title: Never move a free feature behind the paywall
statement: Every paywall regression produced a lasting rating drop; pick the free tier once and hold it. Report 8: a competitor adding a paywall sent its users to a free rival, and free users explicitly warn against gating what is free. Report 10: soundscapes, longer timers, the event micropet and the anxiety breathing exercise all moved from free to paid; paywall-creep is the largest monetization theme (715). Report 11: an app whose third-largest praise theme was 'it's free' ('all functions are free', Dec 2025) retrofitted a paywall by Apr 2026 with no disclosure; five years without a sub-4★ review ended in three 1–2★ reviews in nine days. Report 18: five years of moving existing capability behind Pro — highlighter (May 2023), to-do list (Nov 2023), trackers and statistics (2024–25), free routines 15→8 and short memos →5/week (Dec 2023–Jan 2024), earned friend-invite routines revoked — each produced a rating trough, and dozens of reviewers in three languages stated the rule themselves: 'take back what you gave and people resent it… it may work short-term but long-term I doubt it.' Report 27 (an entirely free app): 'free with no in-app purchases' is the largest theme (47, 34.06%, mean 4.89) and the stated reason users arrived — 13 fled competitors' paywalls, 4 plead 'keep it free', 3 praise unlimited habits, and one is watching ('No ads (yet, but I don't think there are any)'); the report ranks a retroactive gate on existing functionality as the highest-risk action available, and says any future paid capability must attach only to something that does not exist today. Report 29 (free limiting case, second corpus): 'it is actually free' is 46.99% of reviews (mean 4.83 vs 4.31), consistent at 42–69% across every top-five market and every income band; 'no subscription' is the highest-rated sub-theme in the report (44, mean 4.98); four 5★ reviewers publicly condition their loyalty on staying free ('as long as this continues I'm gonna use this app every day'; 'never change'); the report ranks never capping habit count and never adding a subscription among what not to change. Report 31: over ten years one listing moved a £2.99 one-time Pro (2016) → $19.99/yr (31 Aug 2020) → $39.99/yr → bundle-only $59.99–$99.99/yr → a $19.99 'lifetime' against $399–CA$499.99 anchors → ~$60/yr annual only; Touch ID was moved behind the paywall in 2019; the effective entry price rose ~15× in recurring terms and mean rating fell 3.94 → 2.75 in the step that coincided with the subscription switch and ownership change (−1.19). Report 33: the gate tightened in steps — one-time Premium replaced by subscription (17 Jan 2019; price objection 9.4% of 2019, subscription objection 29 in 2019; a buyer two days earlier got one year), notes (with 300 days of history), skip, multiple reminders, dark mode and history beyond 30 days moved to Premium (Apr 2019), a 15-per-week check-in cap (Oct 2020), and the free tier cut to 2 habits (2025–26, cap 9.3% of 2026, 'slowly chipping away at the most basic features') — the spikes in 1★ follow each take-back rather than the cap; 18 reviewers defend the cap and 48 call the free tier sufficient. Report 34: in E5 the objection moved from the habit count to everyday features behind the wall — 'other gated feature' rose to 3.2% of E5 while cap complaints fell 9.7% → 7.1%; widgets, notes, colours and backup behind the paywall average 1.55★ (72.7% 1★), worse than the cap itself (2.44). Report 36: the same retraction was run twice — widgets moved behind the paywall ~4 Oct 2023 (three 1★ from us / eg / in inside 36 hours: 'Tap to Unlock … I am deleting the widget and the app'; 2023 H2 mean 3.56) and unlimited free habits capped at 2 (Dec 2025) then 1 (Mar 2026) — CAP 30 (mean 2.30, 26.9% of E5), REGRESS 19 (mean 1.95, zero 5★): 'Never expect rewards for loyalty … 3 years and all my history is on there'; 'Bait and switch'. 2026 mean 3.636 with 27.3% 1–2★ vs 2024 4.312 / 9.9%, while usability complaints were at their lowest; the report's policy: if a tier must change, change it for new users only. Report 41 (counter-case: a gate that never moved): the 3-habit cap has stayed at 3 since 2020 and is still the only negative worse now than at launch (0.0% → 6.4% in 2025 → 4.2%) as category norms, features and price moved around it. Report 42: three long-tenured users describe free features becoming paid on update — 'I've used the app a long time, until today's subscription screen appeared… forcing subscription, disabling buttons… I and those around me will stop using it and stop recommending it' (TR, 1★); 'An app I used to love… but everything has become paid'; 'after the update, only useful in the paid version' — and the paywall complaint rose 7.7% (2020) → 35.4% (2024) → 57.1% (2026). Report 43 (the positive case): the free tier was loosened around 2021–22 and the cap complaint went 14.1% (2021) → 0.0% (2024, 2026) while 'deceptive free' stopped entirely after Oct 2021 — the reference case for what lifting a gate does. Report 46: dark mode was paywalled in 2020 and again in June 2024 ('New update moved dark mode behind a paywall. Immediate deletion'); the report's rule 19 — do not gate further existing capabilities, each episode produced immediate 1–2★. Report 47: the case study — in May 2024 a free, unlimited tracker with banners added a video ad per check-in, put back-dating behind a video and capped new habits; the following eight months (63 reviews) averaged 2.38 with 61.9% at 1–2★ against 14.9–17.8% in every other era, four themes exist only after the update (ad overload 24 at mean 1.46, 改悪 / free became paid 23 at 1.39, backfill gated 9, habit cap 7), 20 reviewers said they were leaving and 11 of the corpus's 23 self-described two-year-plus users wrote in that window ('改悪前は☆4-5くらいの日常使いでしたが、改悪後は☆1です'; '4年くらい使ってましたが、製作者の方が金儲け主義に走り'; 'ERA DE GRAÇA AGORA É PAGO'). Rolling the videos back to banners by December 2024 ended the complaint completely (0 ad complaints in 146 reviews Jan 2025 – Aug 2026; mean back to 4.02). Report 48: the Strides story is the cap variant — a free tier of ~10 trackers (Oct 2015) tightened to 7 (mid-2018) and 3 (2020 on): 'free cap too low' rose 0.00% → 0.32% → 1.59% → 7.00% → 9.87% of E5 and 12.1% of the last 24 months, the only negative theme still growing, while 'free is enough' fell 7.82% → 4.81% — 'as the free tier shrank, satisfaction with it fell and complaints about it rose, roughly in proportion'; 17 reviews record a feature removed from free (mean 2.82). Report 49: no free tier at any point in 29 months — the free product is the questionnaire, the 'analysis' and the paywall; hard paywall is the largest theme (256, 20.78%, mean 1.31) and a 331-review 'never used it' cohort (26.87%, 1.23) reviews only the funnel. Report 50: the free cap was cut 5 → 3 between 26 Jan and 17 May 2026 (nine reviewers state 5 at mean 3.78, five state 3 at 2.20, zero overlap); monetisation friction rose 3.1% → 35.3% of reviews across six half-years and August 2026 (9 reviews, 2.89) is the worst month; a Turkish-storefront reviewer had unlimited habits 'only for the first few days' then was told to 'buy a subscription or keep only three habits' and locked out of her own statistics. Report 52: year statistics moved from free to VIP at year-end December 2025 (PAY_WALL 12 and PAY_REGRESS in one month, 15 reviews since Nov 2025); the monetisation history is 'a sequence of re-scopings of what was already owned' (one-time → tiers → subscription 2020; free themes → paid → free; free year stats → VIP; ad-free for all → ¥8) and each re-scoping produced its own complaint wave; the money-grab theme (183, mean 1.36, 86.3% 1★) is triggered 'almost always [by] a re-scoping or an unexpected charge, rarely the price level itself'. Report 53: once over the 3-habit free limit, editing an existing habit's settings hits the paywall. Report 54: reviewers report the free cap moving 5 (early 2020) → 3 (late 2020) and one existing user's 'three habits got cut down to two' (CN, 2★). Report 55: 'The makers take the free user seriously too' (2018) described the product the July 2020 every-launch pop-up replaced. Report 56: in a fully free app, 9 of 67 name a competitor's paywall as the reason they left it and 35 (52.24%) restate the free promise — 'paywalling existing free capability attacks the documented acquisition path'; the appeal is flat between high-spend and other markets (47.1% vs 43.8%), so it cannot be paywalled in rich storefronts either. Report 57: the free tier was tightened silently and repeatedly — 'At first unlimited habits were free but now only three are for free?'; multiple daily check-ins became Premium ('did daily check-in suddenly become a paid feature? There was no announcement'); a daily-goal interval removed for a years-long user; free data retention cut to 30 days — monetization_model_change_complaint 10 (mean 1.700, the lowest with n ≥ 5), 8× over-indexed in 2★ reviews from the oldest users; monetisation friction rose 5.18% → 10.56% → 23.47% of reviews across eras as the mean fell 4.38 (2022) → 3.30 (2026). Report 58: a fully free, uncapped launch app whose largest theme family is praise for not charging (52 of 91, 57.14%) — the report's reading is that a future habit cap is 'the single worst monetization lever available' because 15 reviewers name a cap or paywall as what they fled. Report 59 (Tappsk): free habits were removed for some users in the 2021-01 cut and the 20-task cap was later lifted again — reviewers name 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 50 as the free cap in different months, and the report could not establish the cap at any date; a moving boundary is itself a grievance (MON_DISCLOSURE 80). Report 65 (Rabit): premium launched in Nov 2020 by taking a capability that already existed (marking the previous day); in 2023 the to-do list and backup moved behind the paywall; PAY_REGRESS 21 (4.22%, mean 1.48): 'Antes o Rabit não tinha anúncios, e dava para colocar vários hábitos… Eu adorava esse app'. Report 69 (TheFor): stats, day history and back-fill reportedly moved behind a subscription in late 2024 — 'You prided yourself on offering a great app with absolutely no payment or prices for subscription for stats … Now you're just like everything else' (a multi-year user, 2★); not corroborated by later reviews, whose free-tier praise rose to 40.0%. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_FREE_CUT 2 ('free version reduced', 2011 and 2016) — rare here; the free tier held at three items for 16 years. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the home-screen widget — praised in 27 reviews at a perfect 5.00★ — was free until ~mid-2025 ('free for widgets and 3 habits without limitations'; 'Widget without premium(powerpack)') and then gated: 'Useless if you dont pay, can[t] even put a single widget!!' (1★); paywall-shape complaints 0 of 110 before, 6 after; §8.8 #3 put the widget back in the free tier or replace it with an equally visible free surface. Report 84 (HabitGrid): the pre-emptive form of the rule — a free app whose terms reserve the right to 'charge for their services at any time'; two reviewers make continued use conditional on it staying free ('I really hope it stays free, otherwise I will have to find a different habit tracker'; 'I hope it won't become a subscription, or at least that there will be an option to buy it once!'); §8.4 'charge for new capability, never for the free core' — do not cap habits, move widgets or statistics behind payment, or add ads; test an optional one-time purchase or tip for unshipped extras (watch, cloud backup, advanced frequency), announced in advance; 'the baseline is zero'.

title: Ratings follow the offer, not the feature set
statement: Trust (pricing, billing, support, delivering what was paid for) moves ratings more than features do. Report 16: the public 4.81 sat 1.21 stars above the written 3.60 — the largest gap in the set — with only 5.6% of raters writing, two-to-one about money. Report 18: the KR listing showed 4.8★ from ~25,000 ratings against a written mean of 3.824 (gap 0.98); praise for the product and condemnation of the paywall were frequently the same reviews, and more than a third of 1★ reviews (122/332) were about money rather than features. Report 20: the trust family (revoked purchase, restore failure, cancel/refund, billing mismatch, false advertising, silent support) was 810 reviews at mean 1.39 against every feature-gap theme combined at 513 reviews at mean 3.57 — trust complaints outnumbered feature complaints 1.58× and carried 2.2 stars less; the five lowest-mean themes were all integrity failures needing no new product surface. Report 23 (a one-time paid app with no offer change in eleven years): the rating decline 4.56 → 4.08 → 3.83 tracks reliability — sync 7.1×, data loss 14×, widget bugs 52× — while price objection stayed flat; when the offer is stable, ratings follow reliability. Report 24: the cleanest statement of the rule in the set — 43,469 reviews where those that mention money average 2.006 and those that do not average 4.356 (a 2.35-star gap); the 1★ and 5★ populations are talking about different things (billing vs product); the annual mean fell 2.09 stars below its 2021 peak while product-praise themes barely moved, and an earlier 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back for four years. Report 25: a bimodal corpus (55% 5★, 23% 1★) where the 1★ band is 56% money and 11% the app not starting, and the 5★ band is converted power users plus prompt-driven one-liners — two populations reviewing two products. Report 26: engineering fixes moved the corpus mean 4.34 → 4.68 while payer satisfaction stayed flat at ~3.5 for five years — the paid experience is set by entitlement and trial mechanics, not by product quality. Report 27 (the free limiting case): with no offer at all, the app has no structural sources of 1★ — every 1★ ever is a reliability failure in one five-week window, and the 4★ band is a fully specified backlog from people who like the app (17 of 18 would plausibly become 5★ on one shipped item); 5★ here means 'I am grateful', not 'I have no needs'. Report 28: the offer here is an ad load — its half-year complaint rate (3.5% → 39.6% → 16.7%) and the corpus mean (4.729 → 3.810 → 4.048) move together; 2021 had zero 1★ and the launch honeymoon never returned. Report 29: the 1★ band changed composition completely — all 11 one-stars in 2024–25 were functional; 3 of 5 in 2026 were the new monetisation prompt; 'the app fixed its way out of one 1★ driver and introduced another'. Report 30: 16 of 19 one-star reviews (84%) are monetisation or billing and only 3 describe a defect — 'the app is rated down for its business model; engineering work will not move this rating, packaging will'; the organic 1★ rate rose 12.5% → 44.4% as complaints migrated from 'it's broken' (crashes gone after Jul 2025) to 'it's not worth paying for'. Report 31: every one of the fifteen worst-rated themes is money-handling, support or the app failing to run — no feature gap appears; the free cap (2.01) is far milder than purchase integrity (1.14–1.39): people tolerate a gate, they do not tolerate paying for a gate that doesn't open; the product concept is not what failed — simplicity, colour, sounds and streaks are quoted in the 1★ band as reasons the app is worth using. Report 33: the eight worst-rated themes are about leaving, being contacted, being billed or being ignored (account deletion 1.23, privacy 1.35, marketing e-mail 1.41, cannot cancel 1.62, support failure 1.70) and none is a missing feature; the free cap (2.31) and price objection (2.64) are milder — people tolerate a gate, not being trapped, spammed or charged for nothing; the praised qualities (simplicity, design, cross-platform, lifetime) are what the 1–2★ reviews say was lost. Report 34: a 4.58★ app whose 1★ band is the paywall almost alone — 28 of 37 1★ (75.7%) are monetisation friction and only 3 are reliability; 'reviewers love what the app is and push back on what it withholds'; era means drifted 4.71 → 4.40 as friction rose 8.4% → 16.4% / 14.3% with no reliability rise. Report 36: E5's rating collapse (3.722, 25.0% 1–2★) coincides with monetisation friction more than doubling (16.9% → 37.0%) while usability complaints halved (12.0% → 6.5%) and design praise fell 32.5% → 13.9% — 'the product did not get worse; the offer did'. Report 41: a 4.591★ corpus where monetisation friction (46, mean 2.80) produces 47.7% of all 1–2★ and every reliability defect together (50, mean 3.46) only 29.5%; nine of ten paywall 2★ reviewers praise the product in the same sentence — 'the rating is set at the paywall, not in the app'. Report 42: a 3.136★ written corpus (store aggregate 4.6) where monetisation friction (87, 42.23%, mean 1.85) produces 73.5% of all 1–2★ and every reliability defect together (31, mean 2.45) only 20.5% — 'fixing every bug in this app would recover roughly a fifth of its bad reviews; fixing the paywall would address three-quarters'; the written mean fell monotonically 3.96 → 2.69 as the paywall tightened and quality fell. Report 43: a ten-year corpus where the two negatives crossed over — monetisation friction 23.1% of 2020 reviews → 0.0% of 2024 and 2026, reliability 0.0% (2016) → 23.9% (2021) → 26.1% (2026); 'the product traded one problem for another; the monetisation fix was real and complete, the engineering debt that replaced it is not being paid down'; the mean moved 4.34 → 3.90 → 3.88 by era. Report 46: a 4.332★ written corpus (4.7 aggregate) where monetisation friction (373, 17.13%, mean 2.80) carries 66.4% of all 1–2★ in every era while praise almost never coexists with a low rating (15 of 250) — 'when this product loses a reviewer, it is not because they disliked the grid; it is because they were stopped by the paywall, disagreed with the price, or lost data'. Report 47: a 3.818★ corpus whose low ratings are a sequence of distinct causes — crashes (2019–21), monetisation (2024), data loss (2026) — not a slow decline; without the eight-month shock window the mean is 3.99 (n = 526); stated churn 27 (mean 1.48), 20 of them May–Dec 2024 — before 2024 churn was a reaction to one defect, in 2024 to the business model. Report 48: 72.38% of 4,402 reviews praise the product (mean 4.84) and 14.04% attack how it is sold (2.53) — those 618 supply 51.0% of all 1–2★; the 4★ band withholds the fifth star mostly over price (8.4%) and the cap (6.2%); five monetisation regimes over 11 years each produced their own complaint family; 'Nothing in this corpus suggests users dislike Strides. A large, repeated minority dislikes the deal.' Report 49: the widest written-vs-store gap in the ledger — 2.77★ from 1,232 writers vs 4.7★ from ~12,000 ratings; monetisation friction (538, 43.67%, 1.49) supplies 74.6% of all 1–2★ while only 35 reviews carry both praise and friction — 'two largely separate populations, one reviewing the funnel and one reviewing the product'; on the 901 reviews from people who used it the mean is 3.34★; the product improved sharply in 2025 yet the 1–2★ share held at ~50% because 'every improvement in this corpus happened behind the paywall'. Report 50: a 4.263★ corpus (69.3% 5★) where monetisation friction (26, 2.42) supplies 48% of the 25 1–2★ while more reviewers praise the pricing than complain (31 at 4.87 vs 26) — 'this product's pricing reputation was, until 2026, a net asset' — and 40 feature-gap reviewers average 4.38 and supply only 2 bad reviews: 'do not treat the feature backlog as a rating-recovery lever'. Report 52: a 4.25★ written corpus (4.78 public, 562,951 ratings) whose reviews turn negative almost entirely over how it makes money — monetisation friction 2,496 (12.10%, 2.98) and ads 885 (2.46) — while aesthetic praise is 3,537 (4.80) and requests come from satisfied users (4,160 at 4.38). Report 53: a 4.6-public app whose written mean fell from 3.90 (2017–19) to 2.55–2.71 (2023–26) as monetisation friction rose 14.8% → 40.1% → 45.0% of reviews; billing & trust failures (133) average 1.81. Report 55: praised for a decade as a simple, flexible tracker while the written mean fell 4.71 (2015–16) → 3.25 (2020) on crash waves, a paid sync that failed, a 2018 subscription switch and a 2020 pop-up — the complaints are not about the core. Report 56: a 4.91★ corpus with zero 1★ and zero 2★ in 199 days is selection bias, not proof of health — defect reporters average 4.50, two 5★ reviews report functional defects, and the users driven away wrote nothing. Report 57: the three lowest-rated families are all monetisation mechanics — churn 1.593, ads 2.234, paid-user trouble 2.528 — while UX praise sits at 4.753; outside Korea people complain about what the app costs, inside Korea about what it broke. Report 58: 97.80% five-star with zero 1★/2★ in 87 days — explained by removing the paywall grievance, an app too young to hit renewal, data loss or a year boundary, and founder-audience selection; 'Do not treat 4.956 as a quality measurement'. Report 64 (Critique AI): 69.93% of 419 reviews are about money (mean 1.81) while the 126 that are not average 4.41; the 1★ band is 66.7% blocked at the paywall and only 5.6% from inside — 'an acquisition problem, not a quality problem'. Report 65 (Rabit): era means 4.49 → 4.19 → 2.98 → 2.98 track monetization changes, not features; GEN_PRAISE (unqualified affection) 16.2% → 16.5% → 8.7% → 1.6%. Report 67 (Habio): era means 3.03 (free) → 1.73 (paywall) → 1.17 (web funnel) → 2.98 (seeded wave; non-seeded 1.11) → 1.59 — the positive share is the number that moves, and it depends almost entirely on the flagged reviews; billing harm stays high-priority under every exclusion. Report 68 (Ultiself): era means 3.34 → 2.42 (launch failure, tier traps) → 2.99 (web billing) → 2.23 (billing collapse) → 4.03 (five-star wave) → 3.34 (named agents) — the dips track billing mechanics and the peak tracks a review campaign. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 36 of 41 (87.80%) praise the product, including 9 of 12 money complainers and 4 of 5 1★; means 4.50 → 4.28 → 3.53 across free → 3-cap → 5-cap eras while praise themes persist unchanged — 'the rating damage in this corpus is not being caused by the product'. Report 76 (Way of Life): mean rose every era 4.51 → 4.70 while 1–2★ also rose 2.2% → 5.2% — the subscription era is carried by veterans (TENURE_LONG 20.6%) and developer praise, with the offer objection (MON_SUBSCRIPTION 4.4% of E6) underneath; 4★ reviews are 'the same praise with one missing thing' (frequency 96, price 100, free limit 81, sync 62 of 1,281). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 5 of 6 one-star reviews are monetization and nothing else; zero 1★ report a crash or data problem; the product thesis drew zero negative reactions while the free/paid boundary drew every one-star — 'the product thesis is validated and the reliability is fine; everything that costs this app ratings happens at the free/paid boundary'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): mean 4.89 → 4.19 → 4.02 across three eras while craft praise held at 58–76% and COMP_BEST is awarded in the final review — the fall is entirely money (widget gated, subscription added, price ×2.3), broken purchases, a review prompt and a post-overhaul regression: 'Only 2 of 11 one-star reviews are about what the app charges; 6 of 11 are a promise not kept'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the extreme case — the offer is the whole story: U:money_harm 115 (65.71%, 1.13★) vs app-quality complaints 46 (26.29%) and only 14 (8.00%) that criticise the app with no money problem; 83 reviews (47.43%) report money harm and never evaluate the product; APP_UNUSED 14 never opened the app they were billed for; ten reported outcomes against 115 reports of money harm. Report 83 (Roubit): E1 4.69★ → E4 3.52★ with praise 88.2% → 53.0% and defects 14.7% → 73.5% — the fall is reliability, not the offer: paywall friction is lower in E4 (6.0%) than E3 (14.8%) and none of PRICE_TOO_HIGH / WANT_ONE_TIME / PAYWALL_LETTERS appears in E4. Report 85 (Habitica): the offer is free and the ratings still fell — E2 3.52★ and E4 3.37★ are reliability and governance eras; 'Great idea, broken app' is the most typical low-star shape (PR_CONCEPT 285 at 3.40★, 82 at 1–2★); the rating recovers to 4.04★ in 2026 as crashes fall to 4 a year while gem-gating and request shares rise. Report 86 (Today): the offer changed twice (cap 1 → 3 → 1; one-time → subscription + $299.99) and reliability collapsed; the era means 4.16 → 3.07 track defects (12.36% → 50.85%), not the offer — 'In 2016 people left over the paywall. From 2018 they leave over reliability. That shift is the whole story of this product compressed into one table.'

title: Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase — and keep it visibly on the shelf if a subscription is ever added beside it
statement: People buy because it is not a subscription; lifetime is the strongest pricing signal. Report 13: 239 reviews across every year 2017–2026, including 5★ ones ('It would be better to charge only once. It would attract more users, trust me'), asked for the one-time purchase back after it was withdrawn. Report 14: a $1.99–$3 one-time unlock produced zero refund, unexpected-charge or restore complaints in 70 reviews — a materially cleaner record than the subscription apps in the set. Report 16: the price fell ~67% ($119.99 → $40/yr) and the objection rate did not move (31% → 30%); 37 reviews asked for a one-time SKU and Streaks was named eight times, every time for its one-time price — 'I will not rent a checklist'. Report 17 (contested): a $64.99 lifetime beside a $19.99 annual — 3.25 years of payback demanded up front from a developer with an abandonment history — drew 'three times the price of a premium word processor'; the lifetime option must be credible, not just present. Report 18: 34 lifetime buyers averaged 4.12★ against 3.53 for all payers; nine reviewers rejected the subscription outright and asked for a one-time purchase; the report's recommendation is to keep the lifetime tier and protect its entitlement absolutely. Report 20: 35 reviews praised a pay-what-you-want one-time model at mean 4.83 ('£4.99 to say thank you, £6.98 for liking the app and £14.99 for loving it'); after the subscription switch 26 reviewers walked to Streaks explicitly because it is a one-time purchase ('even though I like this app better'); stated willingness clustered at $5–15 one-time, and the report's recommendation is a $15–25 lifetime unlock with legacy buyers grandfathered free. Report 23: a paid-up-front one-time tracker where 'no subscription' praise (398, 5.47%, mean 4.43) rose 3.61% → 5.55% → 8.00% across eras as the category subscription-ised — the one competitive position that strengthened; 'worth it' outnumbered 'not worth it' 3.2:1, and an entire cohort arrived after a competitor revoked already-purchased premium features. Report 25: the lifetime option is a stated purchase driver (44 mentions, 3.36%, mean 3.95; 8 name it as the deciding factor — 'you dont have to do subscription stuff thank you'); subscription fatigue is explicit in German ('One-time payment €50 or subscription. No, on principle'), French and US reviews; one Brazilian buyer could not find the lifetime option and thought only monthly existed. Report 26: one-time pricing is a repeatedly praised differentiator in a calm-aesthetic tracker — 57 (mean 4.18) defend the price, most because it is not a subscription, and 11 name it as the purchase trigger; the lifetime option survived the 2022 restructure ($25) but rose to €40 by 2026. Report 27 (the limiting case): a tracker with no price at all — 47 reviews (34.06%) name 'free / no IAP / no subscription' in a register of relief and disbelief ('How is this free?'; 'In a world where literally every service is locked behind a pay wall, this is like a breath of fresh air'); the free position is the acquisition channel, and the only monetisation the corpus endorses is a voluntary tip jar. Report 29: the one explicit payment offer in a free app is 'please add widget support happy to pay for a lifetime subscription' — lifetime, attached to a new capability; the report's proposed test is a one-time Pro unlock for widget + dark mode + flexible frequency that touches nothing existing users have. Report 31: 27 E1 reviewers (mean 4.78) chose Done because it wasn't a subscription ('happily paid the one-time fee because many other programs are switching to a subscription'), 13 later reviews leave for Streaks because it still is one-time, and one-time pricing praise went 2.9% (E1) → 0 in every later era; the report recommends offering a genuine one-time lifetime price alongside monthly and annual and testing all three on conversion and 1★ rate. Report 33: a lifetime option restored in Apr 2019 alongside monthly and annual is the most-cited purchase trigger (112 payers, mean 3.62; 'Habitify allows you to unlock all premium features with a 1 time in-app purchase of $10'; 'you'll pay double in a year for some other similar apps'); E2, when lifetime coexisted with a stable app, is the payer high (mean 3.77) and price praise never fell (1.9% → 3.2%) — rivals that only rent are named as the reason people chose Habitify; the report says keep it and publish what lifetime includes. Report 34: a $5–9 one-off (2018–19) gave the highest payer share of any era (18.9% of E1 reviews vs 3.9–8.4% later); lifetime (~$40) beside ~$20/yr and ~$9/mo is praised by 15 (mean 4.87) — 'I hate subscriptions so I paid for lifetime … as an investment'; 'you only pay once which is refreshing in the current year' — and is a US differentiator (3.02% vs 1.46%). Report 36: subscription-only for 4.7 years — SUB- 35 (6.48%, mean 2.60, ~6% every era) and ONETIME 24 (4.44%, mean 3.42, only one 1★), volunteering £5, $20–30, €5–7.99, ¥50 and ~$100 ('I would be more than happy to pay for it outright, but that is not an option. So, I'm not gonna be paying anything at all'); a ¥398 one-time price appeared in China in Aug 2026. Report 41: Lifetime Premium ($22.99 beside $4.99/mo and $12.99/yr) is the most-cited commercial feature — 81 reviews (9.94%, mean 4.70, 67 at 5★) and the top purchase trigger: 'Thank you very much for providing a single purchase option. It is much appreciated in the sea of subscriptions'; 'the option to pay once makes this a no-brainer'; zero US subscription objections with lifetime mentioned by 14.4% of US reviewers; a lost sale when it was not visible at the moment of friction ('It's been deleted and I've bought an app that just has one payment'). Report 42 (absence): no lifetime tier — seven concurrent subscription SKUs at $4.99–$59.99; the only explicit lifetime request is 'Нет перманентной, только подписка на год'. Report 43: a single one-time unlock ($2.99 → $4.99) with no subscription in 638 reviews over ten years — monetisation praise (89, 13.95%, mean 4.70) outnumbers all monetisation friction (87) and is rated 2.25 stars higher, the only corpus in the series with that shape; the one-time model is the dominant purchase trigger ('If it was going to be a subscription app I was not going to bother'; 'one wanted 13 dollars a year, while another wanted 7 dollars upfront. I only paid a small $4'); a payer volunteered to pay annually to fund maintenance — the report's shape for recurring revenue is an optional supporter tier, not a gate. Report 46: the one-time ask (53, 6.99% of 2018–20 reviews) was answered with a $99.99 lifetime in May 2021 and fell to 0.68%, while 'lifetime price too high' rose from nothing to 27 (2.02% of the second half); reviewers converge on $30–70 ('I have never seen someone charge more than $30 for it… happy to pay $30'; 'Would probably buy it lifetime if it was 30 or less'; 'asking for almost $100 for lifetime is GREEDY'; '69.99 and I probably would have paid'; '¥30 elsewhere, ¥328 here — I don't dare buy it in case it disappears'); 16 bought lifetime (mean 4.56: 'now there is a lifetime option, so I bought it straight away'); non-English storefronts ask to own it outright 2.1× more, China 4.5× — the report's E1 is a $49 / $69 lifetime test. Report 47: one-time purchase wanted 4 (2022–25: 'opção de comprar vitalícia, sem ser por assinatura'; '買い切り版が出たら検討しますが、とりあえず乗り換えます'), ad-removal-for-a-one-time-fee asked 2019–23 ('一度払い切りで広告を消すことができたら嬉しい'), and a 2026 lifetime price called 'so expensive it's funny' against ¥600 → ¥14,800 listing items; the report's E1 is an ad-free lifetime in Japan priced against the annual plan. Report 48: 58 want a one-time purchase (several naming $10–$20), 48 reject subscriptions in principle, and 28 accept the model but call a $79.99–$149.99 lifetime 'disproportionate for a tracker' (mean 2.46; China frames it as a quarter of a second-hand iPhone); 23 payers name a lifetime purchase (mean 4.52); reviewers who leave for Habitify cite 'one time $10 and comparable features'. Report 49: prefers a one-time purchase 23 (1.87%); a 66-day programme sold as a 12-month subscription is itself an objection (15). Report 50: a lifetime tier existed ('Love that there is a lifetime membership so I don't have to pay monthly', Aug 2025) but later reviewers ask for one as if absent — 'I would like purchase a lifetime access subscription for this' (4★, Nov 2025) — withdrawn or undiscoverable; the report's S2: make it discoverable; subscription-model objectors 4 (mean 2.00). Report 52: a lifetime option drives the strongest payer segment (PAY_LIFETIME lift ×7.39, 199 lifetime buyers at 4.36; 'one time purchase instead of a subscription'); lifetime was withdrawn for subscriptions in 2020 and re-offered at ¥88; honoured lifetime memberships produce the highest-mean theme above 100 reviews (DEV_TRUST 213, 4.93 — 'it said: you are a lifetime member. I nearly cried'). Report 53: 'because unlike many apps you don't need a subscription, you just pay once' (de, 19 votes); PAY_ONETIME lift 3.40 among payers and none after Jul 2023 once only an annual plan was offered; report's M2 — offer lifetime again beside the annual plan. Report 54: a one-time lifetime Pro with 14 advocates at mean 4.93 and zero detractors of the model — 'I love the honesty of a pricier lifetime membership versus the subscription model that so many extortionists are using now'; 'subscriptions totally stress me out' (DE); D2: do not move to a subscription. Report 55: 'Premium worth it' was said while premium was one-time (22 of 27 PAY_WORTH predate June 2018) and vanished after; reviewers repeatedly name $5–$10 one-time as what they would pay ('Would I pay a one-time fee of $5, absolutely, but a yearly fee, nope!'); M1: a lifetime option beside the subscription. Report 57: a one-time lifetime Premium (₩9,900 → ₩29,000; ¥1,600 → ¥4,500; $13 → $30–35) was the purchase reason for 8 (4.875, 6 non-Korean, 4 US — 'Better than the apps that charge hundreds of dollars a year'; 'charging monthly for a simple calendar or diary seems abusive'), then a subscription appeared in 2025–26 and a lifetime buyer was asked to subscribe ('DO NOT BUY IT'). Report 59 (Tappsk): the lifetime unlock is the monetization asset of a 15,176-review app — 396 of 1,090 stated purchases name it (36.3% of purchasers, 12.82× lift), MON_ONETIME_PRAISE 93 against MON_SUBSCRIPTION objections 23 ('the reverse of most habit apps'), MON_VALUE 465 at 4.93★ ('спасибо разработчикам за отсутсвие подписки'; '5€ de por vida que es lo que te cobran las demás al mes' — €5 for life, what the others charge per month); Germany praises the one-time option at 2.95×; the seasonal discount is what sells it (MON_DISCOUNT 129 of purchasers, 8.02× — 'дождался скидку и купил премиум навсегда'; an offer popped up 'с хорошей скидкой, не задумываясь взял') and the free cap barely does (13 purchasers cite it); buying to support the developer is a stated trigger (MON_DONATE_WISH 18). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a one-time option was requested in Apr 2025 and a lifetime purchase reported in Jun 2026 — probably added in between; 'if it exists and is still being asked for, that is discoverability, not roadmap' (M4: surface the lifetime SKU more prominently). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'you might as well just sell your app instead of using subscriptions' — PAY_TIERS 21 (5.01%, mean 1.48) ask for tiers, one-off, monthly split or a teen tier; no lifetime SKU is visible. Report 65 (Rabit): a $40 lifetime tier existed by 2024 and was praised ('I love how affordable it is to get Rabit Plus for $40, which last forever!') while 2023 reviewers still asked for a one-time purchase as though it did not — 'Uma pena a versão paga ser assinatura mensal… se fosse compra única com certeza adquiria' — M2: 'Discoverability, not creation'; two lifetime purchases were blocked by missing notifications. Report 67 (Habio): a $49.99 lifetime unlock is listed but no reviewer says they bought it; 'consideren una que sea de un único pago o Lifetime, anima más a los usuarios'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the add-on moved from a one-off ¥960–980 (2017–2021) to monthly (first described 2022-05-15) — 'it seems it used to be a one-off purchase and has changed to monthly, which is a shame'; 'a one-time purchase option would be nice too'; explicit purchases fell from 3.7% to 1.6% of reviews across that change (directional). Report 72 (Habit Hearts): the listing sells Monthly $3.99 and Yearly $14.99 beside Lifetime, but buyers describe and repeat the one-time unlock — 'Not subscription based. But once keep forever.'; 'бонусом подписка за 899₽ навсегда'; 'Pour 9,99€ à vie, franchement j'aime beaucoup' (PAY_ONETIME 7, 4.71) — and nobody describes a renewal or cancellation. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): the paid tier is a single buy-once SKU ($4.99 / ¥780 today; reported ¥600 → ¥800 → ¥1,000) and the 20 self-stated buyers average 4.15 and name the one-time model — PAY_ONETIME_PRAISE 14 (4.71): 'I hate apps that require a subscription… Best 3.99 I've ever spent'; 「Så skönt att det går att köpa appen för en engångssumma!!!」; 1 of 151 objects to the amount against 23 objecting to how it was revealed; no refund, cancellation or regret exists — 'Keep the one-time price; stop hiding it'. Report 76 (Way of Life): a $4.99 one-time unlock sustained a 4.62★ corpus for 13 years — MON_VALUE 342 (4.40%, mean 4.90★): 'it is a one time charge and it unlocks the full capabilities of the app'; 84.2% of 349 self-reported purchasers rate 4–5★; after the 2023 switch reviewers still ask for it: 'happy to pay up to £50 even for lifetime access' (3★), 'I'm not paying a yearly subscription'; §8.6 experiment: a published lifetime price alongside the subscription, measuring purchase mix and 1★ share among new users. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a lifetime SKU is the only monetization attribute anyone in the corpus praises by name ('The one time purchase rather than a subscription model is also a lovely thing', 5★, who intends to buy 'the moment I can afford it'); a 2★ whose entire text is 'there is no possibility to get a lifetime version of subscription'; MON_SUB_FATIGUE 2 at 1.50★ ('This subscription fanaticism is getting out of hand'); §8.1.3 'if a lifetime SKU exists, say so'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): MON_ONETIME_PRAISE 12 (6.98%, 4.67★), 9 in year one — 'the premium subscription is a one time 10 dollar payment is incredible'; 'in comparison to other habit trackers that are subscription based'; 'best of all — it's a one time purchase!!'; 7 of 12 frame it as the reason to choose this app over rivals; the listing then added Plus Monthly $2.99 / Yearly $9.99 beside a $24.99 lifetime and the corpus records the arrival ('Nutteloos zonder subscriptie'; 'after a while it turns out I have to pay a monthly subscription'); §8.6 E5 lifetime-forward paywall: show Lifetime first and measure whether the 'no subscription' audience converts higher. Report 83 (Roubit): WANT_ONE_TIME_PURCHASE 6 (1.20%: 'a subscription feels like slavery', kr; 'どうしても買い切りが欲しい', jp); Korean users anchor a routine-app subscription against a one-time game — 'Animal Crossing is ₩50,000 for life; a routine app is ₩55,000 a year… the first app where I'm upset that I can't bring myself to pay' (5★); §8.5 test a lifetime or long-term plan and a student price against the yearly ₩55,000. (Consolidation after report 83: title widened from 'Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase' to cover what happens to the lifetime SKU once a subscription is introduced; the original evidence stays in the statement.) Report 84 (HabitGrid): the only payment model any reviewer proposes for a free app is a one-time purchase ('or at least that there will be an option to buy it once!'); zero volunteer a subscription; two reject subscription pricing for the category. Report 85 (Habitica): 'I'd gladly pay $10-$15 for the full program but nickel and diming users is off-putting' — a one-off wanted instead of subscription + consumable gems. Report 86 (Today): a one-time ~$4.99 unlock (2016–~2021) was praised as the reason to choose the app — PR_ONETIME 23 (4.61★), U:pro_pricing 124 (6.95%, 4.75★): 'Paying once (4.99) for all these features is the prime reason I use this app as a Habit Tracker compared to others'; 'some apps out there have a yearly subscription circa £30… this one is a steal at £5'; MON_DEFEND 44 argue against other reviewers' price complaints; the model was then replaced (~2022) by $3.99/month, $9.99/year and a $299.99 'All premium features' tier — MON_SUBSCRIPTION 8, all post-2022, none positive.

merged_from.old_title: Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase
merged_from.note: reports 76, 77 and 79 attached the post-subscription shape: a $4.99 unlock sustained a 4.62★ corpus for 13 years and reviewers still ask for lifetime after the 2023 switch (report 76 §8.6 a published lifetime price beside the subscription); a lifetime SKU is the only monetization attribute praised by name and its existence is contradicted across three reviews (report 77 §8.1.3 'if a lifetime SKU exists, say so'); twelve reviewers chose the app because it was not a subscription and §8.6 E5 tests a lifetime-forward paywall (report 79); the original rule covered only the launch offer

title: Price low and fair, anchored against subscription competitors
statement: 'Cheaper than a coffee' framing produces near-perfect ratings; know the price anchors users cite. Report 23: the one-time price rose ~2.5× nominal over eleven years ($3.99 → $9.99) and the objection rate stayed flat (1.75% → 2.41% → 2.21%); objections are feature-per-dollar and paired with the cap or 'Reminders does this free', never the number itself. Report 25: the lifetime price roughly doubled ($24.99 → $49) between early 2024 and mid-2025 and price objection stayed flat (3.8% → 4.9% → 3.8%); 64 reviews (mean 4.31) call the price cheap or fair ('less than 30 euros for life'; 'Premium is 1000% worth it'). Report 26: lifetime moved $5–7 (2021) → $25 (late 2022) → €40 (2026) — roughly 5× — while price objection stayed the smallest of the four monetisation objections (29, 0.76%); the €40 point 'risks spending' goodwill. Report 28: a $6.98 skin, $9.99–$14.99 consumable packs; 'Study bunny costs like $15-20 so the price could go up for this one too… kind of uncool'. Report 31: 119 price-praise reviews (mean 3.82), 63 of them E1 (6.7% of the era): 'I'm only paying to support the developers'; 'a one-time charge is a lot less exploitative, and doesn't come with the same guilt'; 'Best $8.99 spent in a long time!' — price praise fell 6.7% → 0.7–1.7% after the subscription. Report 33: 99 price-praise reviews (mean 4.85, zero 1★) — 'permanent premium is only equal to other apps' annual fee'; 'I would have paid triple'; 'the best £30 I ever spent'. Report 34: price fair / worth it 34 (4.58%, mean 4.91; US 6.79% vs 3.35%) — 'I never buy apps. This is worth it … Take it from a penny pincher'; the price objection (25, mean 3.16) anchors against an indie game ($5–25) and Netflix. Report 36: $14.99/yr was anchored as 'less than a quarter of the price for competitor habit trackers' (4 of 34 payers); the price objection is about ratio to substance ('$15 for permission to buy a $10 skin. Scam!'), and by 2026 prices of $59–70 met 'the demographic which can drop 60$ on a reminder app'. Report 41: positioned as the value option by 6 reviews ('My favourite app was Strides but I refused to pay the almost £80 premium'; 'die schönste und günstigste') against 1 calling it expensive; 'It is worth the absolutely fair (!) price of only 25 euros for the lifetime version'. Report 43: price / value praised by 57 (8.93%, mean 4.89) — 'I've tried 3 other apps that ranged from $25 to $60 per year'; 'Others… will charge double the one time payment for this as a monthly subscription!'; 'accessible to super low income people like myself'; value praise rose 3.98% → 11.04% → 10.39% by era even as the price rose $2.99 → $4.99, because the alternatives moved to subscription. Report 46: a subscription priced against 'simple' invites 'simple things should be cheap' — '$4.99 a month is too much to ask for the ability to electronically check a box'; 'essentially a checkbox $30 (a year)'; benchmarked against Spotify, Lightroom, 200 GB iCloud + Office, 1Password, Notion; price objections 163 (7.48%, mean 2.84) spiking with each rise ($12 → $30/yr in 2020: 'Most of the worth it reviews reflect the original pricing'; $7.49 / $29.99 / $99.99 in 2023) and fading to 4 in 2026; payers justify the price by outcome ('$29/year for what this app is giving me in terms of mental health is an absolute steal'), non-payers by comparison. Report 47: price is rarely the objection but the shape is — 'このシンプルなアプリに月額320円は高い' ('¥320 a month is too much for an app this simple'); a Korean reviewer would pay about ₩9,000 once for stats, sync and iPad (2020); ¥200/month to log past days (Apr 2024) was refused. Report 48: price complaints fell from 21.43% of the 2015 conversion era to 4.69% of 2022–26 — 'pricing anger has migrated from "too expensive" to "I can't try it"'; Canada (9.47%), Australia (9.68%), Germany (10.92%) and China (10.96%) are the price-sensitive storefronts; 73 say it is worth it at 4.97★. Report 49: 'too expensive' (113, 1.65) is flat-to-rising while 'not worth it' (55) collapses 6.8% → 1.4% — 'reviewers increasingly accept that the product delivers, while continuing to object to what it costs'; 39 defend the price at 4.74 ('Yeah, You Have to Pay. Yeah, it's Worth it'); ten live price points from $12.99 to $59.99 under two product names. Report 50: payers judge the price low for the category ('relatively low compared to similar services'; 'Honestly would pay more for this'); price objectors 3 (a French student: '2,99€/month would be fair'); quoted $5 / €5.99 / ≈$2.99 monthly and $14.99–$20 yearly. Report 52: payers find the price fair (PAY_PRICE_OK 256 at 4.86, payer lift ×4.58; 'less than a Starbucks for a good mood every day', 54 votes) about as often as non-payers call it too high (254 at 3.28); outside mainland China price is praised, not resisted (US PAY_PRICE_OK 23 outnumbers every price complaint combined). Report 53: payers who talk about price mostly call it fair (PAY_PRICE_OK 47 at 4.79, payer lift 3.95; 'RAISE YOUR PRICES… I would genuinely pay more'), then the praise vanished (2 reviews from 2023) when an annual $39.99 plan replaced a ~$8–20 one-time unlock. Report 54: price fair 16 (4.69) against too high 16 (2.75), the objections clustered in lower-ARPU storefronts (CN, TW, PH, TR, CO: 9 of 16); US price sentiment net positive 21 to 1. Report 55: a $3.99–$4.99 one-time premium ('I got Premium, was worth $4') became ~$19.99/yr in June 2018 — 'about 400% increase in price'; 40 of 42 price complaints date from the switch. Report 57: price_too_high 20 — 14 non-Korean (8.05%) vs 6 Korean (0.99%); Japan 7 of 26 (26.92%) after ¥1,600 → ¥4,500 ('I was going to buy at around ¥300'); reviewers name ¥2,000 and 'under ₩20,000'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a $10 one-time price was named as the reason to choose the app over subscription rivals; at €23 the same product loses a supporter-motivated buyer ('23 Euro sind doch recht viel für eine einzelne App mit einer Funktion') while ten others still call it fair — the objection is the multiple, not the level. Report 83 (Roubit): PRICE_TOO_HIGH 10 (2.00%), eight in Korea, anchored on the yearly price (₩39,000 in 2023, ₩55,000 from 2024) and against one-time games; PRICE_FAIR 2 ('honestly isn't that bad at 7.99'); 'about $60/yr' while an ad still plays on every task completion (4★).

title: Know which competitors buyers compare against
statement: Buyers shop around before paying; competitor names and price anchors appear in reviews. Report 19: departing payers named Fabulous and Triimo — the latter because 'customer service aren't trying to rob you'; trust is a feature people comparison-shop on. Report 20: 145 reviews (3.58%) named an alternative — Streaks 26 times, and one churning customer wrote the complete gap analysis: 'it adds things to apple health and has custom icons and you can set multiple reminders. apple watch support and an updated ios14 widget.' Report 23: Momentum 14 (4.64, 'switched from'), Strides 13 (both directions — some leave over the cap), Productive 6 ('Streaks is simpler / not a subscription'), Habitify 5 (year calendar view), Habitica 3 (reward economy), Apple Reminders 9 (mean 3.67, 'does this free'); the frame is Reminders below and subscription rivals above. Report 24: competitors are named rarely (102, 0.23%) and almost always as a switching destination in anger — Finch 19 (mean 1.579) for business-model trust ('Finch is much less greedy'), Noom and Duolingo as comparisons of mechanic (click-through lessons; streak freezes), Notion 13, Stoic 11, Way of Life 6, Habitica 4. Report 25: 37 (2.83%, mean 4.16) arrive after abandoning a named competitor — Streaks 6 (outgrew it), Habitify 4 (cluttered, no widget completion), Habitica 3 (became work), Strides 3 (dull colours, weak sound), Done 2 (buggy), HabitKit/Ripples 2 (better heat-map widget), Me+, Tiimo (calendar import) — 'I have tried them all and this is the one'; among gated users the frame is Apple Reminders and paper. Report 26: reviewers compare against 'too busy', 'too technical', 'aggressively productive' trackers and choose calm; Chinese users compare to the discontinued 种子习惯. Report 27: 13 (9.42%, mean 4.85) arrived from other trackers ('I have tried like 20+ apps including notion, atoms'; 'replaced Streaks'; 'I've tried dozens upon dozens of apps and this is literally unmatched'), and 13 name the competitive paywall — a net receiver of category churn whose position is defined by rivals' monetisation, not its own features. Report 28: 13 (1.58%, mean 4.15) arrive from other trackers — 'a more affordable and functional alternative to another well known self care pet' (Finch), 'Not overloaded with features and tabs (like Finch)', 'didn't need a subscription to add more than three habits'; the losing comparison is a full teardown against Finch where multi-device sync wins and no trial plus ad load lose. Report 29: 52 (14.21%, mean 4.83) tried or rejected other trackers — 65% of them name price or habit caps; one 2★ uses 'Check Me' instead because it has a widget and is waiting to switch. Report 30: a user left for a competitor whose widget is free. Report 31: competitor mentions flipped direction after 2020 — E1 arrivals (89, 9.5% of E1) from Productive ('$5/month??? Have they lost their minds???'), Streaks, Habitify, Habit-Bull / Way of Life, Strides; E2–E5 departures to Streaks, Habit, Way of Life, DayStamp, Onrise, Habitify, Grit, Finch, Daylio, Structured. Report 33: 217 competitor mentions (5.51%, mean 4.31, 152 5★) and Habitify is mostly the destination — arrivals from Productive, Way of Life, HabitBull, Strides, Momentum, Done, Notion, Streaks; departures to Streaks (one-time price, iCloud sync, better Health, 'a tenth of the price'), TickTick, Loop (free), Fabulous, Atoms. Report 34: 98 competitor mentions (13.19%, mean 4.85, only one 1★) — arrivals from Streaks, Ladder, HabitKit, ADHD-specific apps and paper; departures only to an app with more free habits or one with iPad and Mac apps; the US names rivals twice as often (19.62% vs 9.62%). Report 36: rivals named — Streaks (one-time £5.99, where payers say they will go), Atoms, Me+, Onrise, Dayrise (cheaper in India), Habitica, Things, Notion, Habit Grid, Apple Reminders; the app wins on feel and loses on price model. Report 41: 160 comparison-victory reviews (19.63%, mean 4.94, zero 1–2★) — arrivals after WabiTime, Focus, Structured, Habitify, Habitica, Done, Strides, Grit, Loop; Streaks named in 21 as the benchmark being displaced ('I loved Streaks, but hated its UI'; 'Streaks has a limit of 12'). Report 43: 50 comparison winners (7.84%, mean 4.88 — 'I have checked 22 habit tracker apps'; 'I tested 5… It won for its simplicity… also the cheapest') and 22 naming alternatives — Streaks, Strides, Apple Reminders ×4, the phone calendar ×2, MyFitnessPal, paper; the only 'I left for' destinations are Apple Reminders and the built-in calendar; no reviewer in 638 leaves for a named paid competitor. Report 46: 198 competitive-displacement reviews (9.09%, mean 4.92) — 'nearly every habit tracker… all the way back to Chains.cc'; 'so much better than Streaks!!!! It's not even close'; 'habitica but without the stupid game mechanics'; named rivals Streaks, Productive, Fabulous, Done, Habitica, HabitShare, Finch, Momentum, Way of Life, mem:o, TickTick, (Not Boring) Habits, Awesome Habits, Habitty, Onrise, 习惯口袋; departures only to spreadsheets, Reminders, cheaper lifetime trackers ('Awesome Habits is $22.99 for a LIFETIME license'; 'Habit Pocket… buyout is only ¥45') or bundles ('Done app gave me SIX different apps… $25 for the year') — no design competitor, only price competitors. Report 47: 'best of the many I tried' 33 (5.60%, mean 4.88), strongest in Korea (13% of KR reviews — '진심 다 써봤는데 이게 제일 좋음'); competitors rarely named — Dots ('そちらの方が操作性が良い', better to operate), RecStyle as the CSV-export model, Duolingo as the widget benchmark; departures to 'その辺のシンプルな野良アプリ' ('any random simple app'). Report 48: 453 'best of many' (10.29%, mean 4.89) and 105 competitor-named (3.16) describe one trade — wins on tracking flexibility, loses on price model; rivals Streaks, Habitify, Productive, Way of Life, Done, HabitBull, Habit, Loop, TickTick; 'reviewers concede Strides is more powerful and leave anyway' — 'no evidence of a capability gap that is losing users… repeated evidence of a packaging gap that is'. Report 49: rivals named — Me+, Finch, Atoms (the model for customisation), Habitica ('a stylized version of Habitica but with cards'), Habit Legends ('no subscriptions… MUCH MUCH more flexible with editing tasks'), Level-Up ('At least it's free'), Opal, Notion templates; the threat named most is ChatGPT — 36 say the plan can be generated free; 'None of those [loop, art, community, removing the daily decision] is reproducible with a prompt. The checklist is.' Report 50: 37 reviews (18.05%, 4.89) rank it first after trying others — the largest theme — 'I reckon I've tried almost every habit tracking app on the App Store, and this is the one I've settled on'; 'trying different habit trackers since 2018 and HelloHabit is the only one that stuck'; the one counter-teardown says 'Reminders, Things, etc, all do a much better job'. Report 54: displacement 35 (9.49%, 4.83) — 'I literally downloaded 30 different habit/productivity/tracker apps… this is the only one that came remotely close' — halved in 2023–26 (11.3% → 5.0%). Report 55: switchers from Strides, Way of Life, Productive, coach.me, Streaks, Todoist, Habit List and paper (USER_SWITCH 194, 4.68) accept its dated looks for its function ('I'll take function over form any day'). Report 56: 15 of 67 (22.39%, all 5★) describe a search that ended here, rising 17.6% → 31.8% — 'i've uninstalled like 5 habit trackers this year lol… the one i actually kept'; the two named criteria are free and widgets ('I have not found others that have both'). Report 57: 69 (8.86%, 4.884) settled here after trying the category ('I'm a habit-tracker nomad, tried over ten and settled here') — collapsing from 10.36% of 2019–21 reviews to 4.23% of 2024–26. Report 58: 35 of 91 (38.46%, all 5★) rank it against rivals they tried ('I have spent the last 3 years trying out all the different habit tracking apps'); the only rival named is Finch ('really great when I was younger, but now it was just overwhelming'); comparative language fell 37.8% → 15.2% between halves as early category shoppers gave way to later arrivals — composition, not erosion. Report 59 (Tappsk): switchers to the app (COMP_SWITCHED_FROM 110, 4.87★) outnumber leavers to another app (CHURN_SWITCHED 43) — they come from Notes and Reminders ('Гораздо удобней стандартных заметок и напоминаний'), paper, Todoist, Trello and Notion (after those services left Russia) and Things ('Desinstalei o Things por causa desse app'); leavers name TickTick and Things, for the missing Mac support and task time; COMP_MENTION 211 (1.39%). Report 60 (Mindway): the competitors reviewers name are not habit apps but Apple Reminders, Notes, Calendar and a paper planner (6, 2.78%) — the free tools already on the phone ([[C277]]). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'From what i have tested this one is the one i liked the most' (won a comparison shop); a 4★ considering alternatives over statistics and within-day counting; no competitor named except the implied 'original' Streaks. Report 64 (Critique AI): ALT_TOOL 13 (3.10%, mean 1.92) — ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini for the AI half; Apple Notes, Google Sheets, Google Calendar for the tracker; Clearspace for focus mode; Duolingo as the freemium model to copy — 'Nobody names a competing self-improvement app'. Report 65 (Rabit): COMP_BEST 31 (6.22%, mean 4.68) tried others first ('Baixei uma dúzia de Habit Trackers e esse, sem dúvidas, é o melhor'; 'He probado varias y siempre regreso a esta') and still 5.5% of the latest era — 'people who still rate it best while telling you it is broken'. Report 69 (TheFor): 'I've tried almost 10 apps'; 'it's better than so many of the other more expensive paid apps'; the only named competitor is Ripples, for charts. Report 71 (MyStreaks): habit tracking is a commodity and reviewers say so — 'there are so many alternatives'; 'if I find a better one I'll definitely switch'; no competitor is named. Report 75 (Habit Streak): competitors named — atoms, Duolingo (as the streak model), 'apps that charge up to $70 a year'; category fatigue in a 1★: 'Deçu comme tout les apps de routines'. Report 76 (Way of Life): COMP_MENTION 113 (1.46%, 4.29★); PR_BETTER_THAN 428 (5.51%) — the grid of three states and good/bad habits is what users say other trackers lack; leavers name data loss, price or the subscription, returners name simplicity. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): COMP_TRIED_MANY 4 and COMP_BEST 3, all 5.00★, all praising the no-streak concept — the comparison set is 'the streak focus that is everywhere else'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): U:competitive_win 27 (15.70%) — 'spent the past 2 hours comparing which habit tracking app I want to invest into'; the only rival named in 172 reviews is 'Blossom' ('For anyone poor, I recommend Blossom', 3★) and 'other alternatives by chinese developers' (1★). Report 83 (Roubit): COMP_NAMED_APP 8 — Todo Mate (cheaper, Apple Watch), me+, Study Bunny, Finch, Duolingo (as nag and as widget model), Animal Crossing (as a price anchor), iPhone's built-in apps ('no better than iPhone's built-in apps', a regretful payer). Report 84 (HabitGrid): HabitKit named as the paid comparison ('a monthly sub for an app like habitkit, which offers no benefit over this app'); a near-identical name that is paid ('HabitGrid - Goal tracker' by another developer) exists on the store; Apple Reminders is the tool replaced. Report 85 (Habitica): 'this is essentially a planner pretending to be a game' (3★); CMP_OTHER_APPS present; compared as a game against 'tripple AAA' titles on price. Report 86 (Today): CMP_NAMED 48 — Way of Life, Momentum, Coach.me, Streaks, Done, Productive, HabitBull, Habity, Strides, Due, Shanbay, Todoist, Notion, and Apple's Reminders/Calendar/Health/Activity as both the thing replaced and the fallback; the corpus's most-voted review (38 up / 82): 'blew Momentum, Strides, and Way of Life out of the water… Momentum is too minimalistic… Strides has a bubbly interface I can't stand'; PR_BEST 204 (11.43%, 4.78★); the UK writes the most detailed comparisons ('over 15 different habit trackers in the last three years').

title: Stay minimal — every addition is opt-in or off by default
statement: Simple/clean is table stakes and the most praised trait; 'no ads' is the best-rated topic; every feature request comes with 'don't make it complicated'. Report 20: minimalism was the most-praised attribute by a wide margin (1,111 reviews, 27.45%; 42.8% of the pre-conversion era, mean 4.25), framed against 5–20 cluttered or gamified competitors; 'no ads' ran at mean 4.86; 131 one-star reviews still praised the simplicity in the same breath as condemning the company. Report 23: simplicity is the moat — 1,780 reviews (24.48%, mean 4.58) praise it, and it measurably degrades as features are added: simplicity praise fell 32.30% → 20.80% → 18.36% of each era while UI-confusion complaints rose 0.69% → 4.93% → 5.33%; reviewers date the loss to the July 2017 expansion ('like they dipped a pickle in chocolate'). Every addition to a minimal product must be opt-in or off by default. Report 25 (both sides): 126 praise simplicity and 27 call it confusing; 65 praise configurability and others say 'so many options and no guidance that you get lost in configuration' — complexity is both the top praise and a top complaint; any simplification must be opt-in. Report 26: an aesthetics-and-calm product whose four largest themes are design (27.83%, mean 4.64), music/ambience (14.57%), simplicity (10.71%) and the garden metaphor (5.97%), stable across five years — 'A lot of apps in this area are too busy… This app is like a warm hug'; ADHD users say every other routine app 'has been deleted within a day because it's too complicated'; keep new configuration behind an advanced toggle. Report 27: simplicity is the largest theme (52, 37.68%, mean 4.90; 'cuts straight to the point, no fluff'; 'No other shinannigans'), 12 praise the absence of ads (8.70%), and the report's 'what not to do' list is: no gamification, no ads (even one interstitial), no required account, no feature removals without an opt-out, no over-building — 'does everything you need it to do with very little drama' is the product spec; one thing to watch: as refugees from feature-rich paid apps arrive, 'pleasantly minimal' starts shading into 'missing things'. Report 28 (the other side): a gamified pet-and-rooms tracker whose ad load — not its game — is 52% of the worst outcome the store measures; 'do not simplify away the gamification' is the report's first 'what not to change'. Report 29: simplicity (119, 32.51%) is framed as the absence of quizzes, upsells and bloat ('doesn't bombard you with stupid questions and a billion pop ups') and outnumbers 'too basic' 40:1 — 'the clearest do-not-fix signal'; simplicity and zero cost are the same story: 'this app is not trying to extract something from me'. Report 30: minimalism is the only attribute volunteered unprompted (23, 13.86%, mean 5.00; organic 14 — 'minimalist, no unnecessary junk'; 'Good app, minimalistic, effective'), and 'too basic' comes only from people objecting to price — add habit slots, not surface area. Report 31: simple, uncluttered, fast to log is the top praise in every era (458 rated 4–5★; 36.7% of 5★; 'The user discovers value rather than have thousands of distractions flung at him'), and also the top argument against the subscription ('a simple app shouldn't cost…', 104 simplicity mentions are 1★). Report 33: simplicity praise fell 15.9% (E1) → 6.0–7.3% as goals, timer, Health, mood, challenges, friends and AI accumulated, while 'confusing / hard to use' tripled to 5.8% of E5 ('None of the over-designed … gamification' was once the praise); the report recommends 'simple mode' defaults that hide friends, challenges and journal until enabled. Report 34: simplicity praised by 275 (37.01%, zero 1★) — 'no busy visuals, no hokey games'; 'Forget cutesy interfaces, overuse of emojis'; 'too many bells and whistles and I get decision fatigue' — named as the reason people left rivals. Report 36: simplicity 80 (14.81%, zero 1★) — 'Other habit trackers have too much other gunk like blogs or media'; a style-rejecting minority (6, mean 1.17) finds the 3D and piano soundtrack 'viel zu verspielt'. Report 41: 'add nothing' is stated every year 2021–2026 and more emphatically than any feature request — 'Please don't try to be an all in one app!'; 'No plant that grows along, no timer you never use, just habit tracking'; 'no feeling that managing the habit tracker becomes a habit in itself'. Report 42: simplicity ('nothing extra', 'no fluff', 'not over-engineered') is the one stable praise across seven years and six languages (22, mean 4.68) — the complaints are about access, reliability and two missing primitives, not about the app being too simple. Report 43: simplicity 123 (19.28%, mean 4.86), the top theme every year for ten years and in ten languages — 'you don't have to read a bunch of flowery, condescending you can do it! messages'; 'not all illustrated with pink & blue kittens and ribbons… nor is it incessantly asking me to note my feelings' — with the distinction that daily use is simple while setup is configurable ('after a couple days you will appreciate the robust settings over the bare minimum other apps give'). Report 46: simplicity 425 (19.51%, mean 4.87), the top theme and rising every era (16.40% → 21.59%) — 'I don't want to build a new habit of wasting time while tracking habits'; 'I'm really sick of apps with a million features and AI just to convolute things' (Apr 2026); 'A lot of great apps start this way, then they start adding weird features that nobody wants… pls dont do that' — and the same simplicity is the pricing liability ('Simple and overpriced'); rule 16: do not add complexity to justify the price. Report 47: simplicity 126 (21.39%, mean 4.61), the largest theme in every era including the shock; a 5★ who wanted weekly habits concluded '多機能を追加すると、今のシンプルさは壊れてしまう' ('adding features would break the simplicity'); '機能をつけまくった結果UXがボロボロです' ('they bolted on so many features that the UX is in tatters', 1★ 2024, quit) — the report's rule: do not enlarge the feature surface. Report 48: simplicity 817 (18.56%, 4.84) at 16–22% in every era for eleven years, coexisting with four tracker types — 'the most robust habit tracker without being bloated'; reviewers mean both fast to log and uncluttered to look at. Report 50: simplicity (20, 4.90) and flexibility (14, 5.00) praised simultaneously — 'the moat is that the app is both deep and uncluttered. Every roadmap decision should be tested against whether it preserves that'; 'Nothing comes close to the ease in navigation, creativity, options, and customizability'. Report 52: 'product manager, please don't add features blindly — restraint, restraint' (Aug 2026); to-dos, focus timer and AI titles are accepted but ranked below check-in speed; a crowded home screen (DES_DENSE 427, 1.4–3.9% every year) is the persistent fear. Report 53: simplicity is the largest substantive theme (DES_CLEAN 181, 10.38%, 4.66 — 'FINALLY a habit app thats not overpriced or over complicated!', 24 votes); a 21-vote cn reviewer asks the developer not to add a calendar. Report 54: simplicity 60 (16.26%, 4.50) is 'the constraint on every feature request' — 'Other apps feel overwhelming… cluttered with lists, graphs, and other features that can be anxiety producing' — anything shipped must not be visible to the 60. Report 55: DES_CLEAN 475 (23.47%, 4.89) is the largest theme in every era and every eligible storefront. Report 56: simplicity 39 of 67 (58.21%, 4.92), never below half in any period — 'knows what it wants to do and does exactly that and nothing more'; 'I lose interest in things if they're too complicated'; every request is a request to add something, so non-daily frequency must be one field defaulting to daily; do not add social, sharing or AI (zero requested). Report 57: UX praise 198 (25.42%, 4.753) in the same words for seven years (깔끔, 심플, 직관적) — 'Please don't add complexity — keep this leanness'; 'Other apps tried to do way too much'; §8.5: read the 267 requests as settings, not surface. Report 58: UX praise 58 of 91 (63.74%) defined by restraint — 'not overcrowded and overwhelming'; 'no visual noise'; 'doesn't have all the complicated tracking mechanics other apps have'; simplicity and aesthetics are separable, so cosmetic depth can ship without structural complexity; categories only as an opt-in invisible until used. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_SIMPLE 1,704 (11.23%) — 'Ничего лишнего. Удобно' (nothing superfluous); 'the unneeded, obstructive options of the rivals are absent'; PR_KEEP_SIMPLE 49 explicitly ask the developer not to change it; the cost is NEG_LIMITED 115 (0.76%, 3.39★) who find it too basic, against NEG_BLOAT 5 — the trade is worth it at 15,176 reviews. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 11 of 45 (24.44%, mean 4.45) praise simplicity in six languages ('Sade ve kullanışlı'; 'Solo check y a seguir. Como debe ser'), including the user uninstalling over the cap ('Really clean, minimal UI… no-nonsense layout') — the moat is not in dispute even among 1★ reviewers; nothing asks for a busier main screen, the 4★ band asks for depth without complexity ('It's minimalistic I get it, but…'); design implication: every roadmap item additive-on-demand, not surfaced by default. Report 69 (TheFor): design praise 39 (48.75%, mean 4.74), 25 of them for what the app lacks — 'No bloatware, no hassle'; 'No extra junk!'; 'ничего лишнего, только то, что нужно' — 'This is a defended position, not a compliment'; P1: every new capability behind a setting or inside an existing screen — 'nothing on this list should add a tab'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 'The product works by subtraction: one small goal, one tap, thirty days' — PR_SIMPLE 448 (19.56%) in every era; 'At first I thought it was hard to use, with too many restrictions, but I realised they are firmly based on the maker's philosophy of how to keep going'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 「シンプルで使いやすい」 as a review title five times; UX_SIMPLE 36 with no 1★; competitive wins are all against apps described as 'overly complicated'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): simplicity 11 (26.83%, 4.64) stated comparatively — 'What sets apart this habit tracker app from the rest is its simplicity'; 'simple y sin ruido'; 'J'ai testé plein d'apps… (atoms, etc…) et celle ci remplit mieux mes attentes que toutes les autres'; fit 9 (21.95%, 4.89: 'So eine App hat gefehlt!'); a social request is 'lowest confidence… it cuts against the simplicity that 11 reviewers praise'. Report 76 (Way of Life, 7,764 reviews / 16 years): simplicity is the product — U_SIMPLICITY 1682 (21.66%), PR_SIMPLE 17.0–22.5% in every era; PR_KEEP_SIMPLE 64 ('Please do not change a single thing'), 61 of them in E5–E6 where TENURE_LONG is 20.6% of reviews — the request to freeze the product grows with tenure; Germany asks it 4.62× the global rate; 'Product Managers should study this app'; boomerang users come back to it after heavier apps (CHURN_RETURN 60 > U_CHURN 55); the cost is NEG_SIMPLE 43 (2.98★) who leave for a tally sheet. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_SIMPLICITY 14 (19.72%, 4.57★) and UX_TOO_MINIMAL 4 (5.63%, 2.25★: 'Maybe too simple'; 'This app lacks the punch'; 'beyond minimal, it feels bare') — 'minimalism is simultaneously the third-largest praise and the joint-largest non-monetary complaint'; two of the four also praise the design in the same review; the emptiness complaint never resolved across 603 days. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_SIMPLICITY 60 (34.88%, mean 4.98★ — the highest of any theme over 20) described by what is NOT there ('no frills, no 20 taps to log something'; 'No bloat. Just one page for all essentials'; 'no extra gamification, no ads, no BS'; 'Die App erfüllt genau ihren Zweck und nicht mehr'); U:anti_bloat 66 (38.37%, 4.98★); §8.5 do not add gamification, streak pressure, social feeds or AI — 'the product's position IS restraint'; do not rewrite the UI (68.02% craft praise). Report 82 (Lasting Change): the counter-case of a data-hungry tracker — daily long-form self-assessment ('a full blown psych ward evaluation every single day') drives APP_COMPLEX 10 and OUT_ABANDONED 5 within days; the two threads in the only pure product feedback both argue for fewer inputs. Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'simple' and 'complete' are praised together, not traded off — U:simplicity 40 (46.51%): 'Everything you need, and nothing more… no fancy or overly complicated features'; 'A laconic, simple tracker, and yet it has everything you need'; 'more simplistic, but it still has needed features, like reminders'; two US reviewers name feature bloat elsewhere as why they chose it ('too many features for my liking'); §8.8 do not add features for their own sake; the grid is named less often than simplicity (16 vs 40). Report 86 (Today): simplicity is defined negatively — 'No frills, no fuss—no need to sit through way-too-long animations and stories and celebrations every time you do something' (4★); 'a check-in app doesn't need lots of frills; this is just right' (cn); 'It doesn't give you confetti or a cookie but it helps form that path in your brain'; 'Perfect app. Don't ruin it with clutter!'; PR_SIMPLE 361 (20.22%, 4.68★); in China simplicity is valued above beauty (25.21% vs 21.25%, 简约不简单).

merged_from.note: ad-free half split to C246; C006 keeps simplicity / minimalism (report 23: simplicity praise fell 32.30% → 18.36% as features were added; report 30: minimalism is the only attribute volunteered unprompted, and 'too basic' comes only from people objecting to price)

title: Generous fixed habit cap (or unlimited) — never change it
statement: A low or drifting free cap is the #1 monetization complaint; 'unlimited' also sells, so the level is a decision but the stability is not. Report 6: raising a 1-streak cap to 2 did not reduce complaints — the ask was unlimited — though the tone moved from 'scam' to 'love it, want more'. Report 7: a 4-habit cap held unchanged for 3½ years was still the top 2★ theme (0 of 27 complainers paid) while 11 users said 4 was plenty — stable is not enough if the level binds the 5–8-habit user. Report 11: 'First app that has more than 3 habits' was a reviewer's entire body — no cap was the acquisition wedge against the category, and whether it survived the paywall retrofit is unknown. Report 13: the free cap was cut from 5 to 3 in 2018 (the worst year, mean 2.85) and restored in 2020 without recovering the rating; 'hitting the cap while already engaged' is the one purchase trigger buyers name. Report 14: a 3-habit free cap drew its only 1★ free-tier complaint; the report's reading is that the cap must be generous enough to create the streak that creates the desire to pay. Report 16: a free tier of ONE habit drew 76 complaints at mean 2.22 ('a habit tracker that tracks one habit is not a habit tracker') and could not do trial work; 20 reviewers defended the earn-a-slot constraint at 3–6 habits (mean 4.60) — loved at 3–6, hated at 1. Report 20: 'unlimited habits, free' was the highest-mean theme in a 4,048-review corpus (54 explicit, mean 4.94) and the product's entire market position; capping it at 3 deleted the reason to exist — 63 reviews say exactly this, 99 complain about the cap, and 3 is below the threshold of usefulness (the report's defensible line is 7–10 free with paid depth elsewhere). Report 23 (a paid app, cap as design not paywall): raising the cap 6 → 12 → 24 cut complaints roughly in half each time and bought about three years; the request re-anchors on the new number and never falls below ~6%. Report 24 (counter-evidence): a coaching app's highest-rated property is that it refuses to let users add more habits — 'anyone shipping a habit tracker with unlimited habits is competing against the wrong thing'; the generous-cap rule is about paywalls, not about pacing. Report 25: a 3-habit free cap on a product titled 'Routines & Goals Planner' is the single largest fact in a 1,309-review corpus — 138 complaints (10.54%, mean 2.13) and 298 (22.77%) of all monetisation friction, 56% of every 1★; the cap prevents a purchase decision, not just usage ('how do you expect me to subscribe without trying anything??'), and reviewers name their own acceptable number — median 8–10; 19 defend the cap and 64 call the price fair, so the level is not the problem, the gate placement is. Cap complaints fall (17.4% → 6.7%) only because reviewers increasingly describe the whole app as locked. Report 26: a free cap of 3→5→6 habits plus a garden that stops growing at 17% — monetisation gating is 11.36% of reviews (57.8% of all 1★, 21.2% of substantive reviews) while price objection is only 0.76%; 57 defend the price and 45 call the free tier generous; the cap is the single most common reason for withholding the fifth star (47 of 535 4★: 'amazing app, but you can only add 5'); ADHD users who praise the simplicity say five slots cannot hold a morning routine. Report 27: unlimited habits on a free app is praised by name ('unlimited habit tracking without ads'; 'has no limitations'; 'i didn't need to pay to use a certain amount of habits') and 13 reviewers arrived after fleeing competitors' caps — a habit cap on the free tier 'directly attacks the stated reason users are here'. Report 28: a habit-count cap of ~8 (17, 2.07%) plus a priority-slot cap of 1 red / 2 orange (15, 1.83%) and paid moods (10); 'Had trouble finding a habit tracker that didn't need a subscription to add more than three habits' and 'free tier usage incredibly wide compared to other trackers' are stated reasons for choosing it; cap complaints fell 8.5% → 3.8% mainly because the ad load crowded them out. Report 29: 12 reviews (mean 4.92) praise the absence of a habit cap by naming competitors' caps — 'they all made me pay for more than 3 habits'; 'lets you have more than 6 habits'; 'up to 15 to 20 habits without getting charged' — the specific mechanism by which a free app wins comparison shoppers; 'do not cap habit count' is 'the single most protected property in the corpus'. Report 30: a 2-habit free cap (raised to 3 by Apr 2026) is the defining problem of a minimalist tracker — 15 reviews (9.04%, mean 2.00), 31.9% of substantive reviews, 8 of 19 one-stars and all three two-stars; 'if the app is about habits, allowing only 2 is too much'; 'it should be at least 5 free habit entry'; 'It would be smarter to create attractive features that persuade the user to pay rather than limiting tracking to a mere two'; the 2 → 3 raise changed nothing (same rate, same ratings) — an increment below the evaluability threshold does not help; the report's fix is at least 5 free and monetising depth instead of count. Report 31: a 3-habit cap (2 in 2016) drew 670 complaints (12.92%, mean 2.01) at 8–18% in every era, 13.5% in E1 and 14.0% in E4 — unchanged — while the price objection moved 4.1% → 13.0% with the subscription; the plurality objection since 2016 is evaluation ('With only 2 items makes it hard to get a feel'; 'I would like to start by tracking 5 habits, not 3'); a minority defend it ('if you've read The One Thing, three is already a lot!'); the report proposes testing 3 vs 5–6 habits vs a 14-day full trial; Spain shows the highest cap rate anywhere (28.6%).
