Report 84 (HabitGrid): the only acquisition channel named in 86 reviews is an LLM — 'GPT suggested I look at this app' (ru 5★) — plus one App Store search; no ad, article or social post is named; the developer runs Discord, Reddit, TikTok, Instagram, X and LinkedIn and none surfaces in a review. Report 85 (Habitica): therapists, a psychotherapist, a life coach and an autism/ADHD support worker recommend it to clients (SEG_PRO 16, 13 in the US); an AI assistant is a new acquisition route ('I asked ChatGPT for ideas on making my life more like a video game—enter Habitica', 5★, 2025).

title: Be visibly responsive; fixes bring reviewers back
statement: Users who see their bug fixed return to raise their rating. Report 18: the developer shipped what users asked for — widget, Watch, dark mode, bundles, timer, routine modes — roughly 18–36 months after the request, often breaking something else in the same release; six reviewers raised their rating after a developer reply, and one returning churned subscriber wrote '神✨'. Report 20: users restored in Feb 2021 came back and raised their ratings (23 five-star reviews carry the revocation theme as amended reviews); a 20 Oct 2020 launch failure fixed next day drew praise for the speed. Report 23: 12 edited reviews, several visible upgrades after a developer fix; sync-migration recoveries within weeks; reviewers upgraded on learning a backup path existed. Report 24: a 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back from 2.884 to 4.206 for four years; refunds that land turn 1★ into 4★ edits. Report 25: a Turkish localisation request made eight times in Jan–Jun 2026 was answered on 27 Jul 2026 ('Türkçe dil desteği sonundaaa! 🌟') — the clearest shipped-fix-visible-in-reviews event in the corpus. Report 26: a visible 2024 engineering turnaround — crashes 3.37% → 0.13%, the 'music can't be turned off' bug 2.88% → 0.00%, mean 4.339 → 4.675 — with the substantive-only mean rising too; a reviewer thanked the team for adding a calendar; Russian localisation criticised in 2023 was praised by 2025. Report 27: requested features ship on a 6–18 month lag — per-weekday flexibility (Jul 2025 → Mar 2026), reordering (Sept 2024 → Aug 2025), goal end date and archiving (Dec 2025 → on the listing by Sep 2026); the crash was fixed within about four months and the mean recovered to 4.829. Report 28: a 1★ upgraded to 5★ after one support e-mail ('The devs pay attention. 5 stars now'); bugs collapsed from 11.3% (2023) to 0.7% (2025) after a genuine stabilisation. Report 29: the calendar bug fell ~8× between 2025H2 and 2026H1 and the mean rose 4.39 → 4.66; habit editing missing in 2024 was added by May 2025 — but 'a fix ships, and the reviews it caused remain on the store page forever'. Report 30 (counter-evidence): the developer's response to the cap complaint — one more free habit — did not change the rate or the ratings. Report 31: the original solo developer shipped a wished-for feature two days later, replied to a crash e-mail and fixed it 'ASAP', restored a purchase 'within minutes' — support praise 18 (mean 4.78), 11 in E1; after the sale, public developer replies began only in 2024 with split outcomes (restored within days vs a promised refund never issued, 'they sneakily changed their developer response') and support-unresponsive stayed at 20.8% in E5. Report 33: fast fixes after a review earn thanks and rating rises ('thank you for responding right after my review'; a 1★ raised to 4★ after a fix); a public roadmap and feature voting; the Jan 2018 purchase wave fixed in two weeks and the Sep 2025 launch crash in 1–3 days; 'An update improved it' 112 (mean 4.78). Report 34: 52 developer-praise reviews (mean 4.96), 31 naming 'Kevin'; replies turned ratings up ('Updated to 4 stars - thank you devs for the response!'); weekly habits and a reviewer's suggestion built on request; an in-app 'in progress' roadmap list ('this informing and communicative attitude was a huge plus'); the share fell 13.2% (E1) → 5.2% (E5). Report 41: eleven requested capabilities shipped inside the corpus with requesters returning to confirm (notes, Watch, % widget — review edited twice, Shortcuts in the same month, CSV export, vacation mode, heat maps, mood, custom day start 'It was not available at that time, but it is now', Czech / Italian / Traditional Chinese); a support reply 'within hours. Twice' closed a lifetime sale. Report 42: reviewers notice fixes — 'Thanks for the update, it helped remove the lag. I'll bring my subscription back'; 'how much the app has improved in that time! Progress details, results info, charts' — vs 'they just reply the same thing to everyone'. Report 43: at least four verified cases of shipping what reviewers asked — Apple Watch (12 requests, none after it shipped), drag-to-reorder (7 asks, shipped Nov 2025), the timer music fix that turned a 2★ into 5★, and a feature 'added a few days later' (Jan 2026); three of the top four feature gaps have since closed. Report 46: each shipped request stops and a praise theme starts — widgets (Sep 2020), Watch (Mar 2021), journal / calendar (Dec 2023), folders (Aug 2025), no-account use (2024), Turkish and Chinese UI; personal support praised by 53 ('reach out to Joan and received a response in less than 30 minutes'; 'Joan helped me add my previous habit data from a different app'), eight ratings raised after contact. Report 47: 12 reviews (mean 4.42), 10 since 2024, acknowledge a fix — photo multi-select within a week of the request ('まさか本当に意見を取り入れてくださるとは'), late-night gap, Sunday week start, hiding non-scheduled days; stagnant-development complaints 3 ('1年以上更新がないのも残念', 2023). Report 48: 103 praise shipped updates and the public feature-voting board (4.80); 55 confirm a specific fix (4.78); Australia has the highest dev-listens rate anywhere (6.45%); several reviewers raise their rating in place after contact. Report 49: an official Discord with an active developer (17, 4.65) and visible responsiveness (19, 4.74) both rise across eras; an Indonesian reviewer abandoned over rigidity, wrote in, returned months later to find customisation built — 'THIS APP HAS BEEN IMPROVED A LOT'; 8 more noticed. Report 50: 'the developer implemented what I asked and more - he pretty much filled all the gaps I identified'; 'crowdsourcing feature ideas from the community(!!!)'; 'reorder habits without scheduling (*this was updated very soon, thank you)'; requests moved from 'does it exist' (widgets, Watch, to-dos) to 'does it go deep enough' within ~18 months. Report 53: VoiceOver unlabeled buttons reported Dec 2021 and a fix confirmed Mar 2022; an icon suggestion implemented within days. Report 54: 'I know from Reddit that you aren't spending much time on this app anymore, but please fix this small necessary thing! I would pay for the premium version again in a heartbeat!' (4★). Report 55: a reviewer raised their rating when version 1.4.11 fixed the crash, after 'nearly nine months of complaints'. Report 56: 'It didn't have options for reminders & shuffling the order of your habits, but it does now! -Even more happy with it' — visible shipping raised a verdict; 13 of 67 thank the developer by name. Report 57: seven of the ten largest early complaints were fixed (streaks, backup, Watch, custom widget restored after complaints, widget tap, keyboard, past-date, accidental purchase) — 'Recent update is a godsend. They fixed an issue with the widgets and this app is back to being one of my top 3 apps'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_DEV 1,244 (8.20%, 4.96★, rising to 10.0% of the latest era) — reviewers thank the developer by name, praise fast Telegram replies ('Поддержка решила вопрос очень быстро'; 'j'ai réussi à joindre le support par Télégram qui a été d'une grande aide'; 'поддержка подарила мне подписку навсегда другой аккаунт'), and a fixed bug earns a 'P.S. Все исправлено, спасибо'; the report says keep the developer's visible presence. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): zero customer-support mentions in 45 reviews — nobody reports contacting the developer, including the three whose app broke after paying; failed purchasers asked for a fix, not a refund. Report 65 (Rabit): a first-run block (12 of 26 reviews in 16–31 Jul 2021, mean 1.42) was fixed within days and reviewers came back — 'CORRIGIRAM O BUG — OBRIGADAAAA! Amei!' (DEV_FIX 3, mean 5.00) — 'the corpus's proof that fast fixes are visibly rewarded'; the Apr–Nov 2022 crash wave (13 of 67, eight payers) was not visibly fixed and one reviewer could not open the app for seven months. Report 67 (Habio): MKT_REVIEW_MISLEAD 74 (3.61%) cite other reviews, mostly as a warning to would-be buyers — 'the first several top-rated reviews were all previous users warning others not to pay'. Report 68 (Ultiself): named agents answering within hours ('Nick responded within hours. He canceled my subscription, issued a refund…') converted complainants — but partly via gifts and review requests (see C054). Report 69 (TheFor): a widget requested by 20% of 2023 reviews shipped by Jan 2024 and requests fell to zero; 'I reported a bug and the developers responded quickly and resolved the bug soon after. A+ response'; 'the developer reacts quickly to feedback' — 'this developer reads reviews and acts on them'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 'It's also the first app I've seen that replies to every review one by one' — U_DEV_BOND 364 (15.90%, 4.92), release notes written as essays read as content (PR_RELNOTES 28); the bond is what purchases run on, and it is fading (PR_DEV 18.5% → 5.2% of eras); unanswered support mail in 5. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the rename followed a one-line 4★ complaint within 3½ months, while five of six feature requests (widget, cadence edit, retired history, Discover integrity, a larger free cap) stayed open across 25 releases. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): support praise 50 (20.00%, 4.96) — 'a rate this analyst has not seen in any other app in this series'; requests ship ('Atienden tus recomendaciones con actualizaciones (en mi caso poder reordenar los hábitos)'; 'a big thank you for adding a feature I requested—I really feel seen and appreciated!'); a 'Notification bug' review arrives as 5★ because 'they were incredibly kind and patient'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'The undeletable tab was the drawback that had me hesitating on buying. I sent a request through feedback… an update made them deletable, so I bought it immediately!' — 'a specific defect, fixed, converts a hesitant user at full price'; one bought purely to thank the developer. Report 75 (Habit Streak): three reviewers addressed the developer directly with no visible reply — a 2★ who calls the app 'perfekt' asks 'klärt mich bitte auf'; 'The 2★ one would very likely convert to a higher rating on a one-sentence answer'. Report 76 (Way of Life): fast fixes turn regression reviewers around — PR_SUPPORT 68 (4.79★) and REV_UPDATED 74 include reviewers who returned to raise their stars ('Has been fixed - good response', 5★); through 2016 'developer emailed me back in less than 5 minutes', 'solved within a day'; gb over-indexes on support praise 2.75×. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_DEV 3 (5.00★: 'Developer is also very responsive and takes feedbacks very positively'; 'dev actually listens to feedback'; 'the dev updates fairly frequently') all inside the first 90 days and none in the 61 reviews since — 'an early-community signal that is cheap to lose and expensive to rebuild'; three requests visibly shipped (Chinese localisation, more gamification, a widget within 33 days of a day-one request). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_DEV 14 (8.14%, 4.93★: 'Der Entwickler antwortet schnell'; 'developer provided very fast support'; 'Appreciate the updates. Keeps improving'); three E1 request codes shipped and two reviewers came back to acknowledge it — the request pipeline visibly works; SUP_NO_RESPONSE 1 from a lifetime buyer whose purchase broke. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the counter-example in the series — where a request or fix is visibly acknowledged, reviewers edit upward elsewhere; here all five edited reviews stayed negative or became more so, and the four reviewers who received a public developer reply all edited their review to be more hostile. Report 83 (Roubit): a developer reply promising a widget-order fix for October 2024; support that worked raised two ratings; but 2026 brought unanswered email, unread KakaoTalk, a promised same-day fix followed by silence and 'it's starting to feel like the app is being neglected' (NEGLECT_PERCEIVED 7). Report 84 (HabitGrid): DEV_RESPONSIVE 4 — 'send him a bug report, expect to hear back in <24 hours'; 'I suggested adding a watch app; I talked to the developer, he replied quickly and said he would try'; no review reports being ignored; the request → release record is visible: frequency requests 5 before 'Smarter habit goals', 0 of 27 after; categories praised 21 days after shipping. Report 85 (Habitica): REV_UPDATED 35 edited after a fix or relapse ('When that issue is fixed, 5 stars'); PR_UPDATE 170; PR_DEV 11 in Russia; the developer-relationship counter-signal is SUP_NOT_LISTENING 4.7% of E4 and the moderator dispute. Report 86 (Today): responsiveness was visibly the conversion engine early — 'They reply very quickly and kindly' (2016); 'not only did I get a reply, the problem was fixed within days' (cn 2017); FIX_CONFIRM 33 (4.76★), 21 of them before 2019; PR_DEV 39 (4.59★), 30 pre-2019 — 'and it stopped': SUP_NORESP 25 (2.20★), 'haven't heard back from anyone in 6 months +' (2023), a three-week wait for a one-line 'import is currently not possible' (jp); RATING_LEVERAGE 16 withhold a star until something ships.

title: Cross-sell an app family on brand trust
statement: Under-used monetization asset. Report 23: Streaks is sold in a bundle with Streaks Workout and HealthFace. Report 24 (counter-evidence): a nine-app family (Clarify, Shape, Elixir, Lumière, Lune, Ambiance, Sphere, Mind, Enchant), each its own download and subscription, is experienced as advertising inside a paid product and as a billing trap; Clarify, the ADHD sister app, is named almost only inside billing complaints (mean 1.637). Cross-sell on brand trust works only while the trust and the billing are clean. Report 28: cross-promotion from the sibling app Study Bunny drove launch (31.8% of 2021 reviews, a beta-forgiving cohort with zero 1★) and still drives a tenth of reviews, but fell to 3.8% by 2026 — the app now acquires on its own store presence, so the rating and the ad policy are commercially decisive; users ask for single sign-on and a shared bunny across the family. Report 31 (counter-evidence): the Growth Bundle cross-sell became the only upgrade path and a post-purchase 'gift' upsell that broke entitlements — 36 bundle complaints (mean 2.03). Report 36: a 5-app 'Not Boring' membership — SUITE+ 34 (mean 4.41; 'I purchased the S2 for the weather app, but Habits is really the star for me'; 4 of 34 payers bought for the suite) vs SUITE- 9 (mean 3.22; 'Theoretically it includes 3 other apps, but this is the only good one … the calculator app … lags'): the weakest app in the bundle drags the perceived value of the price. Report 52: a studio family (布谷布谷, 须臾, 青子记账, 千结) with common cross-purchasers (USER_CROSSAPP 230, 4.57, payer lift ×3.49). Report 53: WaterMinder buyers arrive happy, but 2023–25 reviewers link the developer to the 'Done' app's degraded lifetime upgrades and call the whole portfolio a scam — 'I will be regretfully avoiding this developer because their pricing policies'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 78 reviews (3.41%, 4.90) use or found the developer's other apps — from 2018-06 the sister app 「集中」 ('Focus'); cross-use peaked at 6.7% of 2020–22 reviews; one multi-app user warns 'after a few months, all of them start producing an absurd run of bugs'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'From the makers of Fleur!' — the app family (Fleur, Floret, Nost) appears in 26 reviews (10.40%, 4.88), rising to 14.00% in 2026; 8 came because of a sister app and 3 of 12 payers bought on that trust ('Yo la compré sin apenas usar la versión gratuita… ya que uso desde hace tiempo Floret… y Fleur'); two ask for the next app (a notes app, a book tracker) — 'this audience asks for more products'; the same trust also produced the only refund request. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the counter-case — six sibling apps under one seller share a billing entity, and a charge that shows a sibling's name spends the family's trust: 'Walking Yoga a scam' in a review of a different app.

title: Goodwill conversion — a generous free tier and 'support the devs'
statement: Small, pure-margin, mean 4.69. Report 5: the dominant purchase path was years of free use followed by upgrading to scale it or to say thanks. Report 20: a large share of pre-2021 purchases were donations — 'I'll definitely choose the highest one because this developer deserves the best'; 'I bought the paid function not because I needed it, but as a thank you.' Report 26: 'bought premium right away just to support the developers'; 45 call the free tier generous (mean 4.49). Report 28: 'I've spent money on this app SOLELY to support the developer because I can't thank him enough'; 'the actual habit tracking is FREE' praised by 13. Report 31: 'supporting a small team' was an E1 purchase trigger ('there is a small team behind so I was happy to pay'; 'happy to support the designers'). Report 33: supporting a small team was a purchase trigger ('I can see this team cares'); 48 call the free tier sufficient (mean 4.85); Vietnamese reviewers take pride in a Vietnamese-built app. Report 34: supporting a solo developer is a named purchase motive ('I paid the app to support solo developer'); 13 of 51 payers praise the developer. Report 36: patronage 5 of 34 payers (14.7%) — 'l'idée de payer 15€ par an pour féliciter, soutenir et remercier le travail d'une équipe indépendante'; proof-first 6 of 34 (17.6%) — 'Have been having it for free until today and decided to purchase'. Report 41: 'Just bought the premium to support the developer i don't even need the features tbh'; decisions made in 20 minutes to a few days on a 3-habit free tier. Report 43: 'I purchased the premium version because I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!'; 'you wouldn't do your job for free. Don't expect programmers to work for free either'; 'I wanna donate the developer'. Report 46: 'I paid the subscription fee because it's a great app with a developer who obviously cares' (ADHD); 'I bought it to support the developer' — 13 (mean 4.92), 12 of them before July 2023; three free users state their condition ('If it helps me build three habits, I'll come back and pay!'). Report 47: gratitude that the app is free 25 (4.24%, mean 4.68 — 'この手のアプリはタスク増やすと課金が必要だけど…'); willing to pay 14 (mean 4.57), 9 before 2022, mostly to remove banners — the 'I'd pay to remove ads' user of 2019–23 became either a subscriber or a leaver after 2024 (ad-removal requests 2.6% → 0%). Report 48: 'free is enough' 248 (5.63%, 4.82) — the load-bearing praise of the freemium era; 38 payers describe months or years of free use before paying 'to support the developers'; pay-to-support-dev 7–9 at 5.00 — 'sustained free use first, then payment as endorsement'. Report 50: free tier praised by 12 (4.92) and price-positive 16 (4.81) — 14 five-stars volunteer the fair price unprompted; 'Has everything that u need and even more for free'; the documented purchase path runs through sustained free use first (a month; six months; 'Once [the habits are] internalised I'll be delighted to pay for more options'). Report 52: supporting an indie developer is a named purchase trigger (DEV_TRUST ∩ paid 52 at 4.98; bought 'so the app can keep running'). Report 54: 4 bought to support the developer, all 5★ — 'make a high quality product, offer it for free without junky ads, and without high pressure sales tactics. Let the app speak for itself'. Report 56: a fully free app with no commercial surface — 0 of 67 mention paying — and exactly one unprompted request to donate ('Eager next for notification and donation options'), backed by 13 (19.40%) who thank the developer; the only monetisation path the corpus supports is voluntary (D3). Report 57: 'you made a good app, so I bought Premium'; 'the purchase option is one-time rather than subscription, so I intend to pay soon as a gesture of thanks'. Report 58: willingness to pay is patronage-shaped, not access-shaped — 'I wish and hope and pray it will continue to be free and to those who can, please support the developers! <3' (PH); 'The framing that works is support the creator, not unlock the feature'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_FREE 493 (3.25%, 4.91★ — 'no limit on the to-do list in the free version'), PR_NO_ADS 127, and buying 'чтобы поддержать разработчиков' (to support the developers) / 'чтобы отблагодарить разработчиков' (to thank the developers) as stated purchase triggers; the report says keep a free tier genuinely usable for tasks. Report 65 (Rabit): 'Rabit's free tier was not a cost — it was the acquisition engine and the review engine' (48 reviews at 4.88); 'no ridiculous paywalls. everything you need is free'. Report 67 (Habio): the non-seeded 5★ reviews are mostly free-era — 'Let's you have as many habits you want for free'; 'This app doesn't ask for payments which I really love'. Report 68 (Ultiself): the free tracker is what earns the praise — 'Free Version is Great' and 'Best habit tracker I've come across' (19 votes each, the most-voted reviews); 'I find the basic non-paid version to be plenty' (PR_FREE 26); only 2 of 408 purchasers mention liking the free version as the path to paying. Report 69 (TheFor): purchases are goodwill, not value exchange — the only stated purchase reason is the design ('clean simple UI loved it thats why purchased the pro plan'), intent is price- or support-led ('the price isn't too much even for my country, so I'll get it'; 'I'm sure to support you… worth every Thai bath'), and no review in 80 describes a single Pro feature — 'fragile in a specific way — it depends on the free tier staying good and the developer staying visible'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the only paid item is an optional message pack named 「無駄機能」 ('useless feature') — 44 reviews name it; 54 bought (mean 4.76), support-the-developer lift 15.22×, developer-bond among 35.19% of buyers; 90 more say they will ('after 30 days', 'when I have money'); 'I felt guilty about using it for free'; 'This app doesn't smell of money at all'. Report 76 (Way of Life): PR_FREE 249 (4.72★) 'free version is enough' and the cap converts only after the free tier has delivered value — 'found myself wanting to add more and shelled out the $5'; 'bought the upgrade to have more than three lines to track'; MON_INTENT 93 (4.65★). Report 84 (HabitGrid, 86 reviews, 4.93★, no IAP at all): the free model is the reason 45.35% of reviewers give (U:free_model_any 39: MODEL_FREE 30, NO_ADS 12, NO_PAYWALL 7, VS_PAID 7, UNLIMITED 3), stable at 44–47% in every era through a language-mix change from 23% to 77% non-English — 'the one reason that does not depend on who is writing'; reviewers thank the developer for keeping it free ('the dev has generously made it free'; 'a big thank-you for keeping it free and without ads'); the free model is usually one item in a list of reasons alongside simplicity, the grid, widgets and fast replies. Report 85 (Habitica): the subscription sells as patronage — MON_SUPPORT_DEV 13 of 55 purchasers (23.6%: 'I upgraded just to help support the developers'; 'I don't mind contributing $5 a month to keep the app and website going'), long-term users 21.8% of payers vs 3.86% of all; 'No annoying pop ups (which makes me actually want to spend money to support the devs)'; MON_ALT_SUPPORT 5 want 'a donate button not add ons'. Report 86 (Today): MON_SUPPORT_DEV 8 ('I bought the full version to support an app I use often'); China frames the price as buying the developer a meal ('what's 30 yuan — think of it as buying the developer dinner'); PR_WORTH 73 at 4.84★; 'because they actually listened to there customers I just paid full price for it!'

title: Weight English-speaking rich markets; volume ≠ revenue
statement: Purchase-signal density is 8.5× higher in the US than China; BR/MX/ES/FR volume is localisation-blocked. Report 16 (contested): the price backlash was STRONGER in high-spend markets — a value-comparison effect ('not worth it at any price', measured against Streaks, Notion, Procreate) — while the rest of the world's complaint was language. Report 20: revocation and delivery grievances were concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (us, gb, de, ca, au, fr: revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua; widget 7×) — the damage landed on the revenue-generating cohort; Russia's higher mean reflected when its users arrived and what they bought, not a better product. Report 23 (counter-evidence): in a paid-up-front app the high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are statistically indistinguishable (4.22 vs 4.22) and only marginally better than the rest of the world (4.12) — what varies by country is which complaint dominates, not how much. Report 24 (counter-evidence): the rich English-language storefronts were the worst — US/UK/CA/AU/NZ/IE (62.87% of the corpus) all above the corpus billing rate and all collapsing to 2.1–2.6 in 2024–26, while Latin America and the Gulf held 4.12–4.59; what varies by country is the funnel, not the product. Report 25 (third corpus in a row): high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are indistinguishable (3.74 vs 3.73) and only marginally above the tail (3.62); monetisation friction is identical (22.5% vs 23.0%) — the paywall objection is global, not a low-income-market phenomenon; what differs is the mix (rich markets praise the price and buy lifetime; the rest hit the launch blocker and billing). Report 26 (the reverse pattern): the high-spend markets (us, gb, de, fr, ca, au = 40.84%) rate lowest (4.489 vs 4.626) and complain most about the paywall (15.3% vs 8.7%; cap 6.2% vs 2.2%) — the free-tier design is costing most where the money is; Russia (19.18%, mean 4.697, 85.3% 5★) and Brazil (4.663) are the happiest markets. Report 27: high-spend markets (92, mean 4.641) and the rest (46, 4.652) are indistinguishable; free-praise appears in 12 of 23 storefronts with no income split — the anti-paywall stance is category-wide. Report 28: the high-spend group (us, cn, jp, gb, de, fr, kr, ca, au, tw = 67.1%) rates lower (3.956 vs 4.181) with ad complaints 5.5pp higher and paywall friction 2.5× higher; GB complains about ads more than the US yet rates higher ('I love this, please fix the ads'); the US carries 71% of payers and the most precise criticism. Report 29 (fourth corpus): high-spend markets rate 0.27 lower and report bugs 3.5× more while praising zero cost at the same rate (48.0% vs 44.0%) — the appeal of free is uniform across income bands; India (mean 4.895, zero bug reports) is not comparable as satisfaction because its reviews are shorter and post-fix, but its dark-mode rate is the strongest country-level feature signal. Report 30 (fifth corpus): the high-spend group (US, GB, FR, DE, JP, KR — 58 reviews) is 67% templated and yields 8 substantive reviews at mean 3.50 vs a 4.79 headline; volume and signal are inversely related — the long tail (36 reviews, 69% substantive) carries the real signal: 47.2% monetisation complaints at mean 3.19. Report 31: high-spend storefronts (78.0%) and the rest of world are almost identical on sentiment (2.34 vs 2.42) but high-spend reports the money story (1.9× cap, 1.4× friction, 1.9× support-unresponsive) and the rest of world the crash wave and language (3.3× localisation); the tail of 71 small storefronts rates better (2.58) than the 9 core ones (2.30) — the more reviewers engaged with paying, the worse the rating. Report 33: high-spend storefronts rate lower (3.60 vs 3.93; ≈3.70 without China) and differ in what money buys — 1.6× payers, 3× Premium not granted, 2.3× billing integrity — with price objection identical (5.2%); the 81-storefront tail rates higher and pays less (3.89 vs 3.71). Report 34: the US (265) is the comparison-shopping market — competitors named 2×, payers 9.06% vs 5.65%, price praise 2× — with less wall friction but 9 of the 14 explicit churn reviews; non-US users hit the cap (6.07% vs 3.77%) and the English-only UI more. Report 36: US 252 (4.095) is the outcome market (outcomes 15.08% vs 6.94%) and reports confusion 3.4× more (onboarding 4.76% vs 1.39%); non-US reviews are feature-request-shaped (unmet 25.69% vs 11.90%) and ask for sync 4× more (9.72% vs 2.38%); the monetisation problem is identical across both. Report 41: high-spend markets self-report paying 2.4× more (9.59% vs 4.00%) and hit the cap 2.3× less; subscription objections are 9 of 10 inside high-spend markets; the UK is the best market (zero cap complaints, 12.5% payers), Canada the most price-sensitive yet most-converting (17.6% objections, 13.7% payers). Report 42: a $39.99–$59.99 app almost absent from high-spend markets (63 of 206; Germany, Australia, China zero) and rated worst there once bursts are removed (2.587); its review base moved to Brazil and Russia, and 20 long-tail storefronts show 46.9% cap complaints with one payer — 'an uncontrolled A/B test of paywall-first onboarding with no trial' (mean 2.906). Report 43: a 64% US corpus where the high-spend group (79.15%) is indistinguishable from the rest (4.006 vs 4.045) and every language request comes from outside it; non-US reviewers self-report paying more (10.04% vs 6.11%, weak) and criticise the dated design more (4.37% vs 1.47%). Report 46: the least US-concentrated corpus (33.43%); the payer rate is twice as high in high-spend markets (5.61% vs 2.85%) and highest in the US (6.04%) while the cap objection is identical everywhere; every regional-price complaint is outside the group; Germany loves the product and disputes the model most (price 2.4×, anti-subscription 3.8×), Russia calls the price fair on an apparently lower tier, China wants a buyout and fears the app will vanish (跑路), India negotiates for 4–7 free habits, Turkey is the clearest regional-price market. Report 47: Japan 369 (62.65%, mean 3.54 — where the full arc plays out) and Korea 92 (15.62%, 4.33 — a requesting market: crash 14%, widget and back-dating over-indexed, praise 4.33) are the only eligible storefronts; the high-spend group is 86.93% of the corpus; Korean reviews fell from 32 (2020) to 1 (2025) — the report's E5 is a Korea re-engagement around the widget and back-dating. Report 48: high-spend markets (US, JP, GB, DE, CA, AU, FR, KR, CN; 77.81%) hold 82.6% of identified payers, complain about price and the model more and about the cap less; the UK is the most paid-engaged storefront (6.51% payers vs 3.91%); Japan (18) and Korea (24) are nearly absent — a distribution gap, not a sentiment one; Brazil is the highest-rated and least analytical storefront. Report 49: US 47.00% at 2.97 (behaviour change +4.58pp); UK 2.43 is 'transaction-damaged' (payers 13.92%, misleading checkout +7.48pp); Germany rigidity-focused (cannot edit +9.70pp, no trial +8.08pp); Australia AI-critical (10.34%); the paywall grievance varies only 14.7–19.8% across five markets — universal; the praise is American. Report 50: monetisation friction 9.0% in the US vs 17.0% elsewhere and 10.8% in the (effectively English-language) high-spend group vs 20.5%; every 3-habit-cap report is non-US (TR, AU, MX ×3) — 'US-only dashboards would not have surfaced finding 1 at all'; Japan returned zero written reviews. Report 54: a developed-market proxy group (70.73%, mean 4.103) vs rest of world (3.685): price resistance 2.7% vs 8.3%, restore failures 0.8% vs 4.6%, outcome language 16.9% vs 4.6%. Report 58: all four 'please stay free' pleas and 3 of 4 budget self-identifications are outside high-spend storefronts (PH 3) while free praise is flat — test any monetisation in high-spend storefronts first because they have not publicly asked for the model to be preserved. Report 59 (Tappsk): the English-speaking group (us, gb, ca, au, in: 725 reviews) and Latin America (br + mx: 639) describe outcomes at about twice the global rate (20.3% / 21.3% vs 9.6%) with billing at 1.0% / 0.8% vs 3.7% Russian-speaking; Brazil is the growth market of the late corpus (32.1% of its reviews in the latest era, lowest 1–2★ share above 500 reviews); continental Europe carries the highest price objection (10.6%) and SA + TR 13.6%; no market uniquely asks for a desktop. Report 60 (Mindway): the US (101 of 216) is simultaneously the biggest market, the only paying market in evidence (11 of 13 payers) and the angriest (3.56★; 26 of the 38 1★; 10 of 11 billing failures) — 'Americans complain about value; everyone else complains about access'; a definitional high-spend group (178 reviews) rates 0.62 lower, complains about money half again as often and holds every confirmed payer, while the rest-of-world 4.11 mean is 'users who never got far enough in to be disappointed expensively'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): on 11 high-spend reviews (3.455) vs 26 high-volume (2.846), high-spend reviewers ask for capability (sync, statistics, granularity, legibility) and none objects to the price, while high-volume and long-tail reviewers raise access (the cap, paying at all) — 'consistent with the corpus but not established by it'; India is the most product-engaged storefront (both widget-outcome reviews, the streak-integrity request, the purchase trigger and the brand risk) and the one the report says to research. Report 64 (Critique AI): the visible real user base is overwhelmingly American — all but two price defenders and 9 of 11 focus-mode mentions are US. Report 65 (Rabit): the inversion — the high-spend tier supplies 61 written reviews (12.25%) at 3.33 while the high-volume tier supplies 433 (86.95%) at 3.74; Brazil holds 77.2% of public ratings at rank 3, the US ranks 39th. Report 68 (Ultiself): the US (724, 3.73; 3.39 outside E5; public 4.33) is 24.9% billing complaint against 48.1% in Ukraine and 56.8% in Belarus. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): a single-market app — Japan 2,259 of 2,290 reviews and 53,106 public ratings — with localised Chinese and English listings rated 4.88–4.96 on under 100 ratings each. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): high-spend markets are more critical (cap complaints 12.1% vs 6.4%, mean 4.589 vs 4.642) and hold the developer relationship (support praise 27.0% vs 11.0%); the UK (cap 26.67%, price 20.00%) and Canada (3.64, public 4.32) are the worst cap markets; France (4.94) and Germany (4.93) the happiest. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): Japan is the home market — 68.21% of reviews and a public base 25× the next storefront — and its risk concentration (grievance 31.07% vs 8.33%); the non-Japanese trial grievances show the disclosure problem 'travels across language and storefront'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): money complaints are slightly more common in the high-spend group (31.0%) than the rest (25.0%) and the two most hostile cap complaints are French (France: 4 of 5 1★, the largest public base, the widest gap) — 'price sensitivity is an emerging-markets problem is not supported here'; the one affordability statement is from Somalia via the ST storefront (n=1). Report 76 (Way of Life): the six storefronts with the most public ratings (us, ru, ca, de, gb, jp — an install-base proxy) run 6.1% price objection vs 7.5% global and 16.9% in East Asia; the US (40.12% of reviews) sets the global profile; cn's second-largest volume in 2014–15 vanished after 2018 (≤12 reviews/yr). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the high-spend group (US, CN, GB, DE, KR, FR, CA) supplies 34 of 71 at 4.62★ with 17.6% money-negative vs 4.03★ / 21.6% elsewhere — direction consistent with higher price tolerance in high-spend markets, not separable from noise; Japan, Australia and Taiwan produced no review at all; Germany (home market, 17 reviews, 4.76★) holds all three named-behaviour-change reviews, the only stated subscriber and the only entitlement failure. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): high-spend (fixed list, 82 reviews) 4.62★ vs rest of world 4.58★ — noise; money-negative slightly higher in the high-volume group (India, Spain) on 6–8 reviews; the five price objectors are all European; 'this corpus does not support' the claim that price sensitivity concentrates in low-income markets; the one-star mass sits in the US (6 of 11) and the single-review long tail has zero 1★ at 4.50★ — the opposite of the usual small-corpus pattern. Report 82 (Lasting Change): 90.9% of the corpus originates in 16 high-spend storefronts; the Anglophone UK+AU+CA block is the most negative (1.20★, 94% 1★) and escalates to trading standards, FTC, FCC and BBB; no price differentiation by market — amounts cluster by billing period. Report 83 (Roubit): the defined high-spend list (US-dominated) is more positive and less broken (defects 28.2% vs 38.0%) but excludes Korea and Japan, the two largest storefronts; outside Korea reliability is the bigger issue (cant_use_app 22.8%, 3.904★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the defined high-spend group (25 reviews) mentions the free model and paywall contrast far more than everyone else (64.0% vs 37.7%; 32.0% vs 13.1%) — the 'no cap, no subscription' argument is a high-spend-market argument; the high-volume group is Russia's profile (gratitude, short reviews, frequency requests). Report 85 (Habitica): payment and gem-gating signals concentrate in English-speaking storefronts (paid signal 2.4% US vs 0.8% non-English eligible) while non-English storefronts carry the language complaint (15.7% vs 0.3% US); defect shares 15.4% (kr) to 53.2% (cn); Germany the lowest-rated eligible storefront (3.31★, 1–2★ 34.3%). Report 86 (Today): the high-spend (us, jp, cn, gb, de) and high-volume (us, cn, gb, ca, de) groups differ only in Japan vs Canada and profile almost identically at 3.96★ — 'there is no market where this app is quietly working well'; the US is the most negative eligible market (3.81★) and China the most positive (4.27★); Japan reports the most defects and rates generously; Germany diagnoses performance; Canada objects to a regional price.

title: Free trial before purchase
statement: Weak but present complaint. Report 9: no trial in most storefronts drew 52 explicit requests, several saying they would have bought — and a trial offered in the US but not Saudi Arabia was compared in public. Report 23: a paid-up-front app with no trial — 15 (0.21%, mean 2.40) name the absence, it recurs as a stated regret in refund reviews, and accidental one-tap purchases drive Korea's 6.5% refund rate (7× global); counter-evidence: 'There's no trial because it doesn't need one'. Report 28: five reviewers wanted to pay and were stopped by the absence of a trial — 'I wouldn't have purchased until I was sure I liked the app, and it was impossible to like the app when it was a slew of ads'; 'Unlike Study Bunny, there is no $2.00 30-day trial… that's a full STOP sign'; the dominant purchase trigger is ad removal after sustained free use, which the 'unusable' churners never reach; the sibling app's reported $2 / 30-day trial is the proposed experiment. Report 30: 'I paid the anual subscription… It doesn't have a trial version and it wasn't what I was looking for' (1★); 'before buying something you should be able to try it' (1★); one 3★ could not tell whether the app was paid or free — introduce a trial or a reversible first purchase. Report 31: trial reaction is net-negative (56, mean 2.16) and the positive outcomes are first-year discount trials, not free trials ('an almost-free year is more than enough to know whether the €60 is worth it'). Report 33: for most of the corpus there was no trial ('Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'), and purchase intent 'would buy if…' appears in 44. Report 34: no trial (2022, 2024, 2026) vs a 3-day trial (2025) — 7 complaints (mean 3.00): 'I refuse to pay the min. $9 just to find out if I like it'; a 2018 reviewer proposes '21 days of all bells and whistles … Once you hook them on, charge them'. Report 36: TRIAL 7 (mean 2.43) — 'any sort of trial period — even just an hour — before you blow $15'; 'these issues aren't readily apparent from the free version when you only have two habits to look at'. Report 42: 'no trial' is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (14, 6.80%, mean 1.29); reviewers name the length they wanted (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, a month) and four met the paywall before any use ('Literally two seconds after downloading'); the report distinguishes it from the cap complaint — a trial asks for temporary full product and is strictly cheaper to grant. Report 43 (counter-case): only 4 of 638 asked for a time-limited trial because a full-featured 3-habit free tier served as one ('The free version has all the features but limits the amount of habits… try it out and if it works for you, you can upgrade as I did') — vs 14 in report 42's 3-habit-plus-paid-basics corpus. Report 46: a 7-day trial is the top purchase trigger ('I paid for the full version after the trial because I could see how much it had helped in just a week'; 'Absolutely did not hesitate to purchase after the week trial'; 'used this app for 6 days and fully expected to delete it… I will be subscribing') — yet 32 (mean 1.88) say the 3-habit free tier is too small to evaluate ('I'd have to subscribe before even trying it'; 'try it for 30 days without limitation'). Report 47: 5-day and one-week trials reported; 'trial not disclosed' 2 (both 1★: '試用期間5日、最初から有償アプリと書け、時間を無駄にした'); a six-year user's app crashed the moment the trial payment went through. Report 49 (the natural experiment): 90 asked for a trial; one arrived 24 Jan 2026 card-gated, auto-charging, annual-only, with a forced loop — hard-paywall complaints went 17.24% → 34.96%, 'advertised as free' 2.13% → 6.50%, 11 new 'trial charged immediately' reviews, mean unchanged (2.77 → 2.78) — 'the reputational cost of a paywall plus the reputational cost of a billing surprise'; reviewers propose 'allow the first week to run freely. Get the user on a run, and they'll pay to continue'; the report: no card and a free first week, or no trial and an honest price — 'The half-measure is the worst of the three options.' Report 50: a 7-day trial ('Download, 7day free trial, then u gotta subscribe') with charges landing before it ended and no expiry reminder (see C029, C152). Report 54: no trial — 7 ask for one ('It's kind of expensive to buy the premium to see if I will like it'; 'use the app fully for 2–3 months before spending the twenty'). Report 57: no trial — 'you only get the urge to go paid after actually trying it free'; 'the Premium features don't land for me — a time-limited trial would be fine'. Report 59 (Tappsk): a trial that needs a card is itself a barrier ('полная версия в пробном периоде требует привязки карты', 1★) and the immediate-charge trial is the 1★ engine ([[C109]]). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'at least bring back the free trial' — the one review implying a trial was removed; 10 reviewers found a 3-day trial while 26 say there is none (possibly A/B-varied). Report 76 (Way of Life): three items is too few to evaluate for some (REQ_TRIAL 4, 1.75★); the subscription era added a free trial ('My trial ends Saturday', 2★). Report 76 (Way of Life): the free trial on the subscription (E6) — 'My trial ends Saturday' (2★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): MON_NO_TRIAL 1 (4★: 'there should be somewhat of a free trial because you can't really explore the app'); zero reviewers mention using a trial; §8.6 E3: a 7-day trial arm vs the 1-habit cap arm. Report 86 (Today): the free tier is the trial and MON_TRIAL_REQ 33 (1.85%) — 'a real one' — was the most-requested monetisation change in 2016 and still asked in 2024.

title: Price level — where 'fair' turns into 'too expensive'
statement: Both coexist for one price; split follows market, payment rails and year. Report 20: $39.99/year for a checkbox app was rejected in every market and language for seven years; Spain, which arrived after the conversion and lost nothing, objected to price (16.9%) but not revocation (2.8%) — the grievance follows arrival date, not nationality. Report 23: price objection 123 (1.69%, mean 2.21, 50.4% 1★) with au 5.7%, de 3.8%, ca 3.6% vs us 1.3%; flat across a 2.5× price rise; China's 1★ reviews are almost uniformly '¥25/30 for a reminder'; Germany objected to €3.99 at launch ('99Ct wären OK'). Report 24: price objection 791 (1.82%, mean 2.248) is about magnitude relative to category ($40/quarter, $80–100/month with bundles vs $5–20/yr rivals), opacity and targeting (premium wellness pricing for people with executive dysfunction and low income) — not the existence of a price; a distinct group calls $20/yr worth every penny. Report 25: only ~12 of 55 price objections are about the level ('£25 for a basic box checker'; '$40??? it's a simple app'); ~8 are stated inability to pay (a student, a child); US names the highest figures ($13/mo, $49 lifetime); Argentina (n=40, mean 2.95, friction 40%) is the most hostile storefront. Report 26: price objection 29 (0.76%, mean 2.76) vs 57 defending the price — 2:1 in favour; high-spend markets (de 19.83%, fr 20.37%, au 18.52%, ca 15.60% friction) are where price-defence arguments are also most articulate. Report 28: 16 price objections (1.95%, mean 2.88) at ~$10–15 consumable tiers — 'too expensive for an unproven, ad-saturated experience, sold as an opaque bundle, with no way to try it'; 'not the level of quality that this kind of money gets you with apps like procreate'; students and minors cannot pay ('strict parents and only my mom knows my Apple ID'); the winning position is 'more affordable alternative' to Finch — do not raise the price. Report 30: the price objection (5, mean 1.40) is price ÷ what you get free — 'Es un check list CARÍSIMO'; 'The price is too high for this quality'; 'para ser de pago es demasiado simple' — while three say the price itself is acceptable, two of them rating 1★/2★ for the cap; 'do not cut the price'. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' ('almost the price of Disney+!'; 'In this economy?'; 'How is this app worth $499.99?') — price objection 379 (7.31%, mean 1.79), 4.1% (E1) → 13.0% (E2); Canada has the highest price objection (11.6%); do not conclude 'lower the price' alone — restore a trustworthy low-commitment path and make it work. Report 33: price objection 203 (5.15%, mean 2.64), highest in Germany (14.7%), Turkey (10.5%) and France (10.4%) — '269 roubles … I pay 400 for Netflix'; '43 euro … for an agenda???'; '€40 … vous vivez où, Monaco?'. Report 34: ~$9/mo, ~$20/yr, ~$40 lifetime — price objection 25 (mean 3.16), many 'great app, too expensive' at 4–5★; €9.99/month called 'completely of the charts'. Report 36: ~$15/£15/€18 a year for Habits alone and ~$30 for the suite (2022–25) rising to $59–70 by 2026; price objection 36 (mean 2.31) and 'not worth it' 21 (mean 2.24, zero 5★). Report 41: lifetime moved €22 (2021) → €28 (2023) → €22–25 / $22.99 (2026) and price objections tracked it (4.2% 2022, 4.6% 2025, 0% 2026); reserve prices named €10, <$5, £3.99. Report 42: $39.99–$59.99/yr (US), ¥6,900 (JP, both reviews 1★), R$79.90 per 12 weeks (BR) vs 500₽ (RU, 'that's nothing'); price objection 18 (mean 1.67, never above 3★) — 'you pay that much for barely any technology'; 'the subscription price is unreal for what the app delivers'. Report 43: at $2.99 the price objection (36, 5.64%, mean 2.31) was almost entirely an objection to being stopped, not to money ('you can easily set timers on your phone for free'; 'I'm a college student so I'm ~broke~'), and it vanished with the cap. Report 46: $12/year (2019) → $4.99/mo or $30/yr (Jan 2020) → $7.49 / $29.99 / $99.99 lifetime (2023); pricing-model union 212 (9.73%, mean 2.92); Canada's CAD $39.99 / $129.99 sharpens it ('Are you out of your mind???'). Report 48: one-time requesters name $10–$20; the lifetime at $79.99–$149.99 is rejected by 28 who accept the model; Canada is the most price-sensitive storefront (9.47%) with praise intact — 'Canadians like the app and resent the deal more than anyone else'. Report 52: a nine-year price ladder ¥6 → ¥12/¥18 → ¥88 lifetime → ¥98, with a Nov 2019 tier rise (¥8→¥12, ¥12→¥18) and price rise complaints 42 (3.19). Report 53: one-time $4.99 → $7.99 → $12–13 → $19.99 (2017–22), then annual only $39.99 / over €40 / AU$99.99; price is Germany's top theme (18.00%, 'why €14?'). Report 55: reviewers name $5–$10 one-time or a $2.99 download as acceptable against ~$19.99/yr (text sub-cut). Report 57: lifetime roughly tripled between 2020–22 and 2024 (₩9,900 → ₩29,000; ¥1,600 → ¥4,500; $13 → $30–35) before a shift to subscription. Report 59 (Tappsk): the monthly at ~300 ₽ is called too high — 'Месячную подписку можно было бы сделать хотя бы 150р, а не 300'; 'Люди куда охотнее отдадут 100р в месяц'; 'Рублей 199-299' — while the lifetime at 449–600 ₽ on sale (list 1,490–2,500 ₽) sells; MON_PRICE 252 (1.66%), distinctive in France (2.16×) and Turkey (4.49×). Report 60 (Mindway): price points $7/week, €8/week, $39.99–40/year, '$60 a year', a $0.99 paid trial; 'a bit expensive for something I could do myself' (payer, 3★); the objection is relative to free substitutes, not to a number ([[C277]]). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): three reviewers volunteer that the price is good ('The price is also very affordable considering the features it offers'; 'the subscription prices are very good'; 'reasonably priced' — and still did not buy, over the sync gap) against two one-line objections ('It's paid'; 'Asked for a payment in simple app like this') — §8.5: do not raise prices and do not cut them. Report 64 (Critique AI): PAY_PRICE 105 (25.06%, mean 1.94) against 11 defenders (2.63%, mean 4.55: '$40 bucks a year is a steal. A human trainer could cost as much as $40 a week!'; 'way cheaper than others'); PAY_PRICE jumped 19.2% → 34.0% in the latest quarter while defect themes stayed flat and defenders rose 0.8% → 8.7% — 'Contested pricing became a topic on the listing itself'; a price rise, a trial withdrawal or an audience widening past willingness-to-pay cannot be separated without pricing history. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): '¥980 is far too much. I'd happily pay around ¥300'; 'It's ¥980 a month as of April 2023, which feels a bit expensive'; MON_PRICE_HIGH 20 and MON_NO_PAY 17 (students, minors: 'my family says no in-app purchases'). Report 75 (Habit Streak): price level (4, mean 3.50: 'like 11 Dollars… I would download it then delete it'; 'man muss zu viel bezahlen') vs structure (7, mean 2.29) — structure carries all the hostile language; one defends the price against 'apps that charge up to $70 a year'. Report 76 (Way of Life): the $4.99 objection peaked when the app was young and the free tier had ads (MON_PRICE 6.7% E2, 6.5% E3) and fell to 1.6% in E5 as it matured; prices users volunteer — 12 yuan (cn), 200 roubles (ru), '.99 for an extra goal' (a per-item micro-price), 'up to £50 for lifetime' (gb); the price objection carries mean 3.71★ and is 23.49% of 3★ — 3★ reviews are the longest because they argue price. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): price level is the smallest of eight upgrade barriers — MON_PRICE_LEVEL 2 (2.82%, mean 3.00★: 'just wastage of funds', 1★; 'a little bit pricey, basic function still worth using it', 5★) against 3 who volunteer the price is right ('really affordable compared to others'); the inference (n=3) is that the app converts against a reference price the user has already formed elsewhere, not against zero; one affordability barrier at 5★ ('the moment I can afford it'). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): price level is not the barrier — MON_PRICE_FAIR 10 (5.81%, 5.00★) including four written after the price rose from $10 to €23 ('der Preis für die Vollversion sehr fair'; 'Simple, barata y eficaz'), against U:price_objection 5 (2.91%, 3.20★: '18€ is way too much for a tracker lmao, pc games cost less than this', 1★; 'etwas teuer', 5★); the five objectors are Italian, Slovak, German, German and Czech — high-income European markets; 'A price cut would buy less than four sentences of disclosure'; the load-bearing case: a German 4★ who 'wanted to buy to support the developer' and did not at €23 'for a single app with one function'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): ~$30.99/month or ~$42–56/quarter for a companion app, billed off-store — the amount is objected to by 4 of 175 and called fair by 2; the entire objection is consent and structure. Report 83 (Roubit): monetisation friction is mild (U:paywall_friction 61, 12.20%, 3.85★) and the free tier is praised more than attacked; the objection is format and the yearly anchor, 'not the value of the character or the letters'; WOULD_PAY_INTENT 11 of 246 in Korea vs 1 of 254 elsewhere; one Korean 3★ payer mainly uses Todo Mate, 'cheaper and works with Apple Watch'. Report 85 (Habitica): MON_PRICE_HIGH 8 — '12 month usage cost as much as a tripple AAA vid game title' (2★); 'I'd gladly pay $10-$15 for the full program but nickel and diming users is off-putting' (2★); regional pricing in Russia and 'a bit expensive' in Turkey; MON_PRICE_FAIR 6; 'I'm a subscriber now, it's not expensive'. Report 86 (Today): $4.99 one-time was defended by reviewers against each other (MON_DEFEND 44; 'a steal at £5'; 'just a cup of coffee') and objected to as 'premium' at CA$7; German reviewers accept the pricing below the global rate (7.79% vs 10.98%); the objection that stuck is structure ($299.99 beside $9.99/yr), not level.

title: Paying customers are the highest 1★ risk — every paid feature must work
statement: Paid cohort rates a full point lower; 28% of payers leave 1–2★; confirmed buyers ×6.7 on 1★. Report 10: paid-cohort mean fell 4.40 → 2.96 across 2022–2026 while the corpus mean barely moved; the five highest paid lifts are all billing mechanics, not price. Report 16: 17 confirmed payers rated 1.21 stars below everyone else; five of the seven billing complaints in the corpus came from them. Report 18: 161 confirmed payers rated 0.30 below the corpus with 21.7% at 1★; their rates of entitlement failure (9.94% vs 1.22%), data loss (12.42% vs 6.01%) and billing dispute (14.29% vs 7.03%) were roughly double the global rates, and by the last era 4.36% of all reviews came from someone who had paid and could not use what they bought. Report 19: 64 of 105 reviewers were confirmed payers and 63 of them left 1★; one third said they could not get their money back and just under one third that they could not stop paying. Report 20: 908 reviewers with payment evidence averaged 1.55 against 3.61 for everyone else — 2.06 stars lower; 76.8% of revocation complaints, 62.1% of widget complaints and 65.5% of support complaints came from the ~22% who paid; the damage was also concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua, broken widget 7×). Report 23 (everyone paid): reviewers who discuss the transaction average 3.52 vs 4.27 for the rest — a dissonance signal; 'I bought this for the Watch and it doesn't work' are the highest-value churn events. Report 24: reviewers who discuss the transaction average 2.006 against 4.356 for the rest. Report 25: explicit payers' mean fell 4.23 → 3.16 → 2.68 across eras (n=13/25/19) while the headline fell 0.27; 14% of payers raise a billing dispute, 8.8% lost access to something bought, 8.8% hit a reliability failure; 52 of 302 one-star reviews (17.2%) show paid evidence — failed customers, not non-buyers venting. Report 26: explicit payers (72) rate a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570), flat across five years; their top problems are losing the purchase (16.7%) and paywall friction after paying (23.6%). Report 28: identifiable payers rate 3.75 vs 4.03 and 41.7% of them report a failed purchase; a 5★ payer still getting ads writes 'Maybe it just needs to sync up'. Report 30: of the six reviewers who reached payment, five had a bad outcome and none describes a satisfactory purchase; the corpus cannot see quiet happy payers. Report 31: explicit payers went from the happiest segment (E1 mean 3.76) to the angriest (E4 1.35) while their share of reviews rose six-fold to 25.0%; 17.2% of 1★ reviews are from people who say they paid; within 625 payers: not granted 48.6% (1.21), support unresponsive 34.2%, still upsold 31.5%, lag 13.3% ($79.99, freezes on the third habit); a share bought only to make the pop-up go away. Report 33: 427 explicit payers (10.84%, mean 3.16) are polarised — 212 rate 4–5★, 172 rate 1–2★; their mood tracks integrity events, not price (E2 3.77 with a stable lifetime app; 2018 2.83 with 25 purchases not applied; E3 2.78 after Habitify X); after paying: reliability 42.6%, integrity 26.7%, support failure 11.9%, regressions 11.5%; nearly one 1★ in five is a payer. Report 34: payers are satisfied (51, mean 4.63) and E5 is their weakest era (4.23) because every low-rating E5 payer reports a broken paid thing — widget, reminders, lifetime entitlement — not price. Report 36: payers are the least satisfied identifiable group — 34 payers average 3.794 (23.5% 1–2★) vs corpus 4.039 and free-tier praisers 4.88 — because paying exposes no sync (9 of 34, 26.5%), entitlements that don't travel, billing edge cases and bugs ('please fix the bugs (paying user)'). Report 41: 5 of 29 1★ (17.2%) are payers whose specific purchase rationale failed — backfill, Mac sync, Watch sync without iCloud, Health sync, refund; 10 of 60 payers report a post-purchase failure. Report 42: payers (29) rate 2.72 vs non-payers 3.20, 44.8% of them 1★, none 4★ — 'no such thing as a mildly satisfied paying customer'; 9 of 29 hit a defect after paying (freezing '5 minutes to mark two tasks', a launch crash, disappearing habits, premium stats miscalculating). Report 43: payers (48, 7.52%) rate 3.58 vs 4.05 and are 1.9× as likely to give 1★; 11 of 48 (22.9%) hit a defect after paying and 10 of 76 one-star reviews are payers — every one a delivery failure (re-buy after reinstall, restore failed, 'Had it for two minutes after I paid for it and it's glitching', won't open with data gone despite iCloud, a lifetime payer with no support reply, the 2025 popup regression). Report 46: payers (97) rate 3.95 vs 4.35, 1.7× as likely to leave 1★ and 2.9× 2★; 21 of 97 (21.6%) hit a defect after paying; every payer at 1★ (12) is a delivery or billing failure, none a design objection. Report 47: 13 identifiable payers (2.21%, 12 JP) average 3.23 vs 3.83; nine of thirteen report a billing, entitlement or reliability problem (ads reappearing, charged twice, crash after paying, the month view showing a week, the AI toggle stuck off, the rating prompt shown to payers); 4★ holds most of the payers — 'one fix from five'. Report 48: 172 payers (3.91%) average 3.92 vs 4.24 — 84 (48.8%) also report a problem (billing 12, refund 8, no support reply 8, crash 9, sync 6); 31 one-star reviews are from payers — 'the most expensive failure mode in the corpus'; 'The paid experience fails at exactly the moments it matters.' Report 49: 106 payers average 1.92 — 97 (91.5%) carry a complaint; reliability 41.5% of payer reviews vs 13.4% of non-payers; login failure 11.32% vs 1.30%; 57 payers at 1★ 'the most serious group in this report'. Report 50 (counter-case): payers are happy — 9 direct at 4.11 (7 at 5★), 13 with probable at 4.23 vs 4.27 for non-payers; both unhappy payers were hurt by billing, not the product; a Premium user who lost data still wrote a 2,020-character defence — 'Every monetization change should be evaluated against whether it risks converting this segment into the angry-payer segment that most competitors have.' Report 52: payers are the most satisfied segment (306 value-reporting payers at 4.92) until something breaks — entitlement broke 80 at 2.62, data loss 33 at 1.73, support silence 52 at 1.92, reliability 286 at 3.04. Report 53: payers went from 143 at 3.44 (2017–22) to 54 at 2.15 (2023–26); paid and reliability failure 82 at 2.46, statistics broken 24 at 2.25, entitlement withdrawn 10 at 1.50. Report 54: confirmed payers average 3.091 against 3.981 and are 3.3× more likely to leave one star (27.3% vs 8.4%); 12 of 31 one-stars are payers — 'the one-star population is, disproportionately, the company's customers'; the payer segment holds nearly all of six failure themes (10 of 12 value gap, 6 of 6 never unlocked, 6 of 7 restore, 5 of 5 refunds) — 'Free users complain about the gate; paying users complain about the goods'. Report 55: payers are the unhappiest group — PAY_BOUGHT 165 at 2.56, 96 (58.2%) at 1–2★, paid mean 4.24 → 2.78 → 1.91 → 1.41 across eras; 41.8% of payers report a data & account continuity failure, 25.5% support silence, 21.8% sync failure; the continuity chain — crash or new phone → reinstall → login fails → data and premium gone → e-mail support → no reply → refund request and 1★; 'Two online reviews that premium customers had posted convinced me not to'. Report 57: 31 of 99 payers (31.31%) report a purchase-side failure, rising 12.9% (2019–21) → 27.3% → 45.7% (2024–26); payers are 12.71% of reviews but 20.8% of one-stars; in 2026 8 of 12 payers report a failure — the rising payer share may be measuring anger, not adoption; refunds rare (2 genuine) because unhappy payers write a 1★ and stay broken. Report 59 (Tappsk): 147 of 1,090 purchasers (13.5%) rate 1–2★; among purchasers BUG_PURCHASE lifts 8.43×, MON_PAID_TWICE 8.89×, SUP_NONE 6.09×, BUG_SYNC 5.71×, NEG_DEV_PROMISE 4.43× — the paid segment concentrates every failure class; 'написано, что поддерживается семейный доступ' (it says Family Sharing is supported) is a paid-twice complaint. Report 60 (Mindway): the extreme case — 13 explicit payers (6.02%), mean 1.38, 11 of 13 at 1★, zero at 5★; 'not one paying reviewer describes getting value for the money… the most consequential single number in the report'; every refund request, cancellation failure and unexpected-charge report in the corpus comes from this segment; five of thirteen say the paid product is a list, not a tracker; the responsible reading — the segment is biased toward the aggrieved — still leaves 'the only payer voices the store shows prospective buyers are 1★'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 5 of 6 self-identified payers report a defect or shortfall — two entitlement failures, two hit by the June build, one lifetime buyer disappointed by the widget; only one paid reviewer is unreservedly happy ('Worth every penny'); notably neither failed purchaser asked for a refund — both asked for a fix. Report 64 (Critique AI): 13 self-stated payers average 1.85 (10 at 1★) against 3.87 for users who got in without stating payment — access more than doubles satisfaction and stating that you paid halves it again; 12 of 13 report a defect or shortfall. Report 65 (Rabit): 49 self-stated payers average 2.061 against 3.677 (27 of 49 at 1★, 3× over-represented), and the 1★ band's top theme is PAY_PAID (29.67%) — 'the one-star band is mostly composed of (a) people who could not get into the app at all and (b) people who paid and could not get what they paid for. Neither group is a pricing problem'; payer complaints peak in 2023, the cap year; only 2 say paid was worth it against 16 who say not. Report 67 (Habio): 35 deliberate buyers (mean 1.23) report the same failures as everyone else plus locked premium; praise among money-left reviewers has a 0.06× lift. Report 68 (Ultiself): 331 of 392 deliberate purchasers (84.4%) carry a billing complaint and 26 (6.6%) rate 4–5★; refund requests 221 (4.90%): refused or ignored 120, received 27 (18 in 2026), partial 4 — 69.7% driven by a charge the reviewer did not expect, not dissatisfaction with the app. Report 69 (TheFor): 'the paid path is the only part of this product with a majority-failure account, and it is the part that generates revenue' (3 of 4 stated payers). Report 75 (Habit Streak): zero self-identified purchasers in 41 reviews — 'this corpus cannot see the post-purchase funnel at all'; §8.6 instrument conversion, refunds and churn 'because the next version of this analysis should not have to say no purchase evidence exists'. Report 76 (Way of Life): 1★ (181) is where purchases go wrong — MON_PAID 16.57%, BUG_PURCHASE 11.60%, MON_SUBSCRIPTION 8.29%, MON_REGRET 7.18%, MON_DISCLOSURE 7.73%, SUP_NONE 6.08%; MON_REGRET is the lowest-rated money code (21, mean 1.52★); 40 of 349 purchasers (11.5%) rate 1–2★; on cn 11 reviews in one week of 2015-01 report crashing immediately after buying premium ('the money was taken and it started crashing, endlessly'). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the four stated payers average 3.75★ (0.56 below the corpus) — a lifetime purchaser whose app crashes on every launch and whose Apple Health connection does not work ('maximum spend, zero delivery — the worst outcome in the corpus'), a premium buyer who uninstalled after 20 days over missing feedback loops, and two satisfied 5★; PAID_ENTITLEMENT_FAIL 1 ('Leider werden mir die Optionen nicht angezeigt', a 5★ titled 'Problem Premium'). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the 11 purchase-evidence reviews average 3.55★ vs corpus 4.599 — the only substantial segment below the corpus — produced entirely by four broken transactions: five of nine stated payers 5★, four 1★, none 2–4 ('paying this developer is, on the evidence of this corpus, a binary experience'); satisfied payers praise craft at the corpus rate; titles 'Estafa' and 'No part of the app is free' are what a prospective buyer reads. Report 82 (Lasting Change): U:paid_evidence 125 (71.43%) averages 1.224★ — 116 × 1★, 0 × 4★ — 92.8% of everyone with purchase evidence rated one star; BILL_NO_CONSENT, REFUND_REFUSED, TRUST_ESCALATED and SUP_NO_REPLY occur only in one-star reviews ('a person who is charged without consent and refused a refund gives one star, without exception, in 1080 days across 26 storefronts'); U:trust_collapse 97 (55.43%): TRUST_SCAM_WORD 65 across seven languages, TRUST_WARN_OTHERS 67 — the largest code — written to warn the next buyer. Report 83 (Roubit): PAID_EXPLICIT 27 (5.40%, 3.67★) — 44.4% satisfied, 51.9% report a defect (one who paid for the letters then lost the diary: 'if it seems fixed after a while I'll subscribe again', 2★), 4 regret ('abandoned a year's subscription as clunky'), 3 not unlocked, 4 churned — 'the product broke under paying users'. Report 85 (Habitica): stated purchasers (55) average 3.25★ and 15 of 55 report a purchase that went wrong — paid then the app would not open ('Paid for premium but can barely use it as it constantly crashes', 1★), gems not credited ('I got a month subscription and the gems didn't credit to my account', 1★), could not cancel ('Habitica keeps charging for new subscriptions', 1★), left over the 2023 changes; MON_PAID_UNHAPPY 17. Report 86 (Today): paid reviewers (188, 10.53%) average 3.69★ vs 3.97 and report defects at 34.57% vs 26.27% — they use it longer with more habits, the condition under which it degrades; 12 of 55 data-loss reviewers paid for the backup that lost their data; MON_PAID_EXPLICIT is 16.13% of 1★ — 'paying does not make people kind'; U:purchase_friction 51 (2.61★): restore 18, IAP failure 11, regret 12, refund 7 (two refused by Apple), overcharge 2, features taken back 3.

title: Focus timer
statement: Meaningful in the US, emerging globally. Report 23: timed tasks and a built-in Pomodoro exist; the Pomodoro break cycle was reported broken in 2022 and timers desync between devices. Report 24: a deep-work ramp-up ritual and per-habit timers are named by long-tenure users as the reason they renew. Report 25: a built-in timer that keeps counting past the goal is praised at mean 4.60 (15, 1.15%). Report 28: a timer with auto-mark-complete exists; three want it to run in the background / on the lock screen. Report 36: a timer / pomodoro requested by 4 (mean 2.50), one because a screenshot habit was named 'Run 15 minutes'. Report 41: a per-habit timer with Live Activities praised by 27. Report 43: multi-step timed routines (morning routines, workouts, kids, ADHD) with background-music fade and voice prompts are a core differentiator and the mechanic the ADHD segment names most. Report 47: timers / time tracking requested by a payer for study logging (average and total study time). Report 48: a built-in timer requested by 5–6; time-duration HH:MM units by 8. Report 52: a pomodoro / count-up focus timer linked to habits (FOCUS 390, rising to 5.5% of 2026) — accepted but ranked below check-in speed; the app-block list works backwards; a solid-red focus page redesign (Aug 2026) clashed with the calm style. Report 59 (Tappsk): REQ_TIMER 43 (distinctive in Ukraine, 3.00×). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a Focus tab ships; the only mention is a Korean 3★ asking why it exists. Report 83 (Roubit): 'a pomodoro timer and the ability to set recurring deadlines' requested (5★). Report 86 (Today): REQ_TIMER 18 (1.01%, 2016 → 2020) — a timer / duration tracking, never shipped.

title: Fitness / health tracking use case
statement: Very strong US use case. Report 31: health and medical routines praised by 36 (hip-surgery physio, Ménière's, a 95-day medication streak); life outcomes 113 (34 kg, 15 lb). Report 33: life outcomes 205 (on the way to 100 books; out of depression; quitting smoking; 1,000+ gym days); medical / mental-health use 20 (mean 4.70). Report 47: fitness / diet users 24 (4.07%, mean 4.08) are the largest named audience. Report 48: fitness / weight 95 (2.16%, 4.87) is the largest segment — 80 lbs lost, 31 lbs and 26 inches; behaviour-change claims 267 (4.95) rising to 8.18% of 2022–26. Report 60 (Mindway): 'Makes me hydrated makes me work out in a lot'; 'work out, drink more water, make my bed, do good in school, and tidy up my room' — health routines are the concrete outcomes named. Report 64 (Critique AI): fitness outcomes carry the corpus's highest mean (12, 4.92); requests for a calorie tracker beside the food scanner, Apple Health and Hevy sync, exercise animations and bodyweight / muscle-group tracking; outcomes run 5× higher in volume markets (11.4% vs 2.2%). Report 76 (Way of Life): USE_FITNESS 98 (1.26%), USE_HEALTH 71, USE_DIET 56 — 'go from 210 pounds to 164 pounds'; OUT_HEALTH 16 at 5.00★. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): OUT_USE_CASE 13 — study hours, gym, medication, workouts, strength training, coding lessons, driving-theory mock tests; a general-purpose 'board' fits any of them.

title: Parents tracking kids
statement: Distinct use case; ties to profiles. Report 23: tracking a child's chores alongside your own is one reason for more capacity (3 reviews). Report 26: one reviewer bought it for an elderly parent and one for their children; ages 10–21 self-identify. Report 31: family/child use praised by a handful — a parent tracking attention to each child; a 5-year-old's morning list. Report 83 (Roubit): 13 reviews from students or children on a 4+ app with a 14+ sign-up gate — '앱이4세 이상인데 14세이상 가입이니 조금 당황스러워요' (5★); §8.3 asks whether minors reach the AI letter despite the gate. Report 85 (Habitica): USE_FAMILY 58 — a chore system for children ('I went from nagging my 11 year old son to do tasks. Now he is asking for more'); gift subscriptions for friends and family (3); a paid group plan for shared task lists is 'not usable in the iOS app' per one reviewer.

title: Check-off sound and haptic
statement: Named as a reason to keep coming back. Report 16: the press-and-hold fill with a haptic reward was the product's most-praised craft ('Pavlovian in a good way'; 'I'm beginning to crave that feeling') — praise fell three-quarters after a redesign replaced the circles with a list. Report 31: musical completion sounds and haptics are free and part of the category-winning basics (82 mentions, mean 3.62); 7 find sounds interrupt audio. Report 36: hold-to-check with haptics, sound and music is the most specific praise (57, 10.56%, mean 4.61) — 'a small dose of dopamine every time you check something off' — 'the hardest for a competitor to copy'; 'the music is absolutely gorgeous, please upload it to Spotify'. Report 43: 'paid for the full version because i really like the happy sound when completing tasks'. Report 46: sounds / stronger completion feedback requested by 5; a December 2022 completion animation was rejected ('please remove the new animation whenever u log a day it's so annoying'; 'Special FX update unnecessary… I'll not renew'). Report 50: vibration cannot be disabled — 'especially for a (supposedly) peace-of-mind application' (1★, KZ). Report 57: the stamp check-in and its sound are the emotional core — stamp satisfaction 19 (4.947: 'there's hardly a reward system more intuitive and efficient than stamps filling up'), sound 5 ('a little thrill in the sound when you check a habit').

title: Use the language users use: Atomic Habits, 75 Hard
statement: Framing seen in US reviews. Report 23: 14 reviews name Atomic Habits (mean 4.79); also Mini Habits, The Power of Habit, Deep Work and The Power of Full Engagement. Report 24: Atomic Habits adjacency is a named purchase trigger. Report 49: 'Solo Leveling' is the language that sells — 38 name the anime as why they love it (4.87, the highest mean above 30), 'I wanted to level up like jinwoo sung and came across this app through an ad'; 15 name Instagram / TikTok. Report 75 (Habit Streak): two users independently arrived wanting 'Duolingo's streak, for anything' — 'Ho scoperto il concetto di strike con Duolingo… Per questo motivo cercavo un'app simile'; 'just like Duolingo, except super simple and you can use any habit you want' — 'a positioning gift'; chess.com's widget cited as a milestone-art model; §8.4 lead with it. Report 76 (Way of Life): Atomic Habits is a named acquisition source in later eras; the app predates the book and reviewers map it onto the grid.

title: Never ship and walk away
statement: Abandonment is visible to users within a year; the app becomes an OS-release liability for paying users with no recourse, while the store rating quietly rises on survivorship. Report 8: a ~18-month pause let iOS updates break the create flow, widget and launch, and users publicly asked whether the app was abandoned ('Wrapped 2022' still in settings in 2025). Report 14: a solo-developer app broke at each major iOS transition ('Same thing happened with iOS 13 and it took them a while to fix it'), went five years without an update, and the last thing the corpus records is the product and its checkout failing at once. Report 17: a developer who in early 2022 emailed users personally when their feature shipped had gone silent by 2023 — not an absence of ability but its exhaustion; bug reports at each iOS transition then had nobody to fix them. Report 20: across 92 months no significant new capability shipped — the only material changes were the paywall, a widget that never worked and two data-destroying updates; 'ZERO updates, content, features… NOTHING that justifies a yearly subscription fee.' Report 25: a solo developer's fast turnaround (24-hour fixes) thinned across eras (support praise 3.0% → 0.9%) while a launch blocker survived two release cycles. Report 28: 'incentives stop after level three hundred… makes me assume the developers have taken their hands off the wheel'; the listing's last version is ten months stale. Report 31: after a Dec 2020 sale ('sold from Tree Betty to this new owner') the new operator went silent on support and legacy purchases while escalating monetisation — 'ever since the original designer/developer sold it … it's stopped working'. Report 47: stagnant development 3 ('作者好像不更新了', 2020; '評価が高いアプリなのに1年以上更新がないのも残念', 2023). Report 53: positives vanished before negatives peaked — SUP_GOOD none after Mar 2022, REM_GOOD none after May 2024, WATCH_GOOD 4.3% (2022) → 0% (2026) — while iOS releases broke widgets, Watch app and statistics for a year ('No update to fix issues on iOS 18 for about a year'). Report 54: abandonment 0.9% → 1.4% → 5.0% and support-unresponsive 0 → 0.7% → 4.2% across periods; reviewers escalate from inferring neglect ('after apparently a year since the last update') to reporting a closed channel; a six-year request backlog (widget since Oct 2020, long-range stats since Apr 2020); F6: publish any maintenance signal. Report 55: 'No updates have been issued in over half a year and the developers are no longer answering emails' (2016); no iPhone X layout from Nov 2017 to Dec 2020 (BUG_COMPAT 53); 'The last update was 9 months ago, this is unacceptable for a subscription based product' (2025). Report 57: 'people have been asking about iPad and Mac for years and you always say it's planned — is it ever actually happening?' — 6 told 'planned', never shipped. Report 59 (Tappsk): NEG_DEV_PROMISE 88 rising to 1.1% of the latest era, 4.43× among purchasers — 'there were added zero new features'; 'Два года прошу добавить эту простую фичу' (asking for this simple feature for two years, 1★); 'приложение вообще не меняется годами'; REQ_TIME, REQ_BACKFILL, REQ_PHOTO, REQ_STATS and REQ_SHARED never stop; SUP_NONE also peaks in the latest era (0.8%). Report 60 (Mindway): after a two-month acquisition burst the app produced roughly one review a month for 15 months with two four-month silences, and no reviewer in 750 days reports a problem being resolved (is_edited false on all 216) — the 2026 tail is 28.57% paywall complaints and zero benefit claims. Report 65 (Rabit): in-app copy still said 'start your 2024 year strong' in Feb 2025 and the purchase screen still said 2024 in Sep 2026 ('Poderiam verificar o anúncio de compra que está em 2024?'); 'Tinha tudo pra ser do topo de app de hábitos mas não atualiza' (DEV_STALE 5, all 2025–2026); review volume 120 → 106 → 67 → 30 → 12 per year with the mean not recovering — 'attrition, not repair'; F10: 'the clearest public signal that the app is abandoned' is a trivial string. Report 69 (TheFor): no update for ~9 months (1.4.6, 2025-12-21) while reviews fell 43 → 13 → 4 per year; no reviewer yet calls it abandoned, but 'the corpus can no longer detect a new problem quickly'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 2023 is the lowest year since launch (4.56 on 108 reviews), the year tone / notification complaints reached 7 and after the add-on went monthly; 2024 recovered to 4.75. Report 76 (Way of Life): NEG_SLOW_DEV 20 (3.50★) and NEG_DEV_PROMISE 6 (2013 → 2026) — 'Can't wait for the promised weekly/monthly options' (2016) is still unmet in 2026; PR_UPDATE 255 (4.91★, 'updates improve it') is the counter-signal in most eras. Report 86 (Today): the extreme case — 1,030 days between releases (2022-11-09 → 2025-09-04, zero releases in 2023 or 2024), beginning with a build that would not launch; DEV_STALE 67 (3.75%, 20.34% of E5 reviews); users audited the developer ('no update in 2 years… copyright dates only thru 2021… email bounces because the embedded address is toda@neybox.com… Odd because sister app Pillow is working well'); 'the pattern is latency, not absence' — dark mode two years after the request, a time-zone bug fixed six and a half years after the first report, and iPad / home-screen widget / bad-habit tracking / archive / overview never in ten years; 11 releases since Sep 2025 but only 13 reviews to judge by; 'what converts a category-leading app into abandonware'.

title: Writes to shared system stores (calendar, health) must be exact and reversible
statement: A paid calendar sync that corrupts the user's calendar is the most severe complaint class in report 2. Report 25: Apple Health values read wrongly — weight interpreted as entry-count, steps off by 568 — in an app whose Health integration is otherwise praised.
