Report 50: the 5 → 3 cap cut reached users without notice — four say they were not told the terms before installing, and the angriest reviews are from people who lost capacity they already had. Report 55: the June 2018 switch from a $4.99 one-time unlock to $19/yr shipped with a release note that said only 'Changes'. Report 57: none of the tier changes was announced — 'there wasn't even an announcement — what's going on?' — F7: an in-app changelog before the next tier change. Report 59 (Tappsk): the January-2021 update capped the free tier at 20 tasks (reviewers also report 10, 3 and '2 habits, 2 recurring'), removed free habits for some ('раньше можно было использовать две, а теперь НИ ОДНОЙ' — before two, now NONE) and simultaneously stopped recognising existing purchases — MON_FREE_CUT 103 (80 in 2021-01→04), BUG_PURCHASE 57 in the era (its peak), any price objection 10.1% of the era (its peak), churn 2.2% (peak), the lowest era mean after launch (4.50★), the second most-voted review in the corpus (94 votes); the developer's reply ('it is 50') did not match the app ('only 20 are available'). Report 65 (Rabit): three model changes in six years each visible in the era means — free 4.49 → optional premium 4.19 → ads + cap 2.98 → notification outage 2.98; the E2 → E3 drop of 1.21 stars coincides exactly with ads plus the cap. Report 67 (Habio): 'I downloaded this app based on the pinned review that stated it had a free version' — the free tier disappeared in 2022 (hard wall 17.74% of that era) while older reviews still said free. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): all 21 release notes are the identical string 'Bug fixes and performance improvements' — nothing records when the free cap moved from 3 to 1 and back, so users discovered it at the paywall and the only record is the reviews; research: check remote-config history against 2024-12-18 and 2025-02. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): an ad-supported free app converted to a ~1-week trial with no notice around 2025-01-04 — zero grievances in 51 reviews over the prior 2.5 years, then 22 of 37 (59.46%); mean 4.43 → 2.78; 1★ from 1 to 17 in six months; still 22.22% of reviews twenty months later — 'an ongoing tax', not a one-off migration cost. Report 75 (Habit Streak): a free, ad-free app ('For a free app without adds, this is great', 2024-07-28) acquired a paywall by 2024-09-19 ('App payante désormais… dommage qu'elle soit devenue payante', 1★); money complaints went from 0 of 6 pre-paywall to roughly a third of every era since, the last review in the corpus (2026-07-15) being one — 'a steady state, not a spent event'. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 2023 move to a subscription was not dated by any reviewer and the corpus cannot say whether lifetime buyers were migrated automatically — the change arrived as a surprise on the restore path ('it said I had to buy premium again', 1★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): no reviewer claims the app used to be free and became paid — the complaint is that the free tier is too thin, not that something was taken away; no paywall-introduction event is visible. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the widget moved behind the wall and subscription SKUs appeared with zero listing text — MON_UNEXPECTED 2 (2.00★: 'after a while it turns out I have to pay'), MON_BAIT_SWITCH 1 ('Just charge for the download instead of the bait and switch'); two reviewers describe the free tier incompatibly fifteen days apart ('not able to use the app whatsoever for free', 1★ vs 'De momento uso la opción gratuita… súper útil', 5★) — a disclosure problem. Report 84 (HabitGrid): §8.4 — if a charge is ever introduced, announce it in advance and measure the review stream for the first price complaints; the terms already reserve charging while the listing and reviews say free. Report 86 (Today): the Notification-Centre widget was removed in 1.9.55 (2021-09-02) with release notes that said nothing about it — 11 complaints in six languages in three months ('No more widget. Which is the main way i used the app. So, I probably won't keep up to be using it', 1★; 'Give it back'; '还我小组件') — restored two months later with a note ('Thank you for making the widget come back!'); photo covers were moved behind payment taking existing covers with them (2023).

title: Widget variants and customisation as the paid layer
statement: Base single-counter widget free forever; multi-counter widgets, custom art, progress rings, reset-from-widget can be paid — and were report 3's #1 purchase trigger. Report 30 (counter-evidence): a paid widget in a capped tracker lost a user to a competitor with a free widget and is the only named paid feature besides more habits; the report proposes testing widget free vs paid as an acquisition driver. Report 36: once widgets were paid, widget-improvement demand peaked (titles, colours, streak display, interactivity) — 'now that widgets cost money, people want them to do more'. Report 41: widgets are icon-only — 'When you have +10 habits, one habit widget with only icon and no clue to remembering the habit is a pain'; one runs a competitor alongside for text labels (8 requests); widget icons 'Make them bigger and it is 5 stars!'. Report 43: per-habit notification sounds are 'too few' — 'hearing the same sound for every habit… mentally makes me mush all my tasks together'; 'you can't use the notification or ringtone sounds from your iPhone'; a snooze wanted (16, mean 3.94). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the large heat-map widget is the only named purchase trigger in the corpus ('I bought the paid version of the app (single month), because I wanted to use the larger widget showing the entire heat map and i absolutely love it') and the credited retention mechanism ('Without it I would underestimate the progress and tend to give up… I was able to successfully track and build new habits for the first time with this app'), while a lifetime buyer's only complaint is that it is too basic ('no dark themed widget? Widget so basic? Please step it up, I just paid for lifetime access') and another wants it to surface the next unfinished habit; M3: make the widget the explicit centre of the paid offer; P2: dark theme and a next-unfinished mode — 'highest leverage per unit of work'. Report 65 (Rabit): REQ_WIDGET 43 (8.63%, mean 4.30), first asked days after iOS 14 widgets launched (Jan 2021) and still asked Aug 2025, never shipped, top theme of the 4★ band, twice as hot outside Brazil; four purchases made conditional on it — 'I'll definitely buy the lifetime plus version if you add widgets'; 'If this app had them I would 100% buy the lifetime'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'более 50 виджетов на выбор' ('more than 50 widgets to choose from'); WID_GOOD 9 at 5.00 rising 2.38% → 6.00% — and the listing does not mention widgets. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): widgets reportedly paid (n=1, a 1★ whose whole text is 'You have to pay for widgets'); the paid layer is the widget itself, not a variant — and it shows one habit only.

title: Goals / targets
statement: Tolerated behind the paywall (mean 4.05) and a stated purchase reason. Report 25: a layer of long-term goals sitting above habits is requested by very satisfied users (7, mean 4.71). Report 41: yearly / long-horizon goals requested by 6. Report 48: numeric Target (a number by a date) and Project (milestones, %) trackers with a pace line and projected completion date are what 485 reviewers switched for; goal pacing praised by 56 at 4.97 — see [[C265]]. Report 59 (Tappsk): REQ_GOALS 52 (4.73★). Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_GOALS 25 (0.32%, 4.20★, 2011 → 2025) — goals / targets; NEG_WEEKLY_GOAL 2.

title: A free trial must be a real trial
statement: It must apply to whichever plan the user picks, and the confirmation must show the exact charge date and amount; a trial that bills at once produced 789 reviews at mean 1.35 in report 4 and must be verified per storefront (Brazil ran 7–11× the global rate). Report 10: 149 users believe they were charged at trial START (mean 1.79) and trial length varied between 2 and 7 days across users. Report 12: a 3-day trial introduced around 2024 shows as subscribed but 'doesn't move past the subscription screen' — the complaint changed shape from 'there is no trial' to 'the trial doesn't work'. Report 13: a trial that cannot start without first authorising a subscription, defaulting to the most expensive annual tier, produced 1,102 auto-charge reviews at mean 1.20 (999 one-star) — the single most damaging mechanic in a 19,850-review corpus; involuntary-charge reviews equalled voluntary-purchase reviews 1:1. Report 18: trials that converted immediately ('in my case there was no free period'; asked for monthly, charged annual; frozen since minute 10, charged a full year) in KR, JP, TW, ID, BR and DE; trial length shrank from 3 weeks to 7 days to 2–3-day variants. Report 19: a 'free trial' that charged (10 of 105) — '$45 for the initial trial', 'free 7 days charged trial' — with the price hidden at decision time and no renewal warning; four non-payers refused precisely because there was no way to try first. Report 24: the 'free trial' charges a 'pay what you can' set-up fee ($1 / $10 / $16.41) on a donation-style screen, classed in the terms as non-refundable — 506 reviews (1.16%, mean 1.136) say the trial was not free and 100 name the fee mechanism (mean 1.110). Report 25: the trial is a net-negative topic (21, mean 2.62, 10 1★) — card required up front, charged inside the window ('it says cost 0 in the trial selector and they charged me 1,500 pesos'), renewal into the wrong plan, and uncertainty about whether cancelling is possible; billing disputes stepped up ~5× after 2024 (0.8% → 3.9%). Report 26: a '3-day free trial' that charges immediately (incl. a lifetime tier charged instantly with no trial disclosed), cancelled before trial end and charged anyway, renewal with no notice — 23 disputes at mean 1.48, the lowest-rated theme in the corpus, and the source of the only accusations of deception ('Scam company. Impossible to cancel and tricks you into renewing'; 'Estafadores'). Report 30: no trial at all, so an annual charge is the first real use. Report 31: a 'free trial' that was actually a paid first year ('told I would be getting one year, 365 days free … now only … a month'), a trial renewing into the most expensive plan, and a trial not visible in iOS subscriptions. Report 33: 2025–26 trials converted to an annual charge unexpectedly ('I signed up for a free trial and somehow got converted to paid'; 'a 7- or 14-day trial, then charged a full year of Pro'). Report 46: two charged on day one of a 7-day trial ('Offerred 7 day trial, but I got charged the same day'); after a trial ends the extra habits are locked, not archivable ('I can't delete them… it falsifies the statistics') — the report's #8: let the user choose which 3 stay and archive the rest. Report 47: no refund requests, but one user cancelled after discovering a half-year plan they did not remember agreeing to ('契約した覚えがないので、もしかしたら無料期間を忘れたのかもしれない。気をつけた方がいいです', 1★, Jan 2026); the fix: a clear notice before a trial converts. Report 48: trial terms 26 (1.65) — charged the full year at the start of a 7-day trial; charged twice after cancelling before the trial ended; refund requests concentrate in 2019+ trial and auto-renew disputes. Report 49: 'I signed up for the 1 week free trial and was immediately charged AU$17.98'; 'immediately charged for one year. It does not show up in your Apple subscriptions and there is no way to cancel your trial!'; cancelled a day early and still charged $50; 'a loop so you can not use the app if you don't accept the free trial'; a 7-day trial only on the annual plan billed €14.99 immediately. Report 50: 'I was charged $30 before my free trial was up'; 'They absolutely DONT SEND THE REMINDER when the trial is about to finish… they charge you automatically the whole year'. Report 53: 7-day trials that several reviewers say billed a full year; M4: charge date and amount on the trial screen and a reminder 24 hours before conversion. Report 55: charged after a trial; a trial that can't be cancelled (PAY_TRIAL 8, 2.12). Report 59 (Tappsk): the 7-day trial that charged immediately or on day six is the largest single source of 1★ reviews across eight years — MON_AUTO_CHARGE 229 (1.51%, mean 1.82★) carries 163 of the 674 1★ (24.2%), co-occurs with MON_TRIAL 111 and MON_REFUND 113; a year's fee (999 ₽ named 73 times) taken at once ('при выборе бесплатной недели сразу списали деньги за год'; '«7 дней бесплатно», а сами втихую списываете на 6 день' — you quietly charge on day 6), charges after deletion ('Списывают деньги, даже если приложение удалено'), peaked 2.9% of 2020 and still 1.2% of 2024–26; the fix list: no charge before day 7, a visible countdown, one-tap cancel inside the app, a confirmation e-mail with the renewal date; a card-required trial is itself a barrier ('полная версия в пробном периоде требует привязки карты'). Report 60 (Mindway): three distinct trial failures from three users — a $0.99 paid trial converting to $39.99 within hours ('with NO EXCEPTIONS OF A REFUND'), a '3 day free trial' that billed a week after cancelling on day two (a 4★ that would otherwise be 5★), and no trial offered at all before purchase ('I'm just out the money now') — 'a flow problem, not three user errors'; F2: audit the trial-to-charge flow end to end. Report 64 (Critique AI): a 3-day trial that requires card details up front, charges the full year on expiry without warning ('it didn't let me know that it was over so it took my money'), cannot be cancelled in-app, and is not reached at all by others — PAY_TRIAL 26 (6.21%, mean 1.58), persistent across 17 months; 3 days cannot test a habit product ('Getting into stuff like this will take at least a month to stick'); M4: 14 days, no card. Report 65 (Rabit): a 7-day trial reported charging the monthly price at once ('isso é propaganda enganosa'), never starting (the subscribe button spins), charging R$199.90 after the app was deleted, and ending free use on day two (PAY_TRIAL_BAD 5); M3: 'the highest-trust-cost surface in the product'. Report 67 (Habio): a $1 / €1 / £1 3-day paid trial (MON_TRIAL_1DOLLAR 148) converting to $40+ plans — MON_TRIAL_CHARGE 173 (8.43%, mean 1.03): 'Factually their 3 days trial for 1,00 Euro is actually a 2 two days trial'; MON_PRICE_MISMATCH 55 charged more than shown; 'they've also never mentioned in their add that the currency is not in AUD'. Report 68 (Ultiself): paid intro trials on the web that auto-convert (MON_RENEWAL_SHOCK 227, 5.03% — an intro plan becoming $39.95–$87 recurring; MON_TRIAL_CHARGED 19); §8.6: replace paid intro plans with a free trial that ends without charge unless confirmed, measuring chargebacks and 90-day retention. Report 82 (Lasting Change): BILL_FREE_CLAIMED 7 (4.00%, 1.57★) — an app presented as free or as a trial that then bills: 'offers what appears to be a free month of membership, but they hide the fact that they will begin charging you monthly many months afterward'; 'I really thought I was going to get a 7 day trial. But, instead it wanted me to pay'; whether a trial exists or its length could not be established from any source. Report 83 (Roubit): BILL_UNEXPECTED_CHARGE 2 — 'I started a 7-day free trial and was charged ₩4,400'; 'suddenly ₩55,000 for a year was charged' (5★, refund requested); TRIAL_USER 4; a trial-ad problem fixed via Restore Subscription.

title: An obvious 'continue free' path on the paywall — the free/paid boundary must be legible
statement: Users wrote 75 reviews teaching each other where the hidden X was while 1,903 said the app was paid-only; legibility of what is free is a rating decision. Report 24: a real free tier (~3–4 habits, coaching locked) exists behind a small 'X' or 'skip' on the trial splash and is hard to find; 77 reviews (mean 4.442) call it generous once found. Report 34: the wall arrives at habit #3 during setup — 'I added 2, tried to add the third and was prompted to pay'. Report 48: 48 reviews (mean 1.65, rising 0.49% → 2.05% of E5) invested setup effort before meeting an undisclosed 3-tracker wall — 'I lost my time encoding 3 trackers for nothing'; 'Wish i knew before i downloaded and set everything up' — the report's fix #1: disclose the limit on the listing and at first run, 'the cheapest 1★ in the corpus to eliminate… about the surprise, not the price'. Report 49: no 'continue free' path exists at all — 256 say the only free thing is the questionnaire and its result. Report 50: a pop-up 'insisting I pay for premium every time I open the app… it stops me from just being able to use the app' (GB, 1★) — the only report of the paywall obstructing ongoing free use; 'it takes 15 Seconds to ask you for 5,99 every month' (DE). Report 52: 2026 onboarding requires picking 5 habits and choosing a 3-day trial; reviewers ask to skip both and for a visible back control on every paywall screen (M6). Report 54: 'told to upgrade, no way to' (1). Report 59 (Tappsk): paywall surprise 64 at 1.70★ — the lowest-rated monetization code — from users who thought the app was free. Report 64 (Critique AI): with no free tier the 'continue' path is only a dismiss control, and a tenth of the corpus cannot find it — 'you are stuck In the buy screen. You literally can't do anything but just stare at it'. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_UPSELL 13 (2.85★, 'upsell nags', 2014 → 2023); MON_PAYWALL 22 (2.68★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'What's the point of making a free app if it's unfunctional unless you buy a premium plan' (1★) — the free/paid boundary is illegible at install and at the wall.

title: No long quiz before the price; show the price up front
statement: A 10–20 minute quiz followed by a paywall turns a price objection into anger (mean 1.98, 71.9% 1–2★); 'lower the yearly price a bit and show it at the very beginning'. Report 24: a large share of buyers take the questionnaire in a web browser and enter payment details before ever opening the app; onboarding-too-long runs at mean 1.600. Report 42: ~15–30 unskippable setup screens before the price, with a rating prompt inside them (3 reviews, all 1★, never used the app). Report 49 (the strongest case): a 10–20 minute questionnaire plus a pledge before a hard paywall — onboarding-before-price 156 (12.66%, mean 1.15, the lowest of any theme above 20; 140 of 156 at 1★); many do not object to paying, only to the sequence ('they ask for tons of personal stuff before displaying the price wall instead of after'; '30分かけて設定したのに…初めに言って欲しい'), identical in 15+ languages; the never-used cohort (331) grew to 33.1% of the latest era; all 40 'scam' accusations are about this payment experience; the report's fix #1: 'A price shown on the first screen converts a one-star review into a non-download.' Report 60 (Mindway): the sequence ad → onboarding questionnaire → price is what the two ad-sourced reviewers (both 1★) and the scam accusers describe — 'Put the price next to your product in the App Store. Its the only correct way to go about selling a product above board'. Report 64 (Critique AI): PAY_QUIZWALL 23 (5.49%, mean 1.35) — a long survey, a physique photo and an account, then the price: 'why the need to do a survey if it isn't free? couldn't it be mentioned before the survey?'; rose from 3.2% to 8.7% in the latest quarter; M1: disclose the price before the quiz — 'Zero engineering cost, zero revenue cost'. Report 67 (Habio): the quiz doubles as the sales funnel — NEG_ONBOARD_LONG 29 ('so we don't waste our time filling up a bunch of useless data in the first place'), paid on the web before installing. Report 82 (Lasting Change): a quiz funnel that never mentions a payment plan (ACQ_QUIZ_FUNNEL 2: 'No where during the process does it mention payment plan'), descending-price urgency (ACQ_PRESSURE 4: 'they continually advertise and offer at lower and lower prices until you bite'; 'fake questions, artificial delays, pseudo customization, pseudo last time offers'), and a listing whose 'SUBSCRIPTION PRICING & TERMS' heading contains no price, period, trial length or SKU ('App does not show there is a payment plan anywhere in description'). Report 83 (Roubit): PRICE_OPAQUE 8 (1.60%) — 'services that don't show the price clearly aren't very trustworthy' (jp 3★); an elementary-schooler asking whether it keeps charging; §8.5 show price and renewal terms before the trial.

title: In-app cancellation
statement: Cancel-by-email with no reply converts recoverable disputes into permanent 1★, legal threats and denied refunds. Report 13: in Korea 24.7% of reviews say they cannot cancel and two reviewers published how-to-cancel guides for other users; an in-app 'Manage subscription' link would address a quarter of that storefront's reviews. Report 19: cancellation required email rather than a button, used bold 'stay' and small 'cancel' buttons, ~10 confirmation steps, was split across two subscriptions, and locked the user out of the account mid-flow; 24 of 105 (22.86%) described it and three asked simply for a cancel button inside the app. Report 20: refund requests ignored in Feb 2021 (Apple refunded where the developer would not), 'cannot cancel' reports 2022–2025 with one alleging an FTC-transparency breach, and accidental Touch-ID purchases during onboarding; 125 reviews at mean 1.28. Report 24: cannot find or complete cancellation 1,146 (2.64%, mean 1.115, 0.3% 5★) because the subscription lives on the developer's website; move billing into IAP or surface the web subscription in-app with one-tap cancel. Report 25: two reviewers could not find subscription settings in the app at all — 'I looked for five minutes… Is that even legal?' Report 26: two reviewers could not find any way to unsubscribe; 'well hidden there is a way to contact support… but the button is not enabled'. Report 30: an accidental subscription with no route to a refund (MX, 1★) — the reviewer blames the app even where the flow is Apple's. Report 31: 66 cannot cancel / charged after cancelling (mean 1.39, mostly E4) — no subscription found in iOS Settings; 'cancelled … TWICE and I'm still being charged'; put 'Manage subscription' in the app. Report 33: web-billed (Paddle) subscriptions had no in-app cancel ('payments … through a third party and there's no unsubscribe button'), 13 cannot-cancel reviews at mean 1.62; a deleted account was still charged; cancelling a renewal after a trial ended current access — show renewal date, price and a cancel link for every billing channel, and keep access through the paid period. Report 36: 'Dark pattern: roach motel … Clicking on link In email returns Cannot cancel subscription' (1★). Report 41: 'I would like to unsubscribe and delete the app but there are no means to do that via the app'. Report 42: two cancelled; one could not find how to refund; 'Don't fall for the free-trial trap.. you won't get a refund even if you cancel two minutes after'. Report 43 (counter-case): a one-time purchase produced zero cancellation complaints; the only refund refusal was inside the EU 14-day withdrawal window. Report 46: six cancellations threatened or described, one on the last day of the trial after a developer reply; 'I just cancelled the subscription. That's $29 down the drain'. Report 48: cancellation difficulty 4 (1.25), retained as compliance-adjacent. Report 55: M4 — disclose cap, trial length, annual price and how to cancel inside the app. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_CANCEL_TROUBLE 73 (1.0% of the latest era, its peak) — the subscription is hard to find and cancel, and the direct-card route for Russian users has no cancellation at all because App Store subscription management no longer shows the app ('В Айфоне в подписках вас у меня нет' — you are not in my iPhone subscriptions, 1★); a cancellation that works without the App Store and stops retries after deletion is an immediate fix. Report 60 (Mindway): M_CANCEL_DIFFICULTY 4 (mean 1.00) plus one who cancelled and was charged anyway — 'There is no way to cancel'; 'Please help me unsubscribe'; 'I am getting no help and stopping the subscription'; an AU reviewer still asking how to cancel 14 months after the first report; F1: make cancellation one tap from the main screen and confirm it in writing — 'the cheapest star recovery available' and 'the highest-severity item in the report'. Report 65 (Rabit): 'Comprei por engano e não consigo cancelar, não tem suporte, não tem orientação como faço?' (PAY_CANCEL 3); M4. Report 67 (Habio): MON_CANCEL 361 (17.60%, mean 1.01) and MON_CHARGED_AFTER 351 (17.11%) — an in-app cancellation confirmation screen with no persistent cancelled status, an emailed cancellation link that expires in 20 minutes, 'email not found' when cancelling, deleting the app believed to cancel (CHURN_DELETE 66); §8.1: every subscription visible in app settings with status, next charge date and amount, one-tap cancel with an on-screen and emailed confirmation, an emailed request effective at receipt. Report 68 (Ultiself): MON_CANCEL_HARD 592 (13.12%, mean 1.10) — 'you can't unsubscribe by your own, you have to email them' (kz); cancellation emails sent on time and ignored; 'Cela fait 2 mois que je demande l'annulation de mon abonnement'; a Manage-subscription button that leads nowhere for web buyers. Report 69 (TheFor): a subscriber used a public 1★ to ask to be unsubscribed and for written confirmation — an Apple-side action the developer cannot perform, but the missing Manage-subscription row is a surface the developer can add. Report 82 (Lasting Change): zero reviews in 1080 days describe a working in-app or web cancel control; CANCEL_NO_PATH 27 (15.43%: 'not… via your App Store account, their website or from within the app itself'), CANCEL_EMAIL_ONLY 12, CANCEL_DARK_PATTERN 2 ('You will forget.'); charged again after cancelling 12, after deleting the account 5 ('They confirmed cancellation and a month later they were charging me again'); cancellation honoured 3 of 175; §8.2 a self-service Cancel control in the account screen and on the web with on-screen and email confirmation — 'the only change that deals with all of the top five 1★ drivers'. Report 85 (Habitica): MON_CANCEL_HARD 4 — 'Habitica keeps charging for new subscriptions' (1★); §8.4 a visible cancel path and clear App Store subscription management.

title: One stable, disclosed price — no discount wheels
statement: Users in the same market reported $19.99–$59.99 for the same thing; that inconsistency is what 'scam' language attaches to; a rigged or broken gimmick makes it worse. Report 10: household members quoted $34.99 vs $41.99 on the same day, support could not explain a $19.99–$99.99 range — perceived as discriminatory pricing inside families. Report 18: four to five concurrently live annual prices per storefront produced 'I paid, then it showed me a cheaper price' — charged ₩33,000 and ₩25,000 both, '40% off' banners not honoured, ¥2,900 checkout billed ¥4,150 — and fraud accusations in six languages; Taiwan (2.60★) was almost entirely this; a Dutch user watched the displayed price move 'from over 200 to 68 to 19.90'. Report 20: the app advertised $5.99 / 499₽ / 85%-off and charged $39.99 / 3,150₽ — 28 reports across eight storefronts, Dec 2021 → Apr 2025; below threshold on volume, a consumer-protection exposure by nature. Report 23: a weak cluster (7, 0.10%) says the price shown and the amount debited differed (au, ru, tr, mx) — most likely tax or currency conversion, but a recurring, avoidable trust event. Report 24: annual, quarterly, 'bimonthly', monthly and weekly cycles at overlapping prices ('this page says $59 for a year… it's $40 billed every three months'), different prices on different screens, and a cancel flow that discounts $19.99 → $12.99 → $5 → $2/month; the inconsistency of what users believe they bought is the direct cause of 'charged twice' reports. Report 25: $24.99 shown and $42 charged; €29.99 lifetime followed by two further €6.99 charges; a German purchase sheet showing no price at all; Mexican reviewers unable to tell whether the price is pesos or dollars (four say so in the review) — show the local currency unambiguously and confirm displayed equals charged. Report 30: two yearly SKUs at different prices ($44.99 and $29.99) beside a $59.99 Lifetime produced 'they tell you the plan is for life and it's only for a year'; the monthly option could not be bought ('it charges for a year'). Report 31: reviewers quote 60+ price points across 15 currencies; a 'Christmas' $11.99 → $39.99, perpetual 72-hour countdowns that reset, 83–90% off banners and $399 anchors — and 69 say the advertised price was not the charged price. Report 33: charged more than shown in ~6 cases (¥4,900 → ¥5,150; $39.99 → $48.97; monthly chosen, annual charged). Report 49: a countdown discount that does not apply (an 80% notification resolving to 70%) and 'limited time offers' that tipped purchases (misleading checkout 17). Report 52: price seen as unstable — ¥18 / ¥28 / ¥88 reported in the same months, a ¥12 buyer finding lifetime at ¥98. Report 53: a perpetual 'limited-time' discount offer (2023–26) reads as deception rather than a deal. Report 59 (Tappsk): the discount that sells the lifetime unlock also generates disclosure complaints — 'Kurz nach dem Kauf wurde der Preis durch einen Zufallsgenerator reduziert' (shortly after the purchase the price was reduced by a random generator); the same lifetime named at 449 ₽ and 2,500 ₽ within a year; offers that vanish ('Предложение куда-то исчезло и желание купить пропало') and a buy button that is inactive; the report's fix: one price per region and no re-pricing within days of a purchase — a predictable seasonal sale rather than random rotation reconciles the two findings ([[C003]]). Report 64 (Critique AI): the same year quoted as $40, £40, £24, 40–45€, $39.99, $45, $50, $60, $100, $192, $200 and ₦69,900, plus weekly and monthly SKUs and an exit discount (£2.08/mo advertised, £24/yr charged) — PAY_SCAM 21 (5.01%, mean 1.05). Report 67 (Habio): 13 price points from $0.49 to $79.99 in the US listing, charges above the price shown (55), and currency not disclosed ('never mentioned in their add that the currency is not in AUD'). Report 68 (Ultiself): MON_BAIT 55 (1.22%, mean 1.05) — 'Ofrecen 4 semanas a 0.35 usd la semana y resulta que cobran 9.92usd por 7 días'; 'Cada que entro a la app me da un costo diferente' (MON_PRICE_SHIFT 6); 'it takes forever to figure out how much it costs a month'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): two different 'Lifetime' SKUs ($9.99 and $15.99) and two prices quoted to one Russian reviewer in one session; reviewers report €10, €9.99, €25, £10, $10–16, R$124.75, 129 kr and 899 ₽ — one checks the 'no further cost' claim with scepticism ('så är jag skeptisk'). Report 76 (Way of Life): 'last week the price was $29, this week is $99' (4★) in the subscription era; §8.1 one stable price per region stating whether it is monthly, annual or lifetime; 'only offer a reduced price in the first days after installation' (br 5★) penalises evaluators. Report 86 (Today): a $299.99 lifetime SKU beside a $9.99 annual — 30× — reads as 'either a mistake or contempt' next to a history of paying customers losing their purchase; regional launch pricing (CA$7 vs US$4.99) drew its own cap complaint in Canada ('$7 in the app world is premium', 2★).

title: Ads must match the app
statement: Advertised features that are absent create a 'scam' cohort before first open (0.62%, mean 2.42).

title: Content library (workouts, meditation, sleep, journal) as the paid layer
statement: Gives a routine app something to sell beyond the core loop and separates it from 'a fancy Reminders list'. Report 13 (contested): Challenges/Explore content tabs added in 2020 drew 'please let me hide them… I will not pay for an app that is 50% useless content'; nobody in 19,850 reviews asked for content, coaching or AI. Report 24: three narrated coaching pieces a day, multi-week Journeys, meditations, a deep-work ritual, music and soundscapes are what paying users value (coaching praised 6,095, 14.02%, mean 4.483; life-changing 4,468, mean 4.799); repetitive content 103 (mean 2.660); the content must be saveable and replayable. Report 26: background music and nature sounds (559, 14.57%, mean 4.68), daily quotes (58, mean 4.74), themes, backgrounds, seasons, app icons and extra gardens are the content layer — partly free, more paid. Report 46: a free Learn tab (articles, videos, James Clear material) and 7-day e-mail course were praised as 'like a life changing book' by early users (107, mean 4.82) and faded 11.02% → 3.30% as the audience turned mobile; English-only; the report's E6 resurfaces it after day 14. Report 48: a free goal-setting course / handbook is credited by 27–29 reviewers (4.93) and several convert from it — a companion-content funnel rather than a paid layer. Report 67 (Habio): articles, courses and quotes criticised far more than praised (57 vs 12 non-seeded) — 'all the typos and language errors'; a therapist 'would never recommend for a client'; 'essentially charging 1 euro per page'; NEG_SHALLOW 102 'You literally pay to track your own habits'.

title: Mascot / companion character
statement: Small, pure praise in report 4; category norm in pet-style apps. Report 10: the pet is the causal story users tell — 'I will do for the bird what I will not do for myself' — at 70,041-review scale (companion 1,309, cute design 10,074); the same attachment makes data loss feel like bereavement. Report 28: the rabbit is the emotional object — 40 (4.87%, mean 4.15) describe attachment ('I named him Paul'; 'so I dont abandon my rabbit child'), the room-cleaning loop is 'an externalised progress bar with an emotional stake' (60, mean 4.25), 244 (29.72%) describe concrete behaviour change ('made me lose 80 pounds'; 'I take my iron pill just to check it off'); the cute art survives even in 12 of 84 one-star reviews; a bug that made the rabbit drift off-screen when tapped ('I WAS TAPPING ON THE BUNNY AND IT FLEW AWAY') drew 12 reports; users want to pet and feed it (9). Report 49: a character / hero mode with equipment, loot and battles shipped late 2025, cut 'just a checklist' to 1.0% of E4 and immediately generated its own bug theme (5). Report 54: an avocado mascot with facial expressions (9, 4.78 — 'the little avocado characters really motivate me'). Report 60 (Mindway): 'LOVED THE SLIMY MASCOT' (one 5★); the cute / bubbly tone draws one 2★ dissent — n=1 each way. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): a stick-figure character shows a different encouragement line after each tap and a reminder says 「やったれ！」 — PR_COMMENTS 428 (18.69%, 4.93), PR_HUMOR 106 — the retention mechanic people name after simplicity; the free lines repeat every 30-day cycle and reviewers notice (REQ_MORE_COMMENTS 21). Report 83 (Roubit): the mascot is the retention engine — U:character_game 192 (38.40%), PRAISE_CUTE 157 (31.40%), PRAISE_GAMIFICATION 76 (4.68★): 'I go in to decorate the room and end up doing all my tasks automatically'; a reviewer who installed five top apps: 'the only one that survived was Roubit'; 'my bunny passed away recently and I kind of enjoy taking care of the rabbit in the app'; SEG_TRIED_MANY 23 at 4.91★; REQ_CUSTOMISE_CHARACTER 14 at 5.00★; a minority is repelled (FEATURE_BLOAT 3: 'I've decided to leave the bunny behind'; a 1★ 'feels too much like a game').

title: Preset routines / templates / programs
statement: Paywalled in report 4 with little complaint. Report 24: multi-week guided programmes ('Journeys' as a mountain map) and the deep-work ritual are the paid layer and the stated renewal reasons. Report 50: habit templates / suggestions at setup exist; recurring journal templates promised by the listing are still missing ('I hope vote templates are coming as it promises'). Report 60 (Mindway): preset routine packs (self-care, hair care, exercise, chores, hydration) and a self-care guide are the praised entry point (P_CONTENT_PACKS 5, 4.80★: 'having a guide to which to refer'; 'rehberle çok yardım ettiler') and the inferred paid asset — but packs loaded by default are also a clean-up burden ('otherwise you would spend all day deleting tasks', a payer; 'It is overwhelming to set up tasks in the beginning'); E6: a bulk-remove-pack control and a first-run 'pick one of three ready-made days'; custom task creation is limited or gated and is the most-requested capability ('I wish there was a way to personalize or make my own'). Report 69 (TheFor): paid 'Routine' packs ($0.99–$2.99) and 'Routine AI' ($2.99) are listed, yet zero of 80 reviews mention buying one; the Explore surface is unfindable to one reviewer and empty to another — M4: make it findable and stocked, or remove it.

title: Redesigns must not regress layout — ship a density / text-size option or an opt-out
statement: A compact-list redesign produced a dated backlash (report 7) while a Liquid Glass refresh drew none (report 8); layout regressions hit neurodivergent users hardest (report 4); a Feb 2024 redesign and continuous UI churn drew a backlash cluster (report 10). Report 23: a list view or density control (45, 0.62%) must be opt-in — 8.9% of that theme's reviews are 1★ precisely because the app changed on them; the v3.0 feature expansion split reviewers the same week. Report 25: complexity is both the top praise and a top complaint (126 vs 27; 65 vs 'too many icons to pick from') — any simplification must be opt-in. Report 27: do not remove features in updates without an opt-out — restore the full-year grid as a selectable view and the 365-dot view as a choice. Report 28: UI bloat / update regression 6 (0.73%, mean 2.50); 'Seems like every update just brings more paywall and more forced advertisements'. Report 30: add a compact list density — rows too large once habit count grows. Report 36: a 2026 layout / scaling regression — font clipped on iPhone SE3, schedule options overflowing on iPhone 13 Plus / iOS 26.2 at first run (an immediate uninstall), an overview 'zoomed in like it was designed for desktop' — 4 of 6 UIBUG records in E5. Report 43: the Oct 2025 redesign split reviewers 4 positive / 7 negative — the negatives are a blocking journal-on-skip modal with no opt-out ('should have option to TURN OFF… the pop up is obscured by my keyboard'), a calendar header 'that takes up too much space', a removed pause button, a scheduling regression and three data losses at the moment the UI changed; the positives are reordering and the restructured routine screen; the report proposes an opt-in theme switch and a one-time 'what changed' screen instead of forced change. Report 48: the 2021 history-logging redesign is the one self-inflicted UX wound (see [[C264]]); 62 call the UI dated but the report advises against redesign for novelty. Report 50: repeated UI redesigns drew three long-term US users in five weeks (Jan–Feb 2025, all churn risk) — 'it's also counter intuitive to create an app about routine and habits and make your users keep adjusting to new layouts'; 'this was perfect as it was when I first downloaded it!… now it's messy' — not repeated in 19 months; 'do not redesign the UI again without a migration path'. Report 52: redesign complaints arrive in release bursts — Oct 2020 widgets (26), Jun 2021 a Success / Pending / Fail sheet on every check-in (29), Sep–Dec 2024 compressed layout (31), Feb–Apr 2026 AI note titles (20), Aug 2026 red focus page (12) — each about losing speed or calm, not a feature; a 5★ reviewer proposes decoupling front-end style from feature iteration; the report's R1: redesigns behind a setting for at least one release. Report 54: §8.5 'Do not redesign' — 128 praise the design and no 1★ criticises it. Report 71 (MyStreaks): 'the user interface can be clunky and unpolished at times. The menu can be slightly inconvenient to navigate' (ZA, 4★) beside 7 praising ease — the check-off and the navigation / social surfaces are different parts of the app; usability-test them separately. Report 75 (Habit Streak): the v1.57.1 'fresh look' widget redesign (2025-10-26) drew a 5★ asking for the old one back — 'earlier version of widget was very attractive. light screen and fire icon can you please bring that back'; widget demand climbed back from 5.6% to 23.5% of reviews; §8.3 #1 restore the look or offer it as a style option. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 2014-06 version 3.0 flat redesign split users — 'new version (3.0) looks awful' (2★), NEG_UPDATE_WORSE 8 of 17 in that era — and marks an era boundary in the review series; NEG_DESIGN 70 (0.90%) runs 2011 → 2023. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the v2.1.0 overhaul (2026-02-11) produced 'UI bugs [that] have made it unusable' for a daily user (1★) and a reorder bug after a drag-and-drop rework — 'Do not rewrite the UI: 68.02% craft praise'. Report 85 (Habitica): the mid-2018 redesign removed sorting pets by colour; a 2026 redesign splits users (two like it, three do not); NEG_REDESIGN present across eras. Report 86 (Today): the November 2018 check-in redesign (NEG_REDESIGN 23, 3.22★) — single-tap check-in became multiple steps, the calendar mark shrank 'from a fully filled-in square to a TINY dot', no visual done-indicator so users tapped twice — was rolled back within months and reviewers upgraded in public: 'Dev Team reacted quite quick… Happy to have single tap check in back… Changed my rating to 5 stars ;-)' (edited 1★ → 5★); 'Thank you for listening!' — 'the corpus's clearest demonstration of responsiveness converting anger into loyalty'.

title: Sequential routine timer with spoken next step and live finish-time estimate
statement: Report 5's product thesis: removes the need to hold a schedule in working memory and says continuously whether you are still on time; 162 reviewers report they stopped being late. The voice needs an off switch. Report 17: a timeline-first day scheduler that 'queues up duties as the time approaches' was called irreplaceable by nearly a quarter of its reviewers and helped one with time blindness; a paying user proposed backward scheduling from a fixed anchor (work out the latest start for a pre-sleep sequence). Report 18: a per-bundle routine timer (46 reviews, 4.37★) converted — one user set every routine to one minute purely to defeat activation energy 'and then I actually started???'; Japan and the US rated it high-priority and asked for it on the Watch and in the widget, and Japanese users uniquely asked for auto-advancing timers. Report 50: stopwatch and countdown for duration habits; Pomodoro / focus music requested (2).

title: Untimed / checklist mode as a per-routine toggle
statement: A real minority of the ADHD audience finds a mandatory timer anxiety-inducing; the fix is an option per routine, not a separate object.

title: Background battery and thermals
statement: A background timer that drains 30–90% of daily battery and heats the device is report 5's worst non-billing theme (mean 2.94) and loses subscribers who otherwise love the app.

title: Notifications are few and finely user-controllable — per-type settings, escalation opt-in, never spammy and never silently retuned
statement: Some users depend on an un-dismissable alarm, others are driven out by it; a global default serves both badly; removing it broke wake-ups for loyal subscribers. Report 24: all-or-nothing notification settings make users disable everything (744, 1.71%); per-type control is the fix. [Merged from C253: Report 36: notification restraint is praised by 12 (2.22%, mean 4.67) and framed as the reason people switched — 'fine-tuned control over the notifications you receive — probably the #1 reason I've deleted other habit apps was that they spammed me with a billion distracting notifications' (13967987039); a US talking point (3.97% vs 0.69% non-US). More / snoozable reminders are also requested (7) — make any escalation opt-in so the restraint is not lost. Report 43 (counter-case): the nag loop is the differentiator — user-controlled frequency ('as often as you want') is what makes heavy notification acceptable; one review in 638 finds it excessive. Report 46: a daily e-mail at exactly 12 with a new sender address each time (3, mean 1.67, 2020–23) was made switchable ('You can turn them off if you don't like it'). Report 48: notification overload 12 (2.33) against 224 reminder praise — custom text and per-tracker control keep the ratio stable. Report 50: per-habit reminders praised by 10 (4.90); notifications broken on the new Watch app (1).] Report 53: suppress reminders once the habit or its Health goal is met ('it should know based on my steps being tracked that I've met the goal'), several clock times per habit, snooze from the notification (R1); a burst of 10–15 notifications at 8 am ('64 notifications in just a few days'). Report 55: reminders only for undone habits, several per habit (R4). Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): notifications that continue after being switched off ('I definitely turned notifications off, yet they keep coming', 1★), remain for deleted goals and duplicate on a new cycle (BUG_NOTIF 38, 1.66%, mean 3.42); §8.2 honour notifications-off, allow weekday / weekend reminder times and later edits (REQ_NOTIF_EDIT 10). Report 76 (Way of Life): NEG_BADGE 13, NEG_NOTIF 11 (2.27★) sit beside NEG_FORGET 14 'forgets to log' — the reminder that nags and the one that is missed are the same design problem. Report 83 (Roubit): NOTIF_TOO_PERSISTENT 3 for alarms that repeat until done; BUG_REMINDERS 6. Report 85 (Habitica): BUG_NOTIF 50 vs PR_NOTIF 24; REQ_REMINDERS 20; pop-ups that derail the task are named by ADHD users.

merged_from.title: Notification restraint — few, finely controllable notifications keep the users that spammy rivals lose
merged_from.note: C253 (reports 36, 43, 46, 48: restraint and fine control are why users switched; heavy nagging is accepted only when the user sets the frequency) is the same decision as C123 (reports 5, 7, 24: escalation must be user-configurable; all-or-nothing settings make users disable everything)

title: Never show ads or upsells to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement — including cross-promotion of sibling apps
statement: Including reward-gated features like streak savers; a 30-second unskippable ad to a payer is the most reliable way to turn an advocate into a 1★. Report 10: a sponsored movie tie-in as the monthly event drew 'I am paying to be advertised to' from multi-year subscribers (mean 3.09, 8× over-represented among payers) after 857 reviews had praised the app for being ad-free. Report 18: 'A pro member should be a pro member regardless of whether they are paying monthly or yearly' — monthly subscribers nagged daily to go annual, and a 'buy the next term' screen that blocked the app entirely. Report 24: in-app advertising of the developer's own sister apps inside paid accounts — 308 reviews, mean 1.932, only 14.6% 4–5★, the lowest satisfied-share of any UX theme ('I'm on the purchased version… I don't want to see adds'); rose 0.11% → 2.03% across eras. Report 28: 'I paid 10$ to remove ads but I still get ads'; a 5★ 'purchased the full version and I am still getting ads' — and even after buying no-ads there is still a prompt to double carrots by watching an ad after every level. Report 31: the promotional banner hid a habit even for paid users (Dec 2020). Report 50: no ads at any tier (5 confirm). [Merged from C248: Report 31: 314 reviews (6.05%, mean 1.57) were upsold after paying — 197 of 625 explicit payers (31.5%) — rising 0.3% (E1) → 12.1% (E4): 'It's not encouraging customer loyalty!!'; mood-disorder tracking interrupted by the offer; a banner in Dec 2020 hid the bottom habit even for paid users. The report's first upsell rule: suppress every offer for any past or present entitlement, and test every-launch vs weekly vs never-for-past-payers on conversion, D30 retention and 1★ rate. Report 33: cross-promotion ads for the developer's other apps (Nirow, Poly) shown to lifetime payers — 'False advertisement – Still get ads with lifetime premium'; a premium user shown notices: 'No. deal with it'; 'I wish the upgrade button would disappear when you buy premium' — 14 + 12 reviews.] Report 52: 40 paying reviewers (including legacy lifetime and ¥8 ad-free buyers) still saw ads — 'I bought lifetime membership before… an ugly ad pops up at every check-in'; F2: verify the entitlement before rendering the first ad. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'never show the lifetime buyer a subscription paywall' is an immediate fix — an app that sells lifetime, annual and monthly SKUs plus a 7-day trial side by side let a subscription charge reach lifetime owners ('купил полную версию на всегда за 1500 тыс, сегодня списалось 999 рублей за подписку' — bought forever for 1,500; today 999 ₽ taken for a subscription); lifetime buyers carry the highest problem lifts among purchasers (MON_PAID_TWICE 8.89×, BUG_PURCHASE 8.43×, SUP_NONE 6.09×) even though the one-time option is praised 93 times against 23 subscription objections. Report 64 (Critique AI): a subscriber reports seeing ads while paying £40/yr (4★) — 'the worst of both models'; F6, verify before acting. Report 65 (Rabit): 'I have ads on a paid subscription- I want a refund'; 'despite buying a premium subscription, I'm still being asked every time I'm in the app to upgrade to premium'. Report 68 (Ultiself): 'I bought a lifetime premium account but I don't get everything'; 'To do that, you have to pay yet another $40'; 'After subscribing, lets you PAY AGAIN' — MON_TIER_TRAP 24 (peak 4.6% in 2023), MON_UPSELL 80 predating the billing wave. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the add-on kept being advertised after it was bought (NEG_UPSELL_NAG 5, mean 1.40); 'I can't tell the difference between the comments before and after paying'. Report 76 (Way of Life): ads briefly appeared for paying users after the 2015-11 update ('Ads when already paid', 2★) and a 2020-01 bundle promotion shown to paying users drew 5 complaints ('Ads now constantly appear in paid version', 4★) — the last ad complaints in the corpus are from payers.

merged_from.title: Never show an upsell to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement
merged_from.note: C248 (reports 31, 33, 47: upsells and cross-promotion shown to payers and lifetime buyers; a rating prompt shown to payers) and C127 (reports 5, 10, 18, 24, 28, 50: ads, sponsored events and renewal nags shown to subscribers) are one rule: a paying user sees no monetisation interruption

title: Use the lead-user market as the beta cohort
statement: Report 5's home market (Korea) carries the deepest engineering feedback and most detailed feature specs — and uses the review page as a support desk. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the developer's home market (Germany) is the largest and strongest storefront — 17 of 71 at 4.76★, 9 written in German and 8 in English. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): Germany (17 reviews, 4.82★, zero 1★) supplies both pre-committed-star requests, both negative-board requests and the only price-rise review — the densest, most articulate storefront; the developer is Ukrainian and Ukraine holds 55 public ratings. Report 83 (Roubit): Korea (home market, 246 reviews, 4.37★) is where the buyers, would-be buyers, price objections, platform requests and widget bugs concentrate (PAID 6.9%, WOULD_PAY 4.5%, IPAD_WATCH 6.1%, BUG_WIDGET 4.9%); other markets report reliability (Japan blank-diary 32.1%, US launch failure 11.5%). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the developer's home region (Romania/Hungary) supplied 6 of the first 13 reviews and then went silent — a launch cohort, not a market. Report 85 (Habitica): the US (42.99%) carries the pay-to-win objection (15 of 19), the professional recommenders (13 of 16), trading requests (11 of 12) and the guild-closure grievance (19 of 32). Report 86 (Today): China (353, 19.78%) values simplicity above beauty, pays more (12.18%), suffers restore failures most (8 of 18), and was the first market to get — and to criticise — a localisation.

title: No default-on social feed in a personal tool
statement: Unwanted by a vocal minority, and a child-safety liability when minors and adults share a feed on a 17+ app. Report 49: social / guild features requested by only 2 — the community lives in Discord. Report 55: a per-habit forum is a support network for most (COMM_GOOD 31, 4.90) but clutter, a one-topic feed and anonymous shaming for some (COMM_NEG 8); R7: topic filters and blocking of shaming replies. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): no review asks for sharing, friends, leaderboards or accountability partners — §8.5: do not chase the 'accountability' positioning with social features.

title: Do not sell in a storefront where the app cannot function
statement: Seven years of 'will not open' from mainland China, with users charged for an app that shows 'no network'. Report 9: in Russia 46% of reviews say the app loads for minutes or only works over a VPN, while 32% of Russian reviewers had paid. Report 33: a mandatory account backend unreachable from mainland China made the app unusable there for eight years — 173 reviews (4.39%; 57.8% of China; 79 of its 101 1★), 18 payers who could not use or restore what they bought (328 RMB lifetime, refunds refused), and an App Store 'Today' feature in Dec 2018 that sent 68 Chinese users into a registration failure ('can't register — and you recommended it on the home page?'); China was lost on reachability, not fit — reviewers praised the design and localisation and asked to pay ('I'd pay 188 RMB lifetime if you fixed the server'). Report 47: registration and login fail from mainland China — 6 of 8 login failures are Chinese ('好像需要vpn'), consistent with a blocked backend; China 32 reviews at mean 4.28 otherwise. Report 76 (Way of Life): Dropbox-only backup was unusable on the Chinese storefront (17 of 18 complaints, 2014–16) — the app was sold where its data-safety feature could not function. Report 85 (Habitica): the service is unreachable from mainland China without a VPN for the whole eleven years (NEG_CHINA_NET 16, 14 of them on the cn storefront, 15× lift) — cn is the second-largest storefront (201 reviews) and its defect share (53.2%) the highest of the eleven eligible.

title: Gate on capability, not on quantity
statement: A quantity cap set above the point of core value is noticed, tolerated and does not convert; move the wall to analytics, sync, Watch, widgets, icons, family sharing. See Research Reports/Feature Gating vs Quantity.md. Report 6 contests the 'icons' part: the listing sold Premium on themes and icons and zero of 44 reviewers mentioned them. Report 18: users who paid said the paid tier 'adds nothing, it only removes limits' — 'not so much an amazing paid service as being forced to pay because the basics were cut'; the corpus's own purchase-condition backlog (export, trend statistics, routine modes, timer with time tracking, Watch parity, themes, web/Mac) is entirely additive capability. Report 20: after the conversion the paid layer was colours, dark mode, extended notifications, manual backup and a non-functional widget above a 3-habit cap — the cap sat below the threshold of usefulness and the paid depth did not deliver. Report 24: the free tier gates coaching content (the product's value) at ~3–4 habits; the constraint that makes the product work is pacing, not a paywall. Report 25: gating expanded over time from a habit count to statistics, the calendar view, group creation and — from Nov 2025 — editing the starter habits the onboarding itself created ('You need to get the premium to edit habits, even the ones they start you out with'), which turns a reduced product into a demo; weak by rate (5, mean 1.20), high by consequence. Report 26: the gate sits on quantity (habit count) and on the visible reward (growth stops at 17%) rather than on capability; extra gardens, themes and 'no wither' mode are the paid layer that users accept. Report 28: capping semantics — how important a user is allowed to say something is (1 red / 2 orange priority slots) — reads as the app overruling the user: 'it feels disingenuous to put exercise as low priority just so that i can put washing my face as medium'; 'if I put hygiene as yellow it's just wrong'; if a cap must stay, rename the tiers as labels or let users choose colours; a to-do list that earns nothing while habits do is the same class of gate. Report 30: 'Quer cobrar? Coloque algumas versões na versão pro. Não faz sentido deixar cadastrar 2 habitos' — users themselves ask to monetise depth (widget, sync, themes, history, stats) rather than habit count; a 2★ says the price is fine ('ce n'est pas cher') and still rates 2★ for the cap — the cleanest evidence the cap, not the price, produces low ratings. Report 31: the cap stayed fixed while packaging changed; buyers valued unlimited habits, reminders, charts, groups and export. Report 36 contests the widgets part: reviewers accept paid skins but reject paid widgets and habit caps — skins-only gate mean 2.77 vs widgets 2.64 vs habit cap 2.30 ('Pay for the skins. I am fine with widget restrictions but 59$?'). Report 41: the report's experiment E1 is to move the gate off habit count onto history depth, statistics, widgets, sync or customisation, measuring conversion and the 1–2★ rate together. Report 42: the report proposes moving the wall to history depth, statistics depth or reminder count rather than habit count — statistics already being the top named purchase trigger. Report 43: the report's experiment E3 is to surface the unlimited-habits unlock at a moment of demonstrated value (e.g. a 14-day streak) rather than at a count limit — the historic cap failed because it blocked before value was shown. Report 46: the report's #9 is 3 → 4 free habits — the smallest change that fixes the widget defect and answers the counter-offer without touching the habit-science defence. Report 47: every purchase trigger reviewers name is additive — accumulated value ('プレミアに入ったくらい重宝してます'), study stats, motivation photos, the AI coach, a platform bundle — and none asks to pay to restore something that used to be free; the report's rule: grow premium only through additive value. Report 48: the cap is the dominant mechanical purchase trigger ('I'll probably upgrade to the paid version soon to get more trackers') but a 3-tracker cap on a multi-goal product blocks evaluation — 'You are not allowing a certain group of people try out your app'; multiple reviewers propose the split themselves: pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports. Report 49: 'just a checklist' 38 (1.68) and 'do it yourself instead' 36 (1.36) — a bare checklist reproducible by ChatGPT cannot carry the price; the level-up loop, art and community can. Report 50: 'the entire monetization surface is one number' — no reviewer reports reminders, statistics, journaling, widgets, Health or the Watch app individually gated — 'That clean one-gate model is worth protecting — and §7.2 shows what happens when the one gate moves.' Report 59 (Tappsk): the quantity gate (2 habits, 2 recurring tasks, a few reminders) is the top objection at 697 reviews while the capability gates (iCloud sync, Mac) draw a fraction of that. Report 60 (Mindway): the purest count gate in the ledger — a free tier of roughly 1–3 tasks in a daily routine planner (M_PAYWALL_BLOCK 19, 8.80%, mean 1.63, 13 of 19 at 1★, in six languages: 'I wanted to add third task to do and I can't do it without paying'; 'you need to pay money to just write some freaking habits'; 'quería organizar mi día y no puedo ya que solo por hacer algo me pide pagar'); the cap sits below the app's own minimum viable use — 'a daily routine of two tasks is not a routine, so the free tier cannot demonstrate the thing the paid tier sells' — and it is the only major theme still growing in the 2026 tail (5.33% → 8.66% → 28.57% of period); D1: gate on depth — multiple routines, history, advanced recurrence, the guided content — rather than on count. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the price is not the problem (three unprompted 'the price is fair' against two one-line objections) — 'packaging (what the free tier contains) and delivery (whether the purchase works) are'; repackage, do not reprice. Report 65 (Rabit): §2.4 — 'Rabit monetises the number of habits. Its behavioural engine — plants, streaks, reminders — is what people love, and it rewards consistency, not volume. So the paywall taxes the axis users do not value while leaving the axis they do value free-but-broken'; a reviewer asks for exactly the inverse ('manter uma versão free com outras funcionalidades pagas mas não bloquear o uso do aplicativo'); M1: raise the cap materially and paywall depth instead of count; the paid tier 'não há grandes diferenças quando paga'. Report 69 (TheFor): 'a product whose free tier is its moat has no obvious upgrade ladder that does not damage the moat' — M2: build Pro from additive capability the corpus asks for (sync free for one device / paid for multi-device, automatic backup, deep analytics, Face ID lock), never by removing free capability; a Pro buyer's only request (auto-backup) is not in Pro. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the clearest case of charging for the commodity — the paywall gates the number of streaks, 'the private, single-player counter' every free competitor gives away ('there are so many alternatives that don't make you pay when you've hit a max of 2 goals'), while the surfaces reviewers praise and competitors cannot copy — community (8, 4.88), sharing, accountability, outcomes (21, 4.95), the book and podcast (8, all 5★) — sit ungated or unclear; §8.4: 'charge for the part that is hard to copy… and stop charging for the part every free competitor already gives away'; §8.1 #1 re-cut the paywall to gate a feature, not the streak count. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'The free tier is an acquisition instrument, and it is currently priced as a monetization instrument' — 24 cap complaints and zero reviewers who say the cap made them buy; eight of nine price objections also carry the cap — 'The price is not the problem; the ratio of what is free to what is charged for is'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 'not one person names a premium capability other than more habits' in 41 reviews — 'the paywall is being read as a quantity gate rather than a value gate'; E1: A/B unlimited habits with premium features gated against the current cap; §8.1 #4 show what Premium unlocks besides more habits — 'if there are not, the offer is a quantity gate and reads as one'. Report 76 (Way of Life): premium = unlimited items only; purchasers still ask for frequency (2.39×) and sync (2.72×) more than the corpus — the paid tier unlocks more of the same rather than the two capabilities people want; §8.5 sync is the paid feature reviewers say they would pay for. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): money-negative reviews object to structure 12 of 14 (85.7%) vs price level 2 of 14 (14.3%); 'the corpus says the price is broadly acceptable and the boundary is not' — a structure problem, not a pricing problem; MON_PAYWALL_BLOCKS 7 (9.86%, 2.86★: 'only a tiny bit of the app's uses are free'; 'most features require the pro subscription') vs MONP_VALUE 3 at 5.00★ ('the price is just right'); no reviewer names a specific feature as the thing they paid for. Report 82 (Lasting Change): consent objections outnumber price objections 56 to 4 (14:1) — PRICE_TOO_HIGH 4 (2.29%) vs U:consent_failure 56 (32.00%); §8.9 do not lower the price; the only clean pricing signal is a 4★ who likes the app and finds it 'too steep… especially for retirees or disabled people'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'the distinction the corpus supports is between charging for what users already have (which is what they chose the app for) and charging for things they have asked for and do not yet have' — watch app, cloud backup, frequency modes are the only asks and none exists yet.

title: Lead the store listing with what users actually love
statement: Report 6's most-loved feature (the free widget) was one bullet at the bottom of the description and its differentiators (no daily check-in, user-defined day boundary) were not marketed at all — yet they are why people switched. Report 23: lead with the streak mechanism and HealthKit automation, not 'to-do list' — the 'just a checklist' 1★ block is an expectation failure; award/editorial traffic (17 reviews naming the Apple Design Award, mean 2.53, the worst channel) arrives expecting 'best app'. Report 24: reviews invoking Apple or Editor's Choice average 1.085 (95.7% 1★) — 'Apple should not feature this'. Report 25: reviewers say the app feels first-party ('went back to check if the app was made by apple') and 37 switched from named competitors — the listing can lead with configurability and Apple-platform depth; measurable outcomes are claimed (45 kg lost in 8 months). Report 26: reviewers convert on the aesthetic within minutes — the listing's visuals and music are doing the selling; the German listing typo 'Gewohnheitstrinker' shows the listing is read closely. Report 27: the origin story in the listing produces 10 all-5★ developer-gratitude reviews; 'From one developer to another — nice piece of work'. Report 28: 'It's a game, not a tracker' (10, mean 2.40 — 'not at all what I was expecting'; 'the only thing I'm tracking is the amount of adds') is a listing and first-run expectation-setting problem costing 2★ reviews with no defect present. Report 31: lead with simplicity, colourful friendly design, build + quit in one list, 'N times per week' and musical sounds — 458 simplicity and 250 design praise reviews prove the brief. Report 41: an app that wins 19.63% of reviews on comparison is under-discovered ('It deserves a way higher ranking and visibility in the search results'; 'I didn't find it the first time'); the listing does not lead with the one-time option, the non-binary ring, full Apple-ecosystem coverage or no ads / no account; outcome stories (10.4% of 2026) are an unused asset. Report 47: why people give 5★ — simplicity 31.8% of the band, the filling grid 18.4%, behaviour change 13.7% ('三日坊主' no longer), design 12.6%, best-of-many 10.5%. Report 48: five-star reviews are simplicity 23.7%, flexible tracker types 13.7%, best of many 13.6%, behaviour change 8.4%; US reviewers talk about outcomes and accountability more than anyone else. Report 50: a Reddit user was acquired by a screenshot of the monthly report ('so pretty'); Instagram-ad and Reddit acquisitions are all 5★. Report 56: the listing leads with the category's language ('simplicity, clarity, and daily consistency') while users say 'actually free, no strings, nothing extra' — E5: rewrite it in the corpus's words; the US over-indexes on outcomes (25.0% vs 9.3%). Report 58: acquisition is founder-dependent and the listing does not claim the ADHD audience that found it; test copy leading with simplicity (the US already leads with simplicity, 50.0% vs 33.8%). Report 60 (Mindway): the marketable asset is concrete habit outcomes in reviewers' own words — 'makes me drink more water'; 'We will drink 4 glasses of water each day'; 'even got me to stretch'; 'This actually helps me with my chores, even though I'm seven'; 'It made me calm'; 'THIS APP MAKES ME FEEL SO MUCH BETTER' — 43 (19.91%) at 4.79★, 'Mindway's value proposition translates' across ten languages, while the listing and the paywall sell task slots. Report 64 (Critique AI): R4 — lead with what works: reported physical outcomes are the highest-rated theme (12, mean 4.92: 'It helped me lost 50 pound'; 'i'm in shape now because of this app') and social / confidence outcomes 4.75 ('you go from not talking to anyone to talking to everyone'), against 2.17 for the AI layer the name sells. Report 65 (Rabit): design is the durable asset — 106 (21.29%, mean 4.57): DES_CUTE 79 ('fofo/fofinho', hand-drawn icons) and DES_SIMPLE 58, 19.4% → 13.0% → 10.2% of eras, praised even inside 1★ and 2★ reviews; 'one of the few apps where UX was taken seriously. 5 stars for that alone' (uk). Report 67 (Habio): what survives among non-seeded reviews is the calm, soft visual design (PR_DESIGN 39, in every era, often from complainants: 'I love the look and feel of the app, it's calming') and the reflection journal — keep them (§8.11). Report 68 (Ultiself): outside E5 47.3% praise something specific — ease of use (255), design (148), tracking (119), library with sources (90: 'large library of habits plus corresponding sources'), routines (78), reminders (68), insights (63); §8.9 keep them. Report 69 (TheFor): the three reasons behind almost every 5★ — it looks good, it has nothing extra, it beat the apps tried before; the listing leads with transformation instead. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): design praise 152 (60.80%, 4.75), flat across eras — 'the design is not a differentiator to be protected alongside features — it is the feature'; the listing omits the 50+ widgets; E5: lead the listing with the aesthetic and icon library. Report 76 (Way of Life): the listing cites Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose and reviewers cite the same source for a decade — earned press in the listing compounds; §8.8 keep the three-state grid, the charts, the 3-habit free tier and one-person development in front. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the title and description already lead with the concept ('The first habit tracker without streaks') — the only thing with no detractors — and it is the paywall that does not; §8.4.1.

title: Offer both check-in tracking and auto-counting (no daily check-in) per item
statement: A counter that runs on its own until you declare a break is report 6's differentiator against every check-off tracker, and fits abstinence streaks best.

title: When an item can be tracked more than one way, make the user choose the mode at creation
statement: Report 6: users who landed in the auto-count mode by default read it as the app fabricating progress (1★), and users asked for a mode that already shipped. Report 48: a decade of setup confusion (118 at 2–3% every era) concentrates on choosing between Habit / Target / Average / Project and on ambiguous yes / no semantics for bad habits (12) — the mode choice needs teaching at creation. Report 49: advanced users given a beginner plan (13) — let users enter existing fitness so the plan starts at the right level.

title: Show the paywall at the moment of need, not on app open
statement: Surface the upgrade when the user tries the gated action (the third streak, a freeze); an upsell on every launch reads as 'begs me for money' and feeds the greed cluster. Report 13: the paywall fired 3–15 times in the first three minutes while the real purchase trigger was hitting the cap after engagement; the report's experiment: delay the first interstitial until habits are completed on three separate days. Report 25: move the paywall to after first value, not after the onboarding survey — the survey-then-paywall sequence averages 1.17. Report 36: the report recommends never showing the upsell before the first habit is created. Report 55: M2 — show the upsell at the moment a sixth habit is added, not on every launch. Report 60 (Mindway): the counter-case — a paywall shown at the moment of need is fine only if the need is real; here the 'need' is the third task of a routine, so the moment-of-need paywall is the wall itself (19 blocked at 1.63★). Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the purchase moment users choose is a completed 30-day cycle — 22 of 54 purchasers report a streak ('I kept it up for 30 days, so I bought the useless feature'; 'I'll buy the useless feature if I last a month'); §8.7: offer the support prompt there. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the subscription prompt fires repeatedly after the first habit is added — the moment of need becomes the moment of nagging when the cap is one.

title: Never let the paywall imply a capability the product lacks
statement: A buyer who paid for a feature that isn't there cancels and says 'there are free ones'; it turns a feature request into a refund cause.

title: Cache entitlements locally — never block a paid surface on a live server check
statement: Report 7: widgets that re-checked Pro against a network service showed 'Upgrade' to paying users for 15 months (100% payers, mean 2.25), 4× more often in markets with VPN/DNS filtering; render from the last-known-good receipt. Report 24: cannot log in / paid but no premium access 96 (mean 1.375, 78.1% 1★). Report 25: three independent reports in three storefronts (fr, fr, nl) that the app stopped working immediately after payment — specific enough to reproduce against the entitlement path. Report 28: 'I paid the 14.99 to unlock the full app 2 days ago and it's still saying I need to purchase it… Total scam'; carrots not delivered after 2–3 hours with restart and restore both failing. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the clearest case — 'If I don't have internet access the app asks me to go premium, when I already bought the app. This is a headache. Can you fix this critical error!' (EC, 5★ despite the bug): a receipt check that requires the network re-paywalls exactly the offline moments (commute, flight, poor signal) when a habit app is used; I1: cache the receipt / entitlement locally and never re-paywall a verified purchaser because the network is unavailable — 'the single highest-severity non-burst finding in this report'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the developer's own v2.7.0 note (2026-09-03) — 'Fixed an issue where Ripples+ features would sometimes become locked while the device was offline' — corroborates MON_ENTITLEMENT_FAIL 3 (every one 1★, 33.3% of stated payers); §8.1.1 an offline grace period for verified entitlements and an in-app 'my purchases' state showing what is owned and when it was verified. Report 83 (Roubit): a Restore Subscription button resolved an entitlement/ad problem for a paying user who then moved to 5★; membership that 'sometimes drops' is the same class.

title: Market the generic-tracker use case
statement: Report 7: users track medication, migraines, supplements for a pet, art-project days — any yes/no daily thing — at mean 4.91, while the listing only says 'build habits'. Report 60 (Mindway): outcomes named are hydration, workouts, tidying, stretching, getting out of bed and chores — a routine planner is used as a generic self-care tracker. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): use cases described — fitness / sport progress, hydration and step counts (unserved by a binary daily check), religious practice, daily task focus; no review describes breaking a bad habit despite the accountability subtitle. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'journals' rather than habits — items can be anything, good or bad; USE_WORK 16, USE_STUDY 18, USE_FAMILY 13 alongside fitness and health; PR_CUSTOM 206 (2.65%). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'boards' with custom units track study hours, gym, medication, music production, driving-theory tests, coding lessons and work days — the generic-tracker use case, praised as 'a task with a completely open schedule'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): USE_NON_HABIT — a Russian reviewer uses it to remember watering plants; one moved from Apple Reminders 'to keep track how many times I actually completed them'. Report 85 (Habitica): Habits (+/− counters with no schedule), Dailies and To-Dos plus custom real-life rewards — 'a planner pretending to be a game'; PR_CUSTOM 66; PR_ORGANIZE 95. Report 86 (Today): 'just a yes/no - did you hit the gym today?' — reviewers draw the line against to-do lists and workout trackers; PR_OUTCOME 106 (4.84★, the highest mean): 60lbs, 50 meat-free days, quitting soda, five languages, 200 days of fitness, quitting smoking, six years of habit-formation.

title: Native iPad layout
statement: A stretched phone UI on iPad does more rating damage than a missing Watch app and is cheaper to fix — a layout, not a new product (report 7). Report 20: an iPad-native app never shipped (43 complaints, mean 3.33). Report 23: iPad layout not optimised 8 (0.11%). Report 24: no iPad app / lost progress on device change 257 (0.59%, mean 2.693) — progress loss on device change is the most-cited reason a multi-year user stops. Report 28: iPad / larger-screen support requested by 6 (mean 4.67); screen-fit / aspect-ratio defects 5. Report 31: native iPad layout with landscape named as the 4★ → 5★ condition ('I will gladly give 5 stars'); Malaysia 21% platform requests. Report 33: iPad layout with landscape shipped Apr 2019; widgets did not refresh on iPad for years. Report 34: 'purchased Premium version for my iPad as well' refers to the iPhone app on iPad; iPad / Mac / web requested by 8. Report 36: landscape / rotation (5) and a real iPad layout (4) requested in early 2022, fading later. Report 43: the listing claims iPad, Mac (M1+), Vision, Watch and TV. Report 46: landscape / wider view requested by 4 ('The rating will change when there's a landscape mode'). Report 47: iPad not supported — the app runs at phone size (11, 1.87%, 2019–2026: 'iPadサイズに対応しておらず、画面が小さくて見づらい'); requested in every era; an iPad layout is a stated purchase condition. Report 48: an iPad app was requested 2013–15 (9) and landscape iPad 2015–16 (8); iPad is now supported. Report 49: iPad layout reported broken (part of device incompatibility 15). Report 50: marking done 'somewhat better on iPad' than iPhone per one teardown. Report 52: iPad HD version, landscape and split view requested (380, 63.7% in 2018–20). Report 54: iPhone only — iPad / Mac requested (7, 4.57; CN 3 of 7). Report 55: iPad runs the stretched phone app (IPAD 30). Report 57: iPad-native layout requested by 21 (18 Korean) — cheaper than full sync. Report 64 (Critique AI): the app 'refuses to work on iPad' for a payer who also could not log in on a second device. Report 65 (Rabit): no iPad layout requested since Feb 2021; crashes on iPad iOS 12.5; reminders absent on iPad. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): iPad layout / landscape requested by 13 (mean 3.92). Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_IPAD 123 (1.58%) dominated the early years (E1 4.7%) and is still the second device most named; §8.5 iPad before Watch; 'you have to pay for each iPhone or iPad you use' (1★) when purchases did not carry across. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): REQ_IPAD 2 (5.00★, 2026) — the listing is iPhone-only; 'a grid view is a natural fit for a larger screen'. Report 83 (Roubit): REQ_IPAD_WATCH_MAC 15 (3.00%), every one from Korea — 'I want to buy premium but hesitate because I use my iPad a lot'; a paying Korean 3★ mainly uses Todo Mate for Apple Watch; §8.8 an iPad layout for Korea. Report 86 (Today): REQ_IPAD 27 (1.51%, 2016 → 2026) — never in ten years; 'Si la tuviesen para Ipad la compraría' (es).

title: Surface existing features where users look
statement: Features hidden behind 'Advanced Options' or unexplained modes are rated as missing — including by payers who bought and then believed the feature absent; report 7's weekly goals, multi-habit widget and notifications. Report 19: the only constructive reviewer found the product's real asset — a web course library — by accident, because the app never linked to it; the thirteen who called the product 'just a checklist' may have been describing the 10% they were shown. Report 23: a hidden backup/restore path, and edit/delete/undo actions hidden behind gestures — 250 UI-confusion reviews (3.44%, mean 2.66, 31.6% 1★) resolve into three actions: deleting a task, editing a task, undoing a completion; a single visible Edit / Delete / Undo affordance plus in-app text would address most of them. Report 26: a calendar/statistics view shipped ~late 2024 and users still cannot find it ('the calendar could be more easily accessible, I currently have to search for it') — a cheap discoverability fix on built functionality.
