Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 10 IAP SKUs from $2.99 to $29.99 under three product names ('Momentumly Plus', 'Premium Habit Tracking', 'Premium'), none showing a billing period, beside a description whose only money paragraph is auto-renewal boilerplate with no price, tier, trial or one-time option — three reviews over 12 months hold three different beliefs about whether a lifetime purchase exists ('I've subscribed for the lifetime version', 2★; 'there is no possibility to get a lifetime version', 2★ — the entire review; 'The one time purchase rather than a subscription model is also a lovely thing', 5★); reviewers name the paid tier five different ways; 'a user who cannot tell what is being sold does not buy'; §8.1.2 show periods and cut the SKU count; §8.7 Q1 'does a lifetime SKU currently exist' is answerable in one minute in App Store Connect. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): five SKUs under three product names (Powerpack $9.99, Ripples Plus Lifetime $24.99, Plus Monthly $2.99, Plus Yearly $9.99, Powerpack Family $17.99) with no billing period shown against any; nine reviews use six different names for the paid tier and two incompatible billing models ('the premium subscription… a one time 10 dollar payment' in one sentence; '$10 for a lifetime subscription'; 'Чекер+'; 'die Vollversion'); 'A customer who cannot tell whether they are buying a subscription cannot consent to buying one'; a 'Чекер+' tier existed under the old app name before today's 'Ripples Plus'. Report 86 (Today): three IAPs — Today Premium Monthly $3.99, Today Premium Annual $9.99, 'All premium features' $299.99 — and reviewers cannot parse them: 'why is Today Premium $10 per year, but ALL Premium Features are $300 ❓ what is the difference' (2★); 'premium used to be $4.99 and now… $299.99' (gt 2★); §8.10 'whatever the intent — a lifetime tier, a price-anchoring device, a legacy artefact — it currently reads to users as either a mistake or contempt'.

merged_from.title: Every SKU delivers exactly what its label says — one clear shelf, a working monthly option, and 'lifetime' that is lifetime
merged_from.note: C245 (report 30: two yearly SKUs beside a 'Lifetime' produced 'lifetime delivered as annual'; the monthly plan could not be bought) and C177 (identically named / period-less SKUs) are the same rule about an unambiguous price shelf; entitlement delivery itself stays in C033

title: A quiet, adult, non-gamified tracker is a positioning some users actively seek
statement: Report 11: 'Functional, no frills and no infantilization. I tested half a dozen similar apps before finding this one'; 'I hate apps that demand set times'; 'without any imposed junk' — four of 33 reviewers chose the app for what it refuses to do, and three switched from gamified competitors. A live tension with the pet/mascot category norm. Report 27: two reviewers name the absence of gamification as the reason they chose the app — 'There's not pets to take care of, there's no flashy graphics or anything, and that is just perfect for me'; 'it removes a direct emphasis on urgency and/or self-competition' — and 52 praise minimalism; in a category converging on pets, gardens and streak anxiety, deliberate plainness is a defensible position that any future monetisation must not contradict. Report 28 (counter-evidence): the gamified pet loop is what works here — 'especially having adhd, this gamification works so well for my brain'; one reviewer chose it because it is less feature-heavy than Finch; the plain/gamified split is a positioning choice, not a rule. Report 29: 'Everything that you need, nothing that you don't' — 119 praise simplicity against 3 wanting rewards or more features; do not add features to the main flow. Report 30: 'понятный и удобный интерфейс. Без заморочек' — a minimalist tracker's one proven strength; the thesis works and the packaging fails. Report 31: the simple, colourful adult tracker is loved consistently in every era, and contrasted with Habit-Bull's 'roided-out CrossFit guy'. Report 34: 'Feels like it was made by Apple'; 'Native iOS gem'; 'The whole app just feels calm and clear' — calm native design praised by 156 at 4–5★, gamification requests (5) outnumbered by praise for its absence. Report 41: 'What you will not find here: being told which habit to do. Challenges against other people'; the report's do-not-add list — to-do list, journal, pet, plant, challenges, social feed, AI coach. Report 43: 'not all illustrated with pink & blue kittens and ribbons, have a psychologist's daily thought for the day baked in, nor is it incessantly asking me to note my feelings for the day'; 'you don't have to read a bunch of flowery, condescending you can do it! messages'. Report 46: 'habitica but without the stupid game mechanics'; no gamification praised (3, all 5★). Report 52: SOC_NOSOCIAL 120 (4.85, payer lift ×4.55; 100% mainland) — 'please never add social features, I just want to check in quietly by myself' (48 votes); 'no ads, no noise' praise rose in 2024–26 as reviewers compared the new ad experience. Report 54: 'Unlike some other apps which include too many unnecessary settings, this app has just what you need. No distractions, and no complications'. Report 56: users praise absence — 'no random pop ups—just put your habits in and track them'; 'track their habits without the faff'. Report 58: 'no visual noise'; 'straight to the point of habit tracking'. Report 69 (TheFor): 19 reviewers (23.75%, mean 4.84) tried two to ten trackers first and kept this one — 'a habit-tracker refugee… looking for less product, not more'; P2: market relief from other apps, not 'Transform Your Life'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'It doesn't reward you for streaks, or show you stats, or remind you to do anything. You don't even enter goals into the app. Everything else I tried failed at one of these points… but for what I need it's perfect' — UX_NO_PRESSURE 3 (5.00); simplicity 65 (43.05%) — do not add streaks, goals, nagging or complexity. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'I've possibly tried every habit app, and keep coming back to this one' (the most-voted review, 20 votes); 'I just always end up coming back to the simplicity of Way of Life'; PR_BETTER_THAN 428 (5.51%) is said comparatively; NEG_SIMPLE 43 / NEG_POINTLESS 15 ('I can do the same with a simple tally sheet', 2★) is the accepted price of the position. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'Momentum based habit tracking feels way more realistic and helpful… than the streak focus that is everywhere else'; COMP_TRIED_MANY 4 and COMP_BEST 3, all 5.00★ — the highest-intent reviews; 'It doesn't feel stressful, like other apps'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'Others are way too expensive or overly animated and cute. This one strikes a great balance'; PRAISE_NO_GAMIFICATION 2 ('Minimal incentive to follow some arbitrary set of rules to make habits stick, leaving it up to the user instead'); a GitHub-contribution-grid identity (7 mentions at 5.00★, developers self-identify: 'As a SWE'; 'I'm a developer so I can definitely understand the GitHub feel'); U:competitive_win 27 (15.70%, 4.93★): 'Tried them all and this is by far the best'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'Nothing superfluous, aesthetic, beautiful, intuitive. What I was looking for!' (ru); 'without extra noise'; OUT_FOUND_IT 15 (17.44%) — the search ended here; ACQ_TRIED_MANY 16. Report 86 (Today): 'No frills, no fuss'; 'It doesn't give you confetti or a cookie but it helps form that path in your brain'; positioned against 'bubbly' rivals; reviewers say it is not a to-do list, calendar or workout tracker — 'Habits are different than to-dos and should be tracked differently'.

title: Do not run a paid twin app beside the free app
statement: Report 11: a separate 'Lifetime Premium' binary collected one rating in six years, ran a version behind, undercut the in-app lifetime SKU by $5 and created a second entitlement surface that plausibly fed the 'lifetime subscription… suddenly cancelled' confusion.

title: No 'wait, don't go' exit discounts or countdown timers on the paywall
statement: Report 12: a lifetime offer at 17.99 that drops to 5.99 when the user tries to close, a '90% off' timer that still grants no access, and a 10× regional price jump were described as 'gross' and 'another major red flag'; 42 reviewers used the word 'scam'. The ladder is also visible to every prospect as ten SKUs on the store page. Report 13: 'Here's one star for you. You can buy the rest at a 49% discount' — the exit-intent discount tells every full-price buyer they overpaid. Report 19: customers charged $98.50/month and $99 were offered $5 and $49 lifetime plans on cancelling; all three left 1★ and one wrote 'That is probably the real value of the service' — a save-offer at 5% of the charged price converts a pricing objection into a fraud belief. Report 24: the cancellation flow offers progressively lower prices and reviewers publish it as a trick ('keep opting for cancel, you'll eventually get $5/month') — it converts some but establishes that the list price is not the real price. Report 31: countdowns that reset — 111 reviews (2.14%) — '72 hour countdown and reset back to 72 hrs'; 'like the DFS adverts, constantly on sale'; 'ran for months'; 'I'm pretty sure this type of fake sale is actually illegal'; fake urgency backfires in a self-improvement category. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'Предложение куда-то исчезло и желание купить пропало' (the offer vanished somewhere and so did the wish to buy, 2★); 'нажимаю на купит, а кнопка не активная' — time-boxed discounts that disappear lose the sale. Report 64 (Critique AI): an exit-intent 'one-time offer' after dismissing the first paywall — 80% / 75% off, '$2/month' — splits 5×1★ / 3×5★ (PAY_DISCOUNT 9, 2.15%, mean 2.44): it produced the only clean purchase-trigger record in 419 reviews and it reads as 'Preis 80% Rabatt, wenn man Zahlung abbricht. Unglaubwürdig.'; a second paywall 8 (1.91%, mean 1.25); M7: at minimum show the billed total on the discounted offer. Report 82 (Lasting Change): descending-price urgency in the web funnel — ACQ_PRESSURE 4 ('offer at lower and lower prices until you bite'; 'pseudo last time offers').

title: If the app is paid-only or trial-gated, say so in the subtitle, first screenshot and first screen — a free download that stops after N days is 'paid-only' to the person who hits the wall
statement: Report 12: the description already said 'purchase is required to access any content' but the price label read Free — 162 reviewers (40%) wrote a 1★ review having never seen the product. A discovery and framing failure fixable at the top of the funnel. Report 25: ~7 reviewers ask for the app to be paid up front instead of 'fake-free' — an honest paid listing is preferred to a free download that gates at habit four. Report 36: 'It's not free. You can't do more than 1 habit without paying'; 'Si c'est payant mettez le là c'est caché après avoir téléchargé' — DISCLOSE 6, mean 1.67. Report 43: 'If it's a paid app then say so. You can only add 3 items before you have to upgrade' (1★); 16 'deceptive free' reviews (mean 1.25), zero after Oct 2021. Report 46: 'free forever' on the listing and website with a 3-habit tier is the angriest cluster (27, mean 1.85 — 'Potential but FREE FOREVER description is misleading'; 'IS NOT A FREE APP, it just has a free try-it-and-see mode'; 'not a one [screenshot] shows what the free version looks like'); the report's #5: remove 'free forever' and add a screenshot of the free tier. Report 50: a listing that says 5 free habits while users get 3; journal-app sync 'as advertised' that does not work; templates the listing 'promises' — fix F7. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'Пишите сразу, что ПО платное, а не встроенные покупки' — reviewers want the paid nature stated in the listing, not hidden as 'in-app purchases'. Report 60 (Mindway): 'Put the price next to your product in the App Store' — a paywalled app advertised as a free planner produced five misleading-advert reviews and five scam accusations, every one 1★. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): a free-download listing on every storefront that enumerates notifications, backup, CSV export and unlimited tabs 'with no statement of a trial, a time limit, or any feature being paid-only' — TRL_NO_DISCLOSURE 23 (15.23%, mean 1.52), 27 of 30 1★ are trial grievances; 14 reviewers write the fix: 'This is a paid app. After the free period ends you need a paid plan to keep using the service'; 'free for one week only, paid after that'; 14 propose selling it as a paid app outright; the most-voted review: 'The listing says in-app purchase, not paid app. It isn't a lie, but I can't see it as anything other than deliberate misleading to grow the user base'; §8.1 #1 state the model — free for N days, then a one-time purchase, price named — in the description and first screen. (Consolidation after report 75: title widened from 'If the app is paid-only, say so in the subtitle and first screenshot' to cover trial-gated apps; the original evidence stays in the statement.)

merged_from.old_title: If the app is paid-only, say so in the subtitle and first screenshot
merged_from.note: reports 74 and 75 attached the trial-gated shape: a listing that enumerates every feature and never the ~1-week free window (27 of 30 1★ in report 74), and a free-download listing that names subscriptions but never the habit cap (report 75); the original rule covered only outright paid-only apps

title: A pre-use hard paywall makes every purchase non-evidence-based and non-durable
statement: Report 12: no reviewer in 404 said they paid because of a feature they had seen working; purchases were made to evaluate, under an exit discount, or on the strength of the intro — and 0 of 80 self-identified payers rated 5★. What the gate protects must be able to survive inspection: 13 buyers said it was a worse version of Apple Calendar. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire followed by an immediate paywall — 'I did the whole survey and at the end I had to pay'; 'first 10 minutes of test… then it turns out you need a subscription' — every such reviewer left 1–2★ (mean 1.17). Report 49: a hard paywall before any use — 43.67% of the corpus attacks how it is sold; buyers convert on a 2am impulse, the Solo Leveling frame or a low point, and payers then average 1.92. Report 60 (Mindway): the pre-value paywall follows a mandatory onboarding questionnaire — 'it was really strange like answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away' (1★); 'Stop playing games and get to plan'; 19 blocked plus 3 interrupted (8.80% + 1.39%) are the largest upgrade barrier. Report 64 (Critique AI): only three first-person purchase accounts in 419 — a $2/month exit discount, 75% off annual, and creator trust; 'No reviewer in this corpus says they paid because of a specific feature' — 'sold on price anchoring and creator trust, not on value demonstration'; 13 self-stated payers average 1.85, 12 of 13 report a defect or shortfall, 1 of 13 unreservedly satisfied. Report 67 (Habio): the purchase path is ad → quiz → small paid trial ('€5.49 seemed like a reasonable amount to see if the app could fulfil on the promises') → immediate add-on → auto-renewal; 995 reviewers say money left their account (mean 1.05) and only 35 describe a deliberate purchase (mean 1.23); very few buy because of the product. Report 68 (Ultiself): purchases are triggered by an ad and a cheap intro plan ('I signed up for this app via an instagram ad and paid £7 for one course'; MKT_AD lift 6.26× among purchasers) and by a problem the ad sold (add-ons 10.14×), rarely by the free tracker. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): stated purchase triggers are trust from another app in the family, buying on sight from the design, a sale price, and wanting to support — never hitting the cap; 'Nobody who bought it thinks it was expensive'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): a subscription-gated app whose purchase happens on a website before the app is ever opened — 'Not one review in 175 describes choosing to subscribe to this app because of something the app does'; 14 reviewers never used, activated or downloaded it.

title: A pre-planned, structured day is the outcome ADHD and autistic users praise
statement: Report 12: 'I lose track of time, forget to do things, and never have a plan, but that girl made sure I DID have a plan' — the one narrow, consistent praised outcome (22 reviews, mean 4.95) is being told what the day looks like. Report 25: an app titled 'Routine / Planner for ADHD' models whether a habit happened, not when — per-habit clock time with a notification at that time is the biggest unshipped feature (29, mean 3.41, 17 of them 4–5★; 9.0% of the 4★ band), clustering with one-off tasks (10), every-N-minutes reminders (4), an hour-by-hour agenda view (4) and long-term goals (7); buyers who expected time structure found a checklist ('Just a to-do list app'; 'I get to see all the things I haven't done and feel bad' — a £29.99 purchaser). Whoever ships routine scheduling rather than routine checking takes the ADHD-planner positioning. Report 43: a red / yellow / green time-window timeline and multi-step timers are what ADHD users name — 'when I don't have the brain power to think it just tells me what to do next'; an adult child with autism's morning routine on timers. Report 59 (Tappsk): the one-screen day plan with habits on top is what forgetful and ADHD reviewers credit ('keeps me together with my bad ADHD'). Report 60 (Mindway): organisation and structure is the most-cited benefit (15, 6.94%, mean 4.80, 13 at 5★): 'I used to be a mess, today I'm organised' (IL); 'Now I have a regular plan' (TR); 'You plan what you're gonna do at the next day'; the ADHD reviewers credit exactly this ('helps me stay on task instead of getting distracted'). Report 85 (Habitica): 'For people with depression, like me, this app is incredible' (18 votes, the most-voted purely positive review); 'Points go in where you can see them, so you want to do it even when you're not motivated' (jp) — instant visible reward as the executive-function aid.

title: Gendered branding narrows the audience; a neutral name is already tested
statement: Report 12: four reviewers objected to a girls-only brand ('I don't think a todo app should be targeted at one certain gender'); the developer ships a gender-neutral name in es/mx, the two highest-rated storefronts in the sample — an existing A/B result to measure. Report 55: a launch-screen photo of a woman hiker (DES_SPLASH 20, 2016–2022) — 'I purchased premium. I am uninstalling due to lack of dev response to the main photo of the girl'; an issue in a NoFap context; some ask only to turn it off. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'the quiz questions are clearly directed toward men, and didn't have a nothing option' (au, 3★, one review) — consistent with the male-coded framing throughout ('looksmax', physique, 'made me more into a man'). Report 68 (Ultiself): 'not designed with women in mind at all' (NEG_INCLUSIVE 2) on a biohacker-branded app. Report 71 (MyStreaks): 'Great habit tracker, really unfortunate name' (4★, seven words, Jan 2024) — v2.61 (Apr 2024) 'Updated Name and Bug Fixes' renamed Streaking → MyStreaks; reviewers switch names exactly at the change — the one complaint demonstrably closed. Report 72 (Habit Hearts, counter-evidence): 12 reviews (4.80%, all 5★) praise an explicitly 'girly' aesthetic ('idealna dla dziewczyn'; 'all girls should have this beautiful habit tracker'), rising 2.38% → 8.11% — a gendered look that attracts its audience rather than narrowing it, on an app with a neutral name. Report 83 (Roubit): 'the gender field has an undecided option besides female and male; I found that thoughtful' (kr 5★) — PRAISE_INCLUSIVE 2.

title: Aesthetic and a polished onboarding convert; they do not retain
statement: Report 12: 17 reviewers praised the design and 11 of them rated 1–2★; nine 5★ reviews praised the narrated intro before using the product; 'The intro before you purchase seems to have more thought put into it than the actual app itself.' See also report 9's warm shell over a thin product. Report 26: Eden converts on beauty and on the absence of a subscription, fast, often before the user has evaluated the functionality — which explains both high purchase velocity and payers rating a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570): 'I bought this one a little too soon I think'. Report 49: the questionnaire and personalised 'analysis' convert the segment it fits, but fit, disciplined reviewers told they have '40% more bad habits than the average person your age' read the assessment as a sales device (13). Report 52: the look converts within days — 'Downloaded, five minutes later bought premium'; 'within 24 hrs of the trial I bought lifetime' — while cuteness praise fell 18.5% (2017) → 2.9% (2026) and calm / clean held. Report 60 (Mindway): design praise sits beside price rejection in the same sentences — 'Es ist eigentlich sehr schön gemacht und gestaltet aber einfach zu teuer'; 'It is a good app well designed but cost abit of money' — P_DESIGN has a mean of 3.00; one dissent finds the cute styling 'too bubbly… better off to be more neutral and simple', and the report says do not redesign on that one complaint. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): praise_ui_design 6 (13.33%, 4.17★) sits beside the cap-driven uninstall — 'Really clean, minimal UI and super easy to use' then 'so I ended up uninstalling'. Report 64 (Critique AI): the onboarding analysis works as a hook — a reviewer praises the personalised analysis then refuses to pay (PERSONALIZE 5, mean 4.40); a physique scan and a projected score are the free teaser before the wall. Report 72 (Habit Hearts, counter-evidence): here the aesthetic is stated as the retention mechanic — 'I am someone who needs things to be pleasing to keep doing it, and this gives me that'; 'When i usually use a routine app, i give up after a few uses as it feels like a chore. But this app … has a gorgeous layout'; OUT_MOTIV 48 (19.20%) framed as a consequence of the design; outcomes 106 (42.40%, 4.97) — the design retains when the product behind it works and the free tier lets people use it. Report 76 (Way of Life): PR_DESIGN 602 (7.75%, 4.78★) and NEG_DESIGN 70 (0.90%, 'dated or ugly', 2011 → 2023) — design praise is high but it is simplicity, not looks, that retains for 13 years. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_DESIGN 17 (23.94%) — 'cute' across four languages — carries a mean of 4.65★, below the concept theme's 4.89★, because two low-rated reviewers praise the design while complaining about something else: 'design praise is not a satisfaction proxy'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_DESIGN 71 (41.28%, 4.87★) and PRAISE_NATIVE_FEEL 11 ('looks and feels like an app made by Apple'; 'even Apple apps don't feel this good'; 'Love the adoption of Liquid Glass') — craft praise persisted at 58.5% even in the era where the mean fell to 4.02★: 'the decline is additive — the same praise, now with something attached to it'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): APP_UGLY 9 ('Very old and simple tracking app design'; 'Very weridly design app, very messy') alongside 'the app itself is well designed' — craft is contested and irrelevant next to consent. Report 83 (Roubit): PRAISE_CUTE 157 (31.40%, 4.50★) and PRAISE_DESIGN_UI 43 — cuteness converts on day one ('paid for premium immediately and don't regret it at all'; paid 'after one day') and is what remains when the app breaks (19 of 40 blank-screen reports at 4–5★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'aesthetic, beautiful, intuitive'; PRAISE_FLEXIBLE 6 (colours, icons, look — 'personalise to your taste'); design praise rides with simplicity rather than standing alone. Report 86 (Today): PR_DESIGN 460 (25.77%) appears in every star band — 10.6% of 1★ still praise the design: 'beauty does not protect the rating; it is what makes the failure worth writing about'; PR_BEST 204 at 4.78★, the highest mean of any large theme; a Good Design Award recipient calls it 'one of the most thoughtfully designed apps I have used' (2026); design praise held at 15.25% even in the abandonment era.

title: Never revoke what earlier buyers paid for when the model changes
statement: Report 13: in Aug 2017 a $3.99 one-time purchase became a subscription, unannounced in the release notes, and prior buyers were downgraded to free ('my purchase was worthless'); the mean fell 1.79 stars in nine months and no month since has been above 4.0. Subscriptions later silently expired after updates. Grandfather, always. Report 17: an abandoned one-time-purchase app relaunched as a subscription with no grandfathering, no discount and the old app left broken split one loyal base into delighted returners (4.46) and betrayed buyers (1.17); the reviewer listed the three remedies himself — grandfather, discount, or leave the old app working — none was done. Report 20: the cleanest natural experiment in the set — on 27 Jan 2021 a pay-what-you-want one-time purchase became a $39.99/year subscription, every prior buyer's entitlement was revoked and the free tier capped at 3; daily review volume went 2 → 61 → 135 at means of 1.15–1.36, 615 reviews (15.19%) describe losing a purchase, and the mean never recovered in five years (4.56 before, 1.62 after). The Feb 2021 patch was three weeks late, offered one free year instead of permanent restoration, was never announced and did not hold — revocation reports recur to Jan 2026. 'I bought your app precisely because it wasn't a subscription.' Report 23 (receiving side): an entire cohort arrived at a one-time-purchase competitor after another app revoked already-purchased premium features. Report 26: the late-2022 move from a $5–7 / €6.99 one-time unlock to $25 lifetime / $19.99 yr / $4.99 mo withdrew the unlock earlier buyers had paid for — 'the premium version I bought was taken away from me… I consider that a breach of contract' (7 in Sept–Oct 2022, recurring in 2024–25); losing what they bought is the top paid-user complaint (16.7% of explicit payers). Report 31: 189 legacy one-time / lifetime buyers (mean 1.38) found their purchase shown as 'Done Basic' after an update, reinstall or new phone, beginning at the Dec 2020 ownership change and spiking Apr 2023 — support 'told me they wouldn't honour my previous purchase', offered a free trial, or removed 'grandfathered access'; one wrote the top 'Done app review' article and then a 1★; validate receipts for every historical SKU and grandfather them automatically — worth more than any feature. Report 33: a lifetime purchase is a bet on continuity — hostile lifetime reviews are about removals, not price ('I paid for the lifetime subscription because the old app was exactly what I wanted. It never occurred to me that they would update it and actually remove things … I wish I had got the monthly subscription so I could cancel'); the 2019 switch converted a £9.99 buyer from two days earlier to one year; a lifetime model obliges the developer to migrate, not delete. Report 34: lifetime holders' only negatives are continuity — the one-time option gone after an update (Nov 2025) and a lifetime licence that 'wont be working anymore' (Jun 2026, 'False claim', 2★); 'a lifetime model obliges the developer to honour and migrate, not withdraw'. Report 42: retroactive paywalling of an installed base — 'forcing subscription, disabling buttons'; 'everything has become paid'. Report 43: a Chinese payer had to re-buy after a system reinstall (1★); 'How do I restore purchase' (1★). Report 46 (fear of it): 'Among apps that charge ¥30 for lifetime, this one wants ¥328 — I really don't dare buy it, in case it disappears'; five Chinese reviews hesitate for fear the app will 跑路. Report 48: the corpus's defining event — a paid app converted on 19 Jan 2015 to a $4.99/month subscription with a mandatory account; nine months at 2.21★ with 68.2% 1–2★ (February 1.66★, 83.9%), 92 'broken bargain' reviews (paid-then-subscription 60, forced account 25, grandfather promise broken 14 — 'Rent what you've paid for'); reversed in October 2015 (free unlimited tier) and the mean jumped to 4.62 — 'The recovery is as clear as the crash'; the theme is extinct after 2016 but still 10.7% of all one-stars. Report 52: in 2020 buyers were told their lifetime purchase is now annual; PAY_REGRESS 75 at 2.15; M1: grandfather every past entitlement explicitly ('you bought X in 2019; you keep X') — 'Honouring old purchases costs almost nothing and is the single strongest trust signal in these reviews'. Report 53: one-time buyers were pushed into a subscription — 'the VIP I bought outright has turned into a subscription? Charging twice is unreasonable' (cn, 2023); 'I had previously PAID to have full access… now they're forcing a yearly subscription' (ca, 2025); 10 in Feb–May 2026 under a new 'AppLife' plan ('all of a sudden I can't use the additional habits I created… without purchasing a $14.99 upgrade'); PAY_REGRESS 16, mean 1.50, payer lift 5.53. Report 55: 'I specifically paid for the app because it was a one-off rather than subscription, so I actually feel I should now get my money back'; 'they offered life time… the people who bought the lifetime pass are no more able to use it' (PAY_REGRESS 9, 1.33, lift 12.27). Report 57: 'I paid for the premium and now it asks for subscription??! DO NOT BUY IT' (HK, 1★, Jul 2026) — §8.2: an explicit, published grandfathering policy; 'One public DO NOT BUY IT on the storefront costs more than the subscription it was protesting'. Report 59 (Tappsk): lifetime buyers are the ones asked to pay again — BUG_PURCHASE 45 and MON_PAID_TWICE 28 of the 430 lifetime reviews; 57 lifetime reviews are 1–2★; the 2021-01 update is the largest cluster and the rest spread to 2026: 'Покупала версию «Навсегда», спустя год написали, что пора опять оплатить «навсегда» ещё раз' (bought Forever; a year later told it was time to pay forever again); 'Купила навсегда, а получается не навсегда'. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 2023 subscription switch — lifetime buyers from 2015 told they no longer have premium (1★, de/kz/cn), restore failures up to 1.55% of E6, 15 of 181 corpus 1★; grandfathering existed ('grandfathered into the new system', 5★) but was unreliable; §8.1 restore for any old App Store receipt on any device without a subscription prompt. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'Lifetime purchase doesn't work. Restore purchases doesn't work. Developer doesn't respond' (1★, 2026-01-01) — consistent with a migration failure when subscription SKUs arrived, though one review is not a mechanism; whether one-time buyers were grandfathered is an open research question (§8.7). Report 86 (Today): 'I bought the one-time version from before the subscription started' — now unable to manage habits at all (jp 1★, 2026); a one-time buyer's covers removed when photos went premium (MON_REGRESS 3).

title: No paid acquisition into an auto-converting trial in frictionless-payment markets
statement: Report 13: a Douyin campaign drove Chinese installs into a 7-day trial that opened a ¥208/yr subscription with password-free payment and no authentication step; China became 73% one-star and 51% of all involuntary-charge reviews. Where the payment rail has no friction, the app must add an explicit confirmation step. Report 67 (Habio): paid Instagram / Facebook acquisition into a web quiz and a $1 auto-converting trial across 81 storefronts; volume tripled in the web-funnel era (572 reviews, mean 1.17, scam language 51.4%). Report 68 (Ultiself): ad → web questionnaire → paid plan by card, Apple Pay or PayPal across 106 storefronts; billing complaints 63.0% of reviews in the Dec 2024 → Mar 2025 era as Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan became major sources.

title: The app must open offline — never block launch on a network call
statement: Report 13: a blocking in-app 'update in progress' migration bricked the app on launch in three waves (Nov 2019, Oct 2020 at 5.9% of that month's reviews, Sep 2025 → Aug 2026), destroyed data on reinstall ('lost almost 3 years of habit tracking') and locked out paying subscribers; 'Will not launch without internet'. Report 14: 'works fully offline' was one of two named reasons a reviewer chose this app over rivals already tried. Report 16: 'why in the world does ticking a box require connectivity!' — 9 reviews, zero 5★; a remote worker without internet for days could not use the app. Report 25: one reviewer names iCloud sync as the stuck state on first run ('shows synchronising with iCloud and nothing happens') — a first-run data path, not rendering; add a skip-setup / continue-offline path. Report 28: offline use is reported as paid and then removed; 6 complain about an internet requirement (mean 3.83). Report 46: free users cannot check off a habit offline ('ticking off habits while offline are locked behind a paywall', 7, mean 2.14) — the mechanism behind China's 'offline mode while online' cluster (16 of 17 Chinese, Sep 2019 – Apr 2020, consistent with the backend being unreachable from the mainland); the report's #14 allows offline check-off in the free tier. Report 47: a crash loop after logging in to the free backup (6, Feb 2024 – May 2025) with log-out as the only workaround; a white screen when typing a habit name (13, 2020–24). Report 53: in mainland China the launch screen hangs for seconds to 10+ minutes from build 2.8.0 (Dec 2022) through Aug 2026 — BUG_LAUNCH 30 of cn's 273 (10.99%); 'with a network connection it won't open; it only works offline' points at a blocking network call (analytics, paywall or ad SDK slow or blocked in China); F5: test cold start with no network and with blocked endpoints. Report 83 (Roubit): BUG_LAUNCH_LOAD 26 (5.20%, 2.85★; US 11.5%: 'i have never been able to use it because it does not load'; 'it just infinitely loads. Unusable.'); BUG_UPDATE_LOOP 7 — §8.2 instrument install → home screen (room loading, routine fetch, forced-update check) and fail open: show routines when the room or store cannot load; 'never block the app on an update that the App Store does not yet offer'. Report 85 (Habitica): NEG_OFFLINE 55 (1.60%) and BUG_SERVER 126 (3.66%) — a server-dependent client that cannot open or tick tasks during outages (2023-09-16: 20 reviews in a day, 17 server errors); NEG_CHINA_NET 16 unreachable from mainland China without a VPN ('翻墙连接也不行' — even using a VPN does not work).

title: Public review replies answer the specific complaint — never canned, never argue price, never press a reviewer to change the rating
statement: Report 13: copy-paste replies restating Apple's cancellation instructions under reviews had a mean of 1.40 with zero 5★, and multiple reviewers edited their rating downward afterwards ('If you're just going to copy-paste an answer again, don't leave one at all'). Report 25: 'the developer preferred to argue about what I could see on my end' — an argumentative support reply ended a trial. Report 31: a support reply 'full of emojis' offered a free trial instead of honouring a purchase; a public developer response was edited after the fact. [Merged from C260: Report 46: 6 reviews (0.28%, mean 1.33, all 2021 or later, five in 2024–26) say a public developer reply was rude or defensive — 'snarky remarks about working for free and making an overpriced app isn't the way to do it'; 'developer takes any criticism with such a nasty attitude'; 'After reading developer's response I am degrading rating to 1 star from 2… 5/5 rating for app but 0/5 for your behaviour' (13298363427) — and 2 say the developer pressed them to change their review ('the developer keeps contacting me to pressure me into changing my review', 11709301622). Every one of these reviews went from 'too expensive' to 'and the developer is hostile', a reputational cost no pricing change recovers, while 53 reviews (mean 4.94) praise the same developer's private support. The report's zero-cost fix: thank, state the free tier and lifetime option factually, never argue value, never ask for a rating change.] Report 60 (Mindway): five explicit warn-offs ('Don't waste your money'; 'Don't ever download this app'; 'Don't download if you need for a routine'), all 1★, remain visible on the listing at the point of decision — an upgrade barrier the report counts alongside billing trust damage. Report 67 (Habio): a templated public developer reply under reviews is mentioned by 19 reviewers; §8.6: no identical public replies. Report 71 (MyStreaks): a public developer reply defending the cap as good for users drew 'Comment from creator that it encourages people to keep it simple? 🙄' in a 1★; §8.1 #4: retire that defence — 'asymmetric downside, and it is free to stop'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): public developer replies on reviews are read as PR — SUP_RESPONSE_FACADE 4: 'The responses on each of these reviews from the company is a facade, and for public appeal only… I have no doubt you will paste it below to seem as though you care'; 'Addendum to developer response: they're full of it… they've ignored my emails'; four reviewers who received a reply edited their review, all hostile, none more positive; the one documented remediation (a disclaimer added beneath the terms consent after an email exchange) came with a denial that it was ever missing, contradicted by the reviewer's screenshots.

merged_from.title: Never argue price in a public review reply, and never ask a reviewer to change their rating
merged_from.note: C260 (report 46: rude or price-defending public replies and pressure to change a rating) and C189 (reports 13, 25, 31, 43: copy-paste and argumentative replies) are one rule about how a developer responds in public; both lower ratings after the reply

title: No weekly billing tier
statement: Report 13: weekly billing introduced in 2024 ($3.99, €6, R$29.90, ₽499 per week) drew the corpus's most hostile pricing language — 'insane', 'immoral', 'Per week! I didn't even test it' — and price complaints rose to 26.7% of 2025 reviews. Report 60 (Mindway): weekly pricing reads as expensive — $7/week and €8/week both cited with outrage ('8€/WOCHE… Frech'), and the annual is chosen to escape the weekly; E3: offer a cheap one-time purchase or a low monthly tier alongside the weekly — nobody objects to paying something (M_COST_NOTED 3 at 4.33★).

title: Never shrink a tier someone already holds — a paid tier's limits, or free capacity a user has already filled
statement: Report 16: Pro was capped at 3 habits, then 6, for 29 months; a cap on the paid tier has no monetisation function (there is no higher tier to drive to) and two of three buyers who paid specifically to escape the free cap hit the next one and rated 3★ — 'A paid user pays $40/year just to create only 6 habits simultaneously?' Report 48: 23 users who built history on 10 or 7 free trackers found the cap shrunk under them (mean 2.22) — retroactive reduction lands on the longest-tenured users; fix #2: never reduce existing users' free capacity. Report 50: grandfather existing free users at 5 — the two cap-cut reviews describe loss, not a low starting cap; experiment: grandfather-vs-migrate. (Consolidation after report 50: the title was widened from 'Never cap the tier someone has already paid for' because the Report 48 and Report 50 evidence is free users losing capacity they had already filled — grandfathering is the fix in both.) Report 59 (Tappsk): the 2021-01 cut shrank free capacity users had already filled — habits removed from the free tier for existing users and a 20-task cap on lists people were using; 2021-01 was the busiest month of the corpus (372 reviews) and 2021-03 the lowest-rated (4.19★). Report 65 (Rabit): capping the free tier after years of generous use drove the E1/E2 cohort out — a user since 2020 uninstalled in 2023 ('antes era mejor'), another had recommended it to about 30 people ('ate eles se importarem mais em ganhar dinheiro que ajudar os outros'); COMP_WORSE 11 (mean 2.09), all Dec 2022 or later — 'The competitive position was not lost to a competitor's feature. It was given away'. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the reported free allowance shrank from 2 to 1 streak between Feb and Nov 2024 while the release notes show 'improved subscriptions' and 'Fix subscription bug'; a 4★ on the 1-streak tier pre-announces churn: 'I like this app but if I find a better one I'll definitely switch'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): cutting the free allowance from 3 to 1 over Christmas 2024 produced 13 of the app's 20 lifetime 1–2★ reviews in six weeks, then was quietly reverted; two reviewers independently concluded 'it should just be a paid app'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): users of a year or more hit the sudden paywall — one bought at once and asked the app not be shut down; others 'had been thinking I might as well pay' and lost the desire to — 'Amazing how much one attitude from the developer changes how you feel' (4/6 helpful). Report 83 (Roubit): the free cap has been moved repeatedly — a 150-record cap in 2021 ('it's like don't use it unless you pay'), 8 routines for most of the window, 9 in 2023-02, 4 in 2025-02 — each move a separate grievance (FREE_LIMIT_ROUTINES 12, a 1★ 'I'll just use another app'). Report 86 (Today): the free tier was narrowed back from three (or five) habits to one in ~2022 and 'the complaint came back with it' — 'I understood the free version allowed up to 3' (pe 1★); premium photo covers were also moved behind payment 'and completely took everything i had on my profile off to do so' (MON_REGRESS 3).

merged_from.old_title: Never cap the tier someone has already paid for
merged_from.note: reports 48 and 50 attached retroactive free-cap reductions (10 → 7 → 3; 5 → 3) to this point; the evidence is about taking back capacity already in use, paid or free — cap size itself stays in C007, slot reuse in C219

title: A trial must end in a usable free tier, not a cliff
statement: Report 16: a well-liked no-card 28-day trial that dropped to a one-habit tier read as a bait-and-switch — 'it encourages people to start habits and continue them for three weeks and then hits you with a steep bill' — and was the fastest-growing negative (2.4% → 7.2%). Taper, warn earlier and in-app, or keep the streak read-only.

title: When a trial or subscription ends, the user lands on a usable free tier with read-only history — never a cliff
statement: Report 16: a cancelled payer could not edit, view or even complete the one habit the free tier allows — 'It's my habit for walking my dog, who is recently deceased… I guess the app is bricked for me now.' A lapsed subscriber with read-only history is a resubscription candidate; one whose data is hostage is a permanent loss. Report 16 (trial side): a well-liked no-card 28-day trial that dropped to a one-habit tier read as a bait-and-switch — 'it encourages people to start habits and continue them for three weeks and then hits you with a steep bill' — and was the fastest-growing negative (2.4% → 7.2%). Taper, warn earlier and in-app, or keep the streak read-only. Report 60 (Mindway): with a free tier of 1–3 tasks there is no usable free tier to land on — a lapsed or refused subscriber has nowhere to go but the wall. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): a free-tier data reset after a month, unexplained — if free data expires, it must say so. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar, 151 reviews): the clearest cost of the cliff — at the end of an undisclosed ~1-week free window the app stops entirely ('after a week you can't even tap'; TRL_SUDDEN_LOCKOUT 20, mean 1.30) and read access to existing records is locked (TRL_DATA_HOSTAGE 6, mean 1.17 — 'the angriest theme'; 人質 'hostage' in two reviews and a title: 'holds the records you've built up hostage and presses you to pay'); the app is used for medication adherence and a locked-out user wrote 'I never thought it would go paid — I wish I'd written down what I'd been taking'; §8.1 #3 'Never lock read access to existing records. Let expired users read, scroll and export their history forever; gate only new entry and premium features' — the report's single highest-leverage change; #4 unconditional CSV export at trial end — 'A user who leaves with their data does not write scam'.

merged_from.title: A trial must end in a usable free tier, not a cliff
merged_from.note: C192 (trial ends in a cliff) and C193 (lapsed subscriber's data held hostage) describe one transition rule from two entry points

title: Do not paywall content the user already bought elsewhere
statement: Report 16: the daily lessons and articles restate the Atomic Habits book; paywalling them was the packaging decision reviewers found hardest to forgive ('I already read the book which only cost me $15 one time') and praise for the content fell 6.8% → 1.2% once it went behind the wall. Content free, slots paid was the corpus's proposal.

title: Premium pricing on a trust-based personal brand spends the brand
statement: Report 16: $120/yr on the official Atomic Habits app produced the lowest-rated theme in the corpus — personal attacks on James Clear ('How to ruin your brand overnight'; 'changed my view of James') — plus 69 'cash grab / greedy / predatory' reviews with zero 5★; the only negative theme still growing in 2026. Report 24: Duke University / Dan Ariely / behavioural-science framing (736, mean 3.865; 1.77% of 5★) is thrown back the moment trust breaks — 'they use behavioural science to help you make positive change, but also to get you to subscribe'; 'discredited for falsifying results… I no longer trust this app'; a credibility asset raises the expected standard of conduct.

title: A subscription is a promise of continued delivery — back it with a visible cadence
statement: Report 17: an app relaunched on a subscription went 3.5 years without a release while still charging; four of its last six reviews were about abandonment and the one paying 3★ stated the deal plainly — 'If we can get iPad and watch apps along with more regular debugging, I will keep paying. Otherwise, I am switching to Blocos.' Subscribers believe they are funding development; when it stops, the subscription has no story, and a 'lifetime' tier sold against a dormant build compounds the grievance. Report 20: an annual subscription was charged for seven years against a product that shipped nothing new; the 4★ band told the developer exactly what would make it a 5 and almost none of it was built. Report 24: repetitive coaching content (103, mean 2.660) in a content subscription. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' — the subscription came with removals, lag and no visible new delivery. Report 41: a German reviewer chose the subscription over lifetime deliberately — 'I want the app to still work in 3 years'. Report 55: 'It's not like a yoga or meditation app, which is constantly adding new videos/content, so why a yearly fee?!?' — an annual fee reads as a promise of ongoing development, and reviewers measured the app by its update log; M3: price the subscription only on features that work. Report 57: 2★ reviews concentrate the oldest users hit by silent tier changes (long_tenure_user 10.3% vs 2.95%). Report 59 (Tappsk): stagnation is the dominant criticism of the latest era — 'nothing changes' (NEG_DEV_PROMISE 1.1%) alongside subscriptions still being sold. Report 60 (Mindway): benefit claims (habit outcome, motivation, wellbeing) peak in the burst period and vanish to zero in the 14-review tail while paywall complaints rise to 28.57% — 'the corpus's least comfortable pattern' for a subscription product. Report 76 (Way of Life): E6 subscription-era reviewers praise 'steady updates' (PR_UPDATE 5.1% of E6, PR_DEV 6.7%) — the visible cadence is what keeps veterans on side while the subscription objection runs underneath.

title: Shift the whole day's schedule at once (global schedule shift)
statement: Report 17: 'there is no other app that allows you to easily globally shift a schedule, rather than moving all tasks individually… invaluable for my erratic work and sleep schedule… jet lag' — named as the one capability no competitor matches, and absent from the store listing. Single source, high value.

title: Edit one instance of a repeating block without changing the series; a slipped block pushes the ones after it
statement: Report 17: two independent 4★ users — 'I can only change ALL workout blocks in the sequence for today and everyday going forward'; adding ten minutes to a block made the next one overlap 'rather than being pushed to 7:16am'. A time-blocking app whose blocks cannot absorb a real day's slippage fails when most needed; 'If these two features are added it is definitely 5⭐️.'

title: System calendar integration — see appointments inside the plan
statement: Report 17: calendar integration existed in the predecessor, was removed at relaunch ('I loved seeing my appointments, too'), and four years later is the single feature keeping the most recent payer from switching to a competitor. Reports 12 and 13 also carry calendar-integration requests. Report 41: calendar view / calendar integration requested by 7. Report 50: Apple / Google Calendar integration requested by 3 (4.67). Report 52: calendar integration requested (41, weak).

title: Never meter the completion action — a free cap may limit habits, never check-offs
statement: Report 18: the free tier advertised 10 habits but ticking a habit consumed a 14-per-week memo quota (two check-offs a day), so tapping 'complete' produced a purchase sheet; 139 reviews (6.79%, mean 2.32★, 19.6% of all 1★) and five years of 'stops working on day 3/5/6/10'. A habit tracker that refuses to record a completion in the first week demonstrates that it does not work, to a user deciding whether it works — 'I was 90% ready to buy… I just lost all feeling for it and deleted it.' Report 25: from Nov 2025 editing an existing habit — including the ones onboarding created — was reported as paid; five 1–2★ reviews, zero before that date; 'never gate editing of habits the onboarding created'. Report 33: a free-tier cap of ~15 check-ins per week (Oct 2020 → 2024) drew 29 reviews at mean 2.00 — the worst-rated monetisation mechanism, 4.2% of E3 — and punished the most engaged free users ('three habits is reasonable. The problem … I can't check into those habits more than 15 times a week'; 'limiting the number of check ins per week ruins the whole point').

title: A user-set partial-completion threshold — a 'good day' below 100%
statement: Report 18: a traffic-light day status that turns green at a user-chosen ~60–80% is the most-articulated praise in a 2,048-review corpus (92 reviews at 4.24★; explicit partial-completion praise at 4.80★): 'with percentage apps you aim for 100 and suffer; here you switch to "green is good enough"'; 'a 60% check feels like 100% achievement'; 'I never feel guilted or pressured'. Rest / postpone / skip options sit alongside it. Some users want it harder (a must-do habit that gates the light, a 90% threshold) — so the threshold is a setting, not a constant. Report 23: a 6-of-8 day rendered as ✗ is named as demotivating and the reason people keep a second app; render a partial ring, not a failure mark. Report 26: partial completion earns nothing (all-or-nothing garden growth, 20 reviews, mean 2.80); ship partial credit as a setting, with full completion still rewarded more — the existing 'no wither' option is the precedent. Report 41: a daily completion percentage ring with partial credit is the quiet differentiator (40, mean 4.67) — 'as someone who suffers from perfectionism and binary thinking… you're never thinking about the cliff edge of losing a streak… made this a thing i actually use and bought over the hundreds of habit apps i browsed'; 'a meh day means about 70%— C work, but a better baseline'; two want weighted habits, one dislikes 'out of 100%'.

title: A light social layer that is explicitly not a social network
statement: Report 18: seeing other users' routines, copying them and sending cheer messages was praised by 66 reviewers (3.22%, mean 4.45★) precisely because 'it isn't like SNS'; a teacher chose the app over rivals because its social features are lighter, and following a friend was described as a shared exchange diary. Very strong only in Korea (3.69%); emerging elsewhere. Report 24: Circles — an in-app feed with comments and writing prompts — runs at mean 3.897 (0.85%), neither a driver nor a grievance. Report 52: a minority asks for accountability buddies (74, weak) against a larger 'never add social' group (120). Report 58: following friends requested once alongside cross-device use. Report 64 (Critique AI): a community feed is 'priceless' to one payer, 'a probably fake community page' to another, and over-moderated to a third (R5: loosen comment moderation); only paying reviewers describe it. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the social layer is the most-praised surface of a streak tracker — community 8 (25.0%, 4.88), positive social union 11 (34.4%, 4.91): 'I love connecting with other Streakers on the community page'; 'it's fun to see other family member streaks and their progress (and we even have competitions sometimes too)'; 'The future of social media' — and thin to two 4★ ('the social feature needs some love'; 'a small community but still great'); community praise went quiet after mid-2023 (8 in E1, 1 in E2), so whether it retains or only delights is untested. Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_SOCIAL 23 (0.30%, 4.30★, 2013 → 2026) 'share with friends'; USE_SOCIAL 4; NEG_SOCIAL 1 'unwanted social sharing'. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): REQ_SOCIAL 1 (3★) — to see other people's progress. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): REQ_STREAK_SHARE 1; zero social/leaderboard requests in 172 reviews. Report 83 (Roubit): REQ_SOCIAL 5 ('please add the ability to msg your friends and give them gifts'); a friend feature shipped in January 2026; SOCIAL_WITH_FRIENDS 10; REFERRAL_CODE 3. Report 84 (HabitGrid): REQ_SOCIAL 1 (shared habits with friends); §8.8 do not prioritise. Report 85 (Habitica): after guilds and the tavern were removed the social requests are small and safe — friend lists, cheering between party members, a party finder for solo players; NEG_COMMUNITY 20 (rude or controlling moderators and party members) shows the moderation cost of the larger version.

title: Onboarding lets the user author their own routine first — suggested plans, surveys and pledges are optional
statement: Report 18: the lowest-rated theme (34 reviews, mean 2.03★) was an onboarding that ran a long survey, built the routine for the user, assumed a 9-to-5 weekday life, demanded a signed pledge and then showed the paywall — 'I wanted to create my own routine not have you suggest one for me. Hence the name of your app. MY routine not your routine'; 'an app that wants to turn you into a very ordinary machine'. Shift workers, night workers and parents were excluded before they reached the product. Report 24: the forced first habit ('drink water', gated three days, then breakfast) is the concrete example inside every larger personalisation complaint; the fix is an 'I already do this' branch, keeping the default. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire suggests starter habits (free) — and from Nov 2025 those starter habits could not be edited without paying. Report 26: onboarding offers preset-only habits and custom habits could not be created (8 verified, mean 2.50). Report 49: cannot add own tasks 80 and cannot edit the generated programme 70 are the top themes of the 3★ and 4★ bands (9.43% / 15.09% among payers) — 'the design is excellent, the idea is right, and I cannot make it fit my life'; custom tasks shipped mid-2025 cut 'cannot add' 10.2% → 1.0%; still needed: week-by-week edits, swapping running, entering existing fitness. Report 60 (Mindway): a mandatory onboarding questionnaire followed immediately by the paywall ('answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away'; 'Stop playing games and get to plan') and preset packs the user must delete rather than a routine they author; one reviewer asks for '3 complete day schedules' to pick from so 'adding and subtracting would not be so overwhelming'. Report 67 (Habio): preset routines only — 'What if I want the routine to include a workout but not meditation?'; REQ_CUSTOM_ROUTINE 18 and NEG_NO_CUSTOM_HABIT 9, 'the most consistent product request from people who got past the paywall'; forced intentions / rewards / reflections steps (7). Report 82 (Lasting Change): 'The ads made it seem like you could track whatever habits you wanted, but you in fact can not add your own habits to the daily activities' (APP_NOT_AS_ADVERTISED 3; REQ_OWN_HABITS 1) — while four other reviewers praise custom trackers, so the capability is either gated or undiscoverable.

title: Never destroy user work at the paywall
statement: Report 18: two users each spent an hour building routines, were asked to pay to save them, and lost the work anyway. Work the user has already done is never the hostage of a purchase sheet — save it, then ask. (The labelling half of the original point — 'reviewers cannot tell what they are buying' — lives on C110 and C218, to which the same cards are attached.) Report 53: reviewers over the free limit hit the paywall when editing an existing habit. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): months of check-ins and memos made unreadable at the paywall; setup effort framed as deliberate sunk cost (TRL_WASTED_SETUP 4, all 1★).

merged_from.old_title: Never destroy user work at the paywall; label paid features before they are used
merged_from.note: the original title bundled 'label paid features before use', which duplicates C110 (legible free/paid boundary) and C218 (listing truth); narrowed to the one rule no other point carries

title: Aggregated, searchable journal / diary across days
statement: Report 18: people wrote daily reflections for years and could read them back only one date at a time; diary/memo aggregation, a calendar of entries and search was the highest-rated request theme in the corpus (22 reviews, mean 4.68★) and the reason a lifetime buyer switched to a competitor. Report 53: a list of all notes, and notes on the calendar (47-vote jp review). Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_NOTES_VIEW 13 — search / view notes across days (2013 → 2026).

title: Swappable day templates / routine modes for irregular schedules
statement: Report 18: shift-work / variable-day routine profiles were a meaningful request (31, 4.03★) from 2022; 'routine modes' shipped Dec 2025 as Pro and won back a churned subscriber ('神✨'; a nurse: 'rain in a drought') but shipped buggy — switching a mode rewrote past days, modes applied forward-only, edits did not persist, and the feature was buried in Settings.

title: Let users hide surfaces they don't use — tabs, social, recommendations, streaks
statement: Report 18: 'UI complexity / can't find things' was the largest negative theme by count (149, 7.28%) and high-priority in all three eligible storefronts (KR 6.75%, JP 10.76%, US 8.33%), rising as features accumulated; an ADHD reviewer asked to hide social, recommendations, to-do, diary and streaks; another asked the developer explicitly not to add more. Report 24: retained users ask for a 'just my routine' mode — coaching, community, discovery and cross-app promotion below the fold or hidden. Report 33: hide friends, challenges and journal until enabled — 'simple mode' defaults. Report 36: daily motivational messages loved by 13 (all 5★) and disliked by 4 ('strangely negative — talking about destruction or a kind of wasteland'; 'Wish I could disable those') — make them switchable, don't rewrite them. Report 43: the report's #2 fix is a settings toggle for the skip-journal popup and calendar header introduced in the redesign — 'should have option to TURN OFF'. Report 52: the 2026 'habit ball' collection could not be hidden. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): UX_FOCUS_TAB_POINTLESS 1 — a tab the reviewer does not use and cannot hide. Report 83 (Roubit): 'I wish I could hide the room-decorating tab' (FEATURE_BLOAT 3); one user left for a more minimal app — 'I've decided to leave the bunny behind'; ONBOARDING_LONG 1 ('endless questions and promotions').

title: Photo / media / URL attached to a habit, memo or diary entry
statement: Report 18: ~25 reviews across KR and JP asked to attach a photo, media or link to a habit, memo or diary entry. Report 47: a photo attached to each check-in ('motivation photos' per habit) is a purchase trigger and part of the named differentiator; attaching a photo crashed the app in January 2021 (10 reviews in 16 days); photo multi-select shipped within a week of the request. Report 52: photos in check-in logs and notes are 'the most repeated single ask' within the largest request theme — 'please add photos to check-ins!! I really want photos!!!' (2017 → 2025). Report 57: photo attachment shipped but capped at 3 even with Premium (9 request more). Report 59 (Tappsk): U_ATTACH_REQ 223 (1.47%) — REQ_PHOTO 124, REQ_NOTES 106 ('ГДЕ ПРИКРЕПИТЬ ФОТО' — WHERE DO I ATTACH A PHOTO); one of the requests that never stops across eight years. Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_PHOTO 9 (4.67★) — photos in notes. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): REQ_PHOTO 1 (4★). Report 83 (Roubit): photos in the diary requested (REQ_DIARY_FEATURES 10).

title: No sign-up wall before first use
statement: Report 18: 'sign-up / login required or broken' was a very strong signal (70, 3.42%, mean 3.13★); a sign-up wall before any trial was a ranked purchase barrier, and Japan's form demanded e-mail, phone and real name before the product was visible. Distinct from having an account system: the account should be offered when there is something to protect. Report 27: 'no account required' is praised as a feature (4, mean 5.00 — 'so many habit apps are expensive and require an account'; 'All this without asking for my personal details') and the listing's no-data-collection label is part of the positioning; a required account 'rules out ad-funded or data-funded models'. Report 29: 'the fact I didn't even have to list my email sold me' — do not require an account; adding one for billing has its own cost. Report 41: 'No account or login is needed' is a reason to choose the app; one payer cancelled rather than enable iCloud. Report 48: 39 reviews (1.64) objected to a forced account on a local tracker in 2015–18; the complaint ended when iCloud sync replaced the account. Report 50: sign-in required before first use, Apple or Google only (see C035). Report 55: a registration screen first; F6 — never block first use. Report 56: 'I tried a couple of them on the App Store and hated them immediately. They usually ask 20 questions just to get started'; 'no sign-in wall' named as why it stuck. Report 58: §8.5 do not require an account to start. Report 76 (Way of Life): 16 years with no account — PR_PRIVACY 12 'local data, no account'; the cost is data loss on phone change (C034) rather than a sign-up complaint. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): no account, no login wall — zero complaints and one request for an account (as a sync/backup path). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): no account, no login ('there's no subscription or sign in/up', 5★); PRAISE_NO_ACCOUNT 1; zero forced-account complaints; iCloud sync without an account. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the web purchase and the app account are two systems that disagree about who the customer is (DEF_LOGIN 14) — an account is required and it is the reliability failure. Report 85 (Habitica): an account is mandatory and sign-up is the harshest failure in the corpus (BUG_SIGNUP 139 at 1.55★); NEG_FB_LOGIN 18 when the rebuilt app launched without Facebook login. Report 86 (Today): no account, no login, no server sync for ten years — praised ('no account') and blamed in equal measure; REQ_ACCOUNT 3 arrive only from users who lost data; §8.4 'optional account-based sync — not mandatory'.

title: Bill App Store users through the App Store — never route them to an off-store subscription the app cannot show or cancel
statement: Report 19: the app was the front door to a web-billed subscription that did not appear in Apple's subscription list, carried non-refundable website terms, and could be cancelled only by email; 18 of 105 reviewers (17.14%) described the consequence, 19 were charged after cancelling, 19 were charged with no subscription they recognised, and 60 distinct reviews flowed from a customer who could not see or stop their own plan. If a web funnel must exist, the app shows the active plan, price, next charge date and a working cancel button. Report 24 (43,469 reviews): the largest theme in the corpus — 5,791 core billing disputes (13.32%, mean 1.110, 94.2% 1★; 52.4% of all 1★; 38% of 2024–26) — follows mechanically from selling the subscription through a web checkout (Chargebee; 'Fabulous SAS' on statements): it is invisible in Apple Subscriptions, cancelling in the App Store does nothing, Apple cannot refund it, and the user is routed to a 250-character web form with no phone; 212 escalated to their bank, the BBB, the FTC or a lawyer. The failure is dated — quarterly rate 5.4% (2023Q1) → 12.0% (Q4) → 33.1% (2024Q4) → ~50% from 2025Q2 — and an earlier 2018–19 episode was fixed in one month (Dec 2019: 12.7% → 2.6%, mean 2.884 → 4.206), so it is recoverable. Reviews that mention money average 2.006; those that do not, 4.356. Report 33: web purchases through Paddle did not unlock the iPhone (18 days; 6+ weeks) and had no in-app cancel; refunds were routed to Apple and then refused ('denied a refund due to the company's arrangement with Apple'). Report 59 (Tappsk): the one case where off-store billing was forced (App Store payments blocked for Russian users from 2022-03) shows the cost: the direct-card route is praised by those who wanted to pay (54 of 74 payment-route reviews are 5★) but produces charges after deletion and a subscription the phone cannot show or cancel ('После отмены подписки приложение каждый раз пытается списать с карты средства' — after cancelling, the app keeps trying to charge the card) — if an off-store route is unavoidable, it needs in-app cancellation and bounded retries ([[C232]]). Report 67 (Habio): a web quiz funnel from Instagram / Facebook ads sold subscriptions billed off-store — MON_OFFSTORE 137 (6.68%) 'not displayed in the AppStore and the receipt comes directly from Habio'; 'even after you delete the app you will still be charged $50 every 180 days unless you redownload the app and cancel through there'; MON_WEB_FUNNEL 30 paid on the website before installing; the listing still says payment is 'charged to iTunes Account' and cancellable in Account Settings; web purchases were not linked to app accounts so buyers could not restore ('couldn't find any purchase history'); U_CANCEL_TRAP 597 (29.11%, mean 1.03); off-store complaints 13.81% of the 2023-07 → 2024-02 era. Report 68 (Ultiself): the same chain across 87 storefronts — purchase on a website or in-funnel Apple Pay / PayPal / card → not in Apple's subscription list → the in-app 'Manage subscription' button opens Apple's list anyway (BUG_MANAGE_SUB 60, from 2025-03-14: 'button directs to the App Store, but the actual subscription is handled outside via their website, to which access is blocked') → email-only cancellation → retention offers or silence → the charge recurs; MON_WEB_BILLING 303 (6.72%), 26.3% of Belarus reviews (two of its reviews are the most-voted complaints: 'DOES NOT show their active subscription'); U_BILLING_COMPLAINT 1,434 (31.79%, mean 1.12) in 88.2% of 1–2★; the listing says only 'charged to your iTunes account… Monthly and Yearly'; §8.1: route Manage subscription to wherever the subscription is billed and add in-app cancellation for web subscriptions. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'This is not a Free app with in-app purchases. This is a $7 app' (1★) — the free listing with a 3-item cap is read as a mislabelled paid app by some. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the subscription is sold on the developer's website and charged to card / PayPal / bank — the listing's own metadata reads hasInAppPurchases: false while its description says 'Payment is charged to your App Store account'; a reviewer quotes the seller's terms: 'subscriptions will not appear on apple or google if purchased through the website'; consequences — it cannot be cancelled in iOS Settings (CANCEL_NO_PATH 27, 15.43%), Apple cannot refund it (36 refusals, zero Apple refunds), 17 discovered the charge from a bank statement, 7 blocked their card or closed the account, 16 escalated to a chargeback, FTC, FCC, BBB or trading standards; 'Apple thankfully denied all three of their attempts'.

title: No second, separately-cancelled add-on subscription
statement: Report 19: an e-book/PDF plan at $17–$45/month was enrolled on top of the programme subscription with its own cancellation path; 11 of 105 (10.48%) across five storefronts described it, and two reviewers on two continents reported the same asymmetry — the main plan cancels, the add-on does not. Collapse add-ons into the main plan or delete them. Report 24: 324 reviews (0.75%, mean 1.398) describe being enrolled in a multi-app bundle (Clarify, Shape, Sphere…) during onboarding through near-identical full-screen offers whose decline is a small corner 'skip'; the $39.99 + $29.99 same-day pair is the signature in hundreds of 2024–26 reviews, each subscription must be cancelled separately, and 338 report a charge with no consent at all (mean 1.047, the lowest in the corpus). Bundle complaints went 0.30% → 0.06% → 0.17% → 2.62% across eras.

title: No conditional refunds — no proof-of-use requirement, and an advertised guarantee is honoured on request
statement: Report 19: refunds were refused for 25 of 105 (23.81%); a 'prove 14 consecutive days of use' condition (6), a 30-day money-back guarantee that was advertised and then denied (3 — all three bought because of it), and retention bots answering refund requests (5) turned refusal into fraud allegations, chargebacks and an FTC report. A guarantee you will not honour is a fraud allegation you have pre-purchased; the refund is cheaper than the dispute. Report 24: refund refusals (968, 2.23%, mean 1.070) quote near-verbatim T&C clauses across years and markets — 'the set-up fee for the trial period is non-refundable' and 'unless cancelled at least 24 hours before the renewal date'; 227 reviewers hold an e-mail or screenshot confirming cancellation and were charged anyway. When a refund is actually reached it works and reviewers upgrade in place (1★ → 4★), so the failure is reaching it. Report 30: 'quise cancelar suscripción… no puedo recuperar el dinero' — a refund dead end for an accidental subscription. Report 33: refunds routed to Apple, then refused — a child's 598 RMB refused twice; 45 refund reviews (mean 2.16), 13 from Korea. Report 43: a refund refused inside the EU 14-day withdrawal period (DE, 1★). Report 48: refund requests 23 at mean 1.04★ — the lowest-mean theme in the corpus with n > 10. Report 49: a marketed '66-day money-back guarantee' cited 13 times (1.85) with undisclosed conditions (66 logged days at ≥ 50% completion — 'Very misleading'), met conditions and no refund, a confirmed PayPal transfer that never arrived, 'nowhere to be found'; 21 of 36 refund requests refused or ignored (1.14) — 'a marketing promise generating one-star reviews at a higher rate than having no promise would'. Report 54: every refund request (5, all 1★) was caused by a failed entitlement, not dissatisfaction with the feature set. Report 55: refund requests 19 (1.11), 17 from payers, 9 from the UK. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_REFUND 159 (1.05%, 1.94★) — refunds reported granted ('Все вернули! Оперативно') and refused ('техподдержка не видит причины возврата' — support sees no reason for a refund; 'I was rejected to refund of 20$ annual subscription'). Report 60 (Mindway): four refund requests, all 1★, all US, all after an annual charge — refused ('NO EXCEPTIONS OF A REFUND'), no route found, 'this needs to be reported', 'I wish I could get my money back'. Report 64 (Critique AI): a parent bought for a 12-year-old found it too advanced and asked for a refund in a review; 'would not let me have my money back' after a 'cancel anytime' promise. Report 67 (Habio): MON_REFUND_DENIED 242 (11.80%, mean 1.01); an advertised money-back guarantee cited as not honoured by 42 (2.05%) — 'Money back policy requires that you use the product for 21 days consecutively!'; 10 invoke the EU 14-day withdrawal right; refunds granted in 10 (mean 2.80), 3 of them via the bank or PayPal rather than the developer. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): a buyer who trusted the sister apps, disliked this one and was refused a refund (2★); an accidental purchase from a sale pop-up — 'If there's a way to get my money back please let me know😭. I'm to tight for money'. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_REFUND 9 (0.12%, mean 1.89★) — drivers are a purchase that did not work, an unexpected subscription charge, or a product that did not meet the price ('got my money back', ch 1★); purchaser churn 3 of 349 (0.9%). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): zero refund and zero cancellation mentions in six languages — 'read as unobserved, not absent'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): zero refunds, cancellations or renewals reported in 172 reviews; one refund threat resolved by its own later edit. Report 82 (Lasting Change): REFUND_REFUSED 36 (20.57%, every one 1★), 12 shielded by pointing at the T&Cs or asserting the service was delivered ('no refunds as we delivered the service — which is simply not true'; 'they don't issue out refunds unless it's their fault directly'); several asked for a refund on the same day as the charge and were refused; one refund obtained 'after insisting' — and that reviewer was then charged 50€ months later; §8.5 experiment: refund any charge disputed shortly after renewal or after a documented cancellation, and measure the 1★ rate — 'the current policy produces the most-repeated public warning'.

title: If you position on ADHD or executive-function help, cancellation must be the easiest flow in the product
statement: Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) accused the product of targeting people with ADHD because they will forget to cancel — 'preying on ADHDers they know may not remember to cancel'; friction a neurotypical user calls annoying this audience calls predatory, because the marketing itself asserts they cannot complete multi-step tasks. The ADHD positioning and a retention funnel are incompatible; six reviewers escalated to banks, card networks and the FTC. Report 24: an app whose subtitle is 'ADHD Help' has ADHD users as its angriest segment (933, mean 2.747, 54.2% 1–2★) and 201 of them (mean 1.159) say the cancellation design exploits the condition — 'they know because of your poor executive function that you won't take the extra effort to find the cancel button'; the segment grew 30× across eras (0.20% → 6.01%) as the marketing worked, and the outcome got worse. Either build for the condition or stop claiming it. Report 25: the same segment that rates the product highest (ADHD, mean 4.44) writes the most cutting paywall criticism — pop-ups 'hyper désagréable et malvenu pour des TDAH'; 'profit off of your disability'. Report 60 (Mindway): an ADHD-positioned routine planner whose subscription four users could not cancel and whose paid trial billed within hours — the positioning makes the billing failures a betrayal of the audience it names. Report 67 (Habio): ads pitching ADHD help and a 'bionic reading' tool; USE_ADHD 97 (4.73%, mean 1.25 — below even the non-seeded 1.31), 35.05% refund denied, 23.71% describe dark patterns: 'en sachant pertinemment à quel point le TDAH est difficile à vivre au quotidien notamment vis à vis de la gestion financière'; 'they're using your own ADHD against you' (UK, where ADHD is 14.47% of reviews).

title: A bare checklist or task-slot paywall cannot carry a premium price — it is compared to Reminders, Notes, alarms and paper, free on every phone, and loses
statement: Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) said the phone's alarm, Notes, calendar, paper or Excel did the same job for free ('If you can set an alarm on your phone you don't need this app'); at $45–$99 that ceiling read as theft rather than expense and produced 96 one-star reviews. A product charging above a few dollars must deliver what a checklist structurally cannot — real personalisation, coaching content, human accountability, or data the user could not assemble. Report 23: 68 one-star reviews (0.94%) make the coherent case 'this is a checklist, iOS Reminders does it free, and it cost me money' — a positioning failure: the listing sold a to-do list rather than streak psychology plus HealthKit automation; Apple Reminders is the low-end competitor (9 mentions, mean 3.67). Report 25: among people who hit the paywall the comparison set is Apple Reminders, Health, Notes and a paper notebook (nine reviews explicitly) — a free tier must beat Reminders, not beat Streaks; ~7 reviewers would rather the app were honestly paid up front than 'fake-free'. Report 27 (the other side): a free, minimal, account-less tracker wins the category comparison outright — 13 reviewers explicitly rejected rivals over price ('Don't get streaks for $6. 👎 Get this!'; 'way better than those paid apps'), and switched-from-competitor rose 0% → 16.7% across eras without the app changing; as the category monetises harder, the free position sharpens by market drift. Report 29: 52 comparison shoppers (14.21%) arrived after rejecting paywalled trackers ('downloaded 20 habit tracking apps and none was satisfactory'; 'premium this, subscription that… here it's just free, like properly FREE') — the app 'wins a bake-off it never enters', so competitors' pricing drives its installs. Report 30: every reviewer calling the app 'too basic' also objects to paying — 'a value complaint wearing a feature costume'; do not add features in response. Report 31: 'How is this app worth $499.99?'; '$90/pY for what?' — simplicity is quoted both as the reason to use the app and the reason a subscription is unjustified. Report 60 (Mindway): the same verdict from buyers — 10 (4.63%, mean 1.50), five of them confirmed payers, say the paid product is 'nothing more than preloaded to-do lists'; 'just a suggestion list'; 'basically just a load of lists and reminders'; 'I cannot believe I spent $40 to use this app for one day' — and six non-buyers price it against Reminders, Notes, Calendar and paper ([[C277]]). (Consolidation after report 60: C277 was created by the report 60 merge and folded in here the same pass — the report's D2 'sell the outcome, not the task slots' is the constructive half of this rule.) [Merged from C277: Report 60 (Mindway, 216 reviews): price objections are relative, not absolute — 13 reviewers (6.02%, mean 1.69, no 4★ or 5★ among them) reject the price by comparing it to a substitute they already own, and 6 (2.78%) name it: Apple Reminders, Notes, Calendar, a paper planner — '8€/WOCHE für einen Tagesplaner, den man sich auch selbst im Kalender bauen kann. Frech.' (€8 a week for a day planner you could build in your calendar. Cheeky.); 'einfach zu teuer dafür dass ich das auch gratis in meinen Notizen machen kann'; 'paper planner is cheaper than this LOL'; 'Just use your remind app it's the same thing'. The report's reading: 'the competitive set Mindway is being priced against is not other habit apps — it is the free tools already on the phone', and a count-based paywall ('you have used your 2 free tasks') invites exactly that comparison because task slots are what those tools give away, whereas guided routines, progress history and a self-care library are not comparable to Reminders — 'the corpus shows Mindway losing a fight it chose' (D2: sell the outcome, not the task slots).
