Related: [[C214]] (a bare checklist cannot carry a premium price), [[C133]] (gate on capability, not quantity), [[C004]] (price against subscription competitors).] Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Asked for a payment in simple app like this' (MN, 1★) — an objection to paying for simplicity, the flip side of the app's own positioning; one of only two flat price objections in 45 reviews. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'I don't think any one is gonna pay 40$ just to check off a list'; 'I lost 40 dollars on something I could've just done on the notes app'. Report 68 (Ultiself): NEG_SIMPLE 97 (2.15%, mean 1.40) 'just a manual checklist' — thin union 137 (3.04%), 32 of them also objecting to price; lift 4.15× among purchasers. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'Excel would do this' — PAY_FEATURES_THIN 4 (1.75), three of four written while angry about the trial. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'Ich kann das gleiche auch mit einer einfachen Strichliste machen' (I can do the same with a simple tally sheet, 2★; NEG_SIMPLE 43 at 2.98★, NEG_POINTLESS 15 at 2.53★) — the tally-sheet comparison is the ceiling on a $4.99 unlock for a minority. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'nothing special.. just wastage of funds' (pk 1★, spend implied) — the too-minimal reading at the paywall. Report 82 (Lasting Change): APP_SHALLOW 13 and APP_NO_VALUE_FOR_PRICE 14 at ~$30.99/month — the recurring comparison is paper: 'Nothing you couldn't do yourself with a piece of paper and pen'; 'You can use a paper checklist for the same results'; 'the to-do lists I make on my notes are better than this app'; 'the app itself is well designed, but it's basically a glorified tracker and not at all worth the monthly cost' (2★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the counter-case from the free side — 'Why anyone would be pay a monthly sub for an app like habitkit, which offers no benefit over this app, I haven't a clue' (5★); a developer 'sat down to write a similar app because the alternatives have paid subscriptions… I downloaded it and immediately closed Xcode' — a free, uncapped, ad-free grid tracker is the reference point the category's subscriptions are now compared against.

merged_from.title: Price the paid tier against what the phone already gives away — a paywall that sells task slots, reminders or a checklist is compared to Apple Reminders, Notes and paper, and loses
merged_from.note: C277 (report 60: price objections are relative — 13 reviewers compare a $7/week task-slot paywall to Reminders, Notes, Calendar and paper; 'the competitive set is the free tools already on the phone') restates C214 (reports 19, 23, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 34, 42, 46: the phone's alarm, Notes, calendar, paper or Excel do the same job free, so a checklist priced above them reads as theft); one pricing rule, so the newer point is folded in and the title widened to name the paywall shape that triggers the comparison

title: Support reply time must be shorter than any cancellation deadline it serves
statement: Report 19: a 24-hour pre-renewal cancellation cut-off was served by a support queue that replied in 48 hours — 'They said cancel within 24 hours before and they take more than 48 hrs to get back to you' — an unsatisfiable deadline by construction; support otherwise ran silent, circular, or hostile ('a rude lecture via email about how I signed up on purpose') for 17 of 105. Report 24: support unresponsive or automated-only in 947 reviews (2.18%, mean 1.528); the specific obstacle named 17 times is a web contact form with a 250-character limit and no telephone number. Report 49: reviewers emailed for days about refunds, were told the app is not eligible for an App Store refund, then hit a 404 on App Support. Report 59 (Tappsk): payment-route questions were answered 'within 10–20 minutes' in 2022 and earned 5★; billing e-mails that go unanswered earn 1★ — the same company, different channels. Report 60 (Mindway): five of thirteen payers used a 1★ review as their support channel; 'I am getting no help and stopping the subscription' — a support route that is slower than the review prompt turns billing tickets into permanent 1★ reviews. Report 67 (Habio): 19 reviews quote a published support response time of up to four business days against a three-day trial — 'How convenient when they offer a 3-day trial'; MON_TRIAL_SHORT 9; §8.3: make the trial longer than support's own response time; §8.6: first human reply within 24 hours.

title: A forgiving long-run measure — cumulative or decaying credit that a missed day does not zero — alongside streaks
statement: Report 20: a non-streak percentage that drops when a day is missed rather than zeroing — 'missing one day and breaking my streak tends to send me into a spiral where I give up'; described as logarithmic and 'much closer to psychological reality'. The product's one genuine differentiator (38 explicit, the highest-affection language in a 4,048-review corpus; unclaimed by any competitor), broken by a 2021 rewrite when the score stopped decaying and never restored — 'Please bring that algorithm back!' Users who asked for a streak counter asked for it alongside, never instead of, the strength score. Distinct from C201 (a day-level partial-completion threshold): this is the long-run measure. Report 10: replacing cumulative Journeys with consecutive-streak Self-Care Areas was the lowest-rated change in a 70,041-review corpus (mean 2.76, 21 of 49 one-star); chronic-illness and ADHD users say a streak-only model is structurally incompatible with their lives. Ship the forgiving measure next to streaks, not instead of them. Report 24: paying users name 'missing a day is not punished' among the things they value most. Report 25: a paying user describes the day view as 'all the things I haven't done' and feeling bad — the un-forgiving frame is a churn reason. Report 26: the garden only grows if every habit is checked that day — 'If I miss only one out of 6 of my habits, nothing happens. Behaviourally this means people will say it's not worth trying'; 'doing 90% should be rewarded'; 'No room for off days… I'm human' (20 verified, mean 2.80) — while 25 (mean 4.76) praise the app for being gentle and streak-free; partial credit as a setting reconciles the two. Report 28: decay that resets 'ALL of your progress' after a bad week is read as data loss; a gentler or optional decay with a visible backup state would separate punishment from bugs. Report 41: the non-binary percentage ring rather than streaks is why a perfectionist bought. Report 54: 'the evidence of consistency and the punishment for breaking it are separable, and this user base wants the first without the second' — colour-density calendars, per-habit completion counts and monthly totals, not a streak counter with a reset (D4, 48 reviewers). Report 57: 'This is the only habit-building app that didn't make me feel like a failure for missing a day'; a detailed proposal asks for a skipped / failed distinction to keep it that way. Report 58: 'an effective habit tracker that did not discourage me when I missed a day'. Report 65 (Rabit): streak-only scoring is 'too all-or-nothing' — a completion-% score alongside the streak requested by a payer (S7). Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): finishers want to keep counting past the fixed 30-day cycle ('I want to see how far I can extend the record beyond 30 days!'; REQ_PERIOD 13); the same 2018 update removed a 90-day option (NEG_90_REMOVED 3). Report 76 (Way of Life): the percentage/grid measure is what users protect — misusing skip to emulate a weekly habit 'distorts the percentages they value' (NEG_CHART 38); OUT_AWARENESS 181 (self-awareness) is the outcome the grid produces. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a momentum score that decays instead of resetting is the whole product — 'the first habit tracker without streaks'; 19 of 71 (26.76%, mean 4.89★, zero below 4★) praise it by name: 'I used to drop habits the second I missed a day — all because of streak pressure'; 'removes all the frustration of having to start over from zero. It takes the 2-day rule even further'; 'motivates me to get things done but without the feeling of punishment when life gets in the way'; the streak is still visible alongside; 11 outcome reviews (15.49%) all 5★; PRAISE_MOTIVATING 11 all 5★, described as 'positive reinforcement', 'nudges that feel thoughtful, not annoying', 'without making me feel anxious'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): v2.4.0 added a toggle to disable streak/consistency stats — a partial answer to weekly-schedule requests where a 3×/week habit 'can never build a streak'. Report 85 (Habitica): PR_GRACE 10 and PR_REST 6 vs NEG_PUNISH 23 — a health bar that regenerates and an inn to rest in are the forgiving elements; users ask for them to be discoverable and time-limited. Report 86 (Today): a skip day is used as a mental-health tool — 'to sort days when I felt bad out of the streak. Over time it became easier to assess my successes' (de 5★, depressive phases) — and the skip feature that exists is misunderstood by three reviewers and reported as damaging streak statistics.

merged_from.title: Credit for non-consecutive, cumulative progress alongside streaks
merged_from.note: C158 (report 10: cumulative credit next to streaks) and C216 (report 20: a decaying strength score instead of resets) are the same product principle stated by two corpora

title: An unexplained metric reads as broken — explain the score on-screen
statement: Report 20: a weekly habit completed once showed 4%, not 100%, and users could not work out why; the developer's answer (~91 repetitions to reach 100%) read as arbitrary. A documentation failure, not a maths failure — one explainer screen and an optional 'this period' toggle was the cheapest satisfaction win in the corpus (20 classified, undercounted). Report 59 (Tappsk): 'не очень понятно что значит 115' (not clear what 115 means) — the productivity score is unexplained on screen. Report 60 (Mindway): 'It's just a basic to do list' — the absence of any metric at all (no completion %, no consistency view) is read as the product being unfinished. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'you see a sea of dots without being able to distinguish month, week and day' (IT, 1★) — the dot / heat-map grid others paid for carries no time axis, and a 4★ asks for the options to be explained: 'the UI is legible to people who already understand it'; P8: a visible month / week / day framing as a design test; P7: one-line hints on first use. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the momentum number is unexplained in-product — 'I can't really tell on what basis momentum arises, or why it's good that it's displayed' (kr 3★) vs 'At first I had some trouble following the points logic, but now that I've grasped it, I'm thrilled' (de 5★) — 'same obstacle, two outcomes… the gap between those two reviews is the whole opportunity'; §8.3.1 a one-tap explanation where the number is displayed; U:comprehension 4 (5.63%, 3.00★). Report 86 (Today): the custom chart, counter and milestone cards go unexplained (UX_CONFUSE 74; NEG_FEATURE_UNUSED 15) and a skip state is misunderstood by three — the depth layer that converts power users confuses everyone else.

title: Store listing and paywall copy stay true — disclose limits, and never advertise a feature you removed, lack, or don't integrate
statement: Report 20: the listing said 'Unlimited amount of habits. You don't need to pay a penny' for at least two years after the free tier was capped at 3; 24 reviews (mean 1.21 — the lowest of any theme) called it false advertising by name. Zero engineering cost, unmade for over two years. Report 18's screenshots advertised a timer a buyer could not find. Report 6 / 19: a buyer who paid for a feature that isn't there cancels and says 'there are free ones' — it turns a feature request into a refund cause. Report 2: sibling apps implied an integration that did not exist; the purchases it drove ended in 1★. Report 25: the App Store listing showed Apple Watch support that could not be installed. Report 26: the German store listing carried a typo — 'Eden-Gewohnheitstrinker' (habit drinker) for 'Gewohnheitstracker'. Report 28: a listing that says 'habit tracker' for a product that is a pet game produces 'it's not what it says it is' 2★ reviews. Report 29: a privacy label saying 'analytics and diagnostics' while the app asks to route third-party traffic through the user's IP — the store disclosure must cover what the app actually does. Report 30: the listing still says 'Track up to 2 habits' after the cap became 3, the advertised streak/interactive widget is not the shipped widget, and one reviewer says the IAP was not visible at the decision point — correct the listing to remove expectation-mismatch 1★. Report 23: reviewers said the task cap was not disclosed in the description and asked for refunds on that basis; the 68 'it's just a checklist' 1★ reviews are an expectation failure the listing could pre-empt. Report 30: the listing still said 2 free habits after the cap became 3. Report 31: 57 say the price was hidden or the listing implied 'free' ('needs an in-app purchases mark'; 'online ads … said it was under $10 one time'); 50 describe an intro price renewing much higher only 'in the small print' (9.99€ → 100.99€; £5.99 → £51.99, 'just hoping someone doesn't cancel'). Report 33: 'you finally mention that habits are limited … after they've created it'; 34 price-hidden / misleading 'free' reviews. Report 34: users who searched for free apps met a 2-habit wall — 'only to find out AFTER downloading the app that there is a fee'; 'I just wish it was said earlier (for example, here)'. Report 36: a store screenshot showing a habit named 'Run 15 minutes' made a buyer expect a built-in timer (2★). Report 41: Spanish and Portuguese are on the listing while reviewers in ES / CL / BR report them missing (2024–2026). Report 42: the listing names 36 languages including Hebrew and Ukrainian which the app does not deliver — 'They present it as if it's in Hebrew. In practice there's no option for a Hebrew interface' (IL, 1★); 'Preview on AppStore was on Ukrainian, I don't like that it's on russian' (three of Ukraine's eight reviews) — a factual misstatement, not a backlog item; a 'goal for the day' advertised and absent. Report 43: 'Not a free app. The whole app is an in app purchase'; 'Bait and switch. After 3 they make you pay' — 14 of 16 such reviews US, none after Oct 2021. Report 46: 'Every picture shows a bunch of colorful habit trackers, not a one shows what the free version looks like' — a screenshot of the actual 3-habit free view is the fix. Report 47: the Japanese listing (12 Sep 2026) says the free version offers 'unlimited task registration' while reviewers from Dec 2024 to Mar 2026 report a free cap of 6 ('6 habitudes gratuites'); two say the paid nature was not disclosed — state the cap and trial length on the listing and at the paywall. Report 48: the listing states 3 free trackers while reviewers report 10 / 8 / 7 / 6 / 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1 across eras; 48 hit an undisclosed wall after setup (1.65★) — disclose the limit on the listing and at first run. Report 49: 'Free with In-App Purchases' and an ad saying 'get your free life reset plan today' front a product with no free use — advertised as free 37 (1.08), tripling after the trial launched. Report 50: search summaries of the listing state a 5-habit free cap, 1 reminder per habit and 3 journal notes per day while five 2026 reviewers in four storefronts get 3 habits and nobody mentions the other caps — 'Either way this is a disclosure problem'. Report 53: the listing claimed Family Sharing that in-app purchases don't support (M5: remove it). Report 54: three reviewer-reported listing-versus-product disagreements — 'Advanced Statistics' that is a calendar, a €2.50 subscription on the listing the app did not sell (a reader who 'would book that immediately'), and a listing that said 5 free habits when the app gave 3. Report 56: a store preview shows a widget-transparency setting the user cannot find in the app. Report 57: 'I bought Premium and nothing differs from before — I can't use the features shown in the screenshots'; Family Sharing advertised but not delivered. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_DISCLOSURE 80 (1.95★) and MON_PAYWALL_SURPRISE 64 (1.70★) — 'Пишите сразу, что ПО платное, а не встроенные покупки' (say up front that the software is paid, not 'in-app purchases'); 50 + 44 of the 674 1★; the listing does not state the caps and the report's experiment is to state them. Report 60 (Mindway): M_MISLEADING_ADVERT 5 (all 1★: 'Click bait'; 'Not set up as advertised'; 'is it free? No. So Change to paid.'; 'it said it was free') and both ad-sourced reviewers at 1★ — F4: state the subscription price and the free-tier limit in the App Store listing and in the first ad frame, which 'removes the click bait / it said it was free class of review entirely'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a Health integration a reviewer believed was advertised does not work — 'either make it work, or remove the claim'. Report 67 (Habio): the listing claims App Store billing, 'optional subscription', 'designed in collaboration with mental health professionals' and sharing with friends, while reviewers describe off-store billing, a hard paywall ('Optional subscription was a lie') and no sharing; an old pinned 'it has a free version' review misled later installers. Report 69 (TheFor): the subtitle leads with 'Journal' while the listing body never mentions journaling and one reviewer uses it — P4: make it visible or stop leading with it; 'Unlimited Habit Creation' is a listing promise the corpus confirms is kept. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): a listing that lists every feature and never the time limit — 'This is the gap the corpus is complaining about, and it is verifiable from outside the corpus'; the listing also claims cross-device and cross-OS restore while 7 say sync does not work and 2 paying users could not move the purchase. Report 75 (Habit Streak): the description says 'Subscription options are: 1 month and 1 year with 7 days of free trial' while the IAP table sells a 'Premium Lifetime $79.99' — 'One of the two is wrong'; the cap the corpus complains about most appears on neither surface. Report 76 (Way of Life): the listing still marks 'backup to cloud' as premium while 4.3.0 release notes say it is free for all; declared languages omit Kazakh and Galician that reviewers asked for; the listing cites Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose and reviewers name the same source — the listing's press citations are corroborated by the corpus. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the description states the concept well ('The first habit tracker without streaks') but never states the one-habit limit, names no price / tier / trial / one-time option, and omits widgets, Apple Health, the calendar, badges, the Habit Forest and iCloud — six capabilities reviewers discuss, two of which (widgets, Health) generated complaints from users who did not know what tier they were in; §8.1.4 name the features. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the description runs five headed sections and contains no monetization paragraph whatsoever — no free-tier limit, no Plus, no subscription, no price; §8.1.2 four sentences would close it: what the free tier includes, that the board limit is three, what Plus adds, and that both a subscription and a one-time option exist — 'the cheapest high-value change in the report'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the listing states four checkable falsehoods — a payment rail it does not use ('charged to your App Store account' while hasInAppPurchases is false), a cancel path that does not exist ('manage or cancel anytime in account settings' vs 27 CANCEL_NO_PATH), a pricing heading with no prices, and a support address at a non-existent domain; it never mentions the book that 43 reviewers actually bought; §8.1 repair the listing is 'the cheapest item… with the most direct evidence'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): the listing understates the product — Languages: English only while 1.0.9 'Added languages', 62.79% of reviews are non-English and a Vietnamese UI is in use; 'No servers. No cloud.' contradicts the analytics label; the website's opt-in cloud backup is absent from the listing; §8.1 four text fixes, none a product change. Report 86 (Today): the listing says 'Quit bad habits and stay on track' and the feature does not exist — REQ_BREAKBAD 15 (2016 → 2026), USE_QUIT 16 trying anyway; 'the description talks about losing bad habits: we need an explanation. In what way does this app concern itself with our bad habits?' (fr 4★); §8.7 'advertising a capability, collecting users who need it, and having them discover the gap after purchase' is not defensible — build a 'maximum N per period' type (Done and HabitBull named as having it) or remove the promise.

merged_from.title: Never let the paywall imply a capability the product lacks
merged_from.note: C138 (paywall implies a capability the product lacks) and C218 (listing advertises a removed feature) are the same rule on two surfaces

merged_from.title: Never imply cross-app integration you don't have
merged_from.note: C087 (implied cross-app integration) is a third surface of the same rule

merged_from.title: Disclose product limits in the listing — an undisclosed cap or scope becomes a refund request
merged_from.note: C224 (report 23: an undisclosed task cap became refund requests) is the omission side of C218 (the listing advertising what the product does not do) — one listing-truth rule

title: A free cap must be concurrent, never lifetime — deleting a habit frees a slot
statement: Report 20: the 3-habit free cap behaved as a lifetime cap — users who deleted a habit to make room could not add a replacement and the add button routed to the paywall; this turned a pricing decision into a functional dead end and was the mechanic that converted annoyance into uninstalls. Report 31: a minority reported 2 or 4–5 free slots after deleting and re-adding, which the free tier did not always allow. Report 36: archived / completed habits counted against the cap — 'when I went to archive one of my completed habits and tried to make a new one it wouldn't let me … seems like kind of a ripoff'. Report 48: users who deleted a tracker to make room found the slot gone (23, mean 2.22, 'the most damaging variant') — fix #2: restore slots freed by deletion. Report 50: 'unlimited for the first few days' then 'keep only three habits' — the cap applied retroactively to habits already created.

title: Never take a paying user's reason to buy away — the widget sold the upgrade and never worked
statement: Report 20: the widget was by a wide margin the most-named purchase trigger and the feature that most often didn't work — 182 reviews (mean 1.94), 113 from confirmed payers (12.4% of all payers), reported broken for five years with an in-app FAQ offering 'restart your phone'; even when present it was a Today-view widget while screenshots implied Home Screen. Ship it properly or remove it from the paywall copy and refund on request.

title: A receipt with a working product link after every charge, and a renewal reminder before it
statement: Report 19: reviewers could find no record of what they bought — 'no confirmation email anywhere'; support's answer 'we sent you an EMAIL notification' conceded that one e-mail with the fine print in a footer link was the whole safeguard, and 'the ONE SINGLE EMAIL they sent confirming my purchase with no actual link' left an ADHD buyer unable to find the product at all. Every charge produces a receipt that names the plan, the amount, the next charge date and links to the product; every renewal is preceded by a reminder. Related: C152 (the trial-end reminder) and C177 (SKU names). Report 24: 197 reviews (mean 1.168, 0% 5★) say the renewal came with no notice — the cheapest item on the report's list; 1,412 edited reviews are largely downgrades added after a later charge. Report 26: renewal with no advance notice (2) inside the lowest-rated theme. Report 31: show the renewal price before purchase — 50 renewal shocks (mean 1.44). Report 59 (Tappsk): 'списали деньги за приложение, которого у меня нет' (money taken for an app I no longer have) — without a receipt naming the product, a renewal on a deleted app reads as fraud. Report 65 (Rabit): renewed after months of non-use with no warning — 'Achei que agiram de má fé… Espero que repensem o formato de receita'. Report 67 (Habio): the charge appeared under the company name, not the app — 'Tuve que investigar que aplicaciones tenía GOTOTOP LTD para saber que me estaban cobrando'; no receipt or reminder before the charge in 68 reviews. Report 82 (Lasting Change): BILL_NO_NOTICE 11 ('I do not even have an email stating this would occur'), BILL_SURPRISE_CHARGE 17 discovered from a bank statement ('if it wasn't for my bank I probably never would have known'); BILL_UNKNOWN_DESCRIPTOR 5 — the card descriptor reads a sibling app (Effecto, Walking Yoga) or the legal entity (Medical Score), so buyers 'had to google search their customer support email to figure out why I was being charged' or call the bank; §8.4 a pre-renewal email naming product, amount and a one-click cancel link, and a descriptor that reads the app's name; the order confirmation email must carry the recurring terms — 'It's such a small change to your email template'.

title: A hard habit cap is a defensible design position only with an opt-in pressure valve — the default never changes
statement: Report 23: a paid one-time tracker capped at 6 → 12 → 24 tasks drew the largest request in twelve years (620, 8.53%) in every market and every year; each raise cut the complaint rate roughly in half (8.76% → 5.06%; 11.90% → 6.16%) and bought about three years before it rebounded, and it never fell below ~6%. Against it 118 (1.62%) defend the cap as the reason the app works, and nobody in the 620 asks for the default to change — they ask for the ceiling to move. The cap is a durable position and a permanent 6–12% complaint tax; ship extra capacity off by default behind a setting that states the rationale. Report 24 (the same principle from the coaching side): the product's real moat is a refusal — it declines to let users add more habits; small-steps pacing is the highest-rated theme of any size in 43,469 reviews (1,817, mean 4.692, 2.0% 1★; 'I stacked everything I wanted to change and failed miserably; this time I followed the program'), and the same constraint produces the four complaint shapes ('I already do this' 124, 'it ignored my answers' 175, 'too slow' 168, 'doesn't fit my week' 31). The corpus asks for one branch — declare a habit already-held and start at habit two — not for the constraint to go. Report 25: 19 reviewers (mean 4.32) defend a 3-habit free cap on principle ('helps me to only keep track of what is the most important to me') while 138 object — and the objectors name the number they would accept, median 8–10. Report 26 (the reward side): the cap is 3→5→6 habits plus a growth ceiling; users who love the constraint-free gentleness still say five slots cannot hold a routine, and propose their own valve — one full garden free. Report 46: 66 reviewers (3.03%, mean 4.92) defend a 3-habit cap on habit-science grounds ('shouldn't be tracking more than three in the first place'; 'the limit is beneficial since it kept me from piling expectations onto myself') while the counter-offer is 4–7 — the defensible cap is disclosed and framed as focus. Report 47: a user proposes buying slots — 'タブ数だけ買わせてください' ('let me buy just the number of tabs I need', 4★, 2025); the report's E2 is a per-slot purchase for free users at the cap. Report 48: the pressure valve reviewers propose is a cheap, narrow tier that only unlocks trackers — pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports (58 one-time requesters, $10–$20); 15 ask to raise the free cap. Report 49: 40 want a free tier, ads or donations instead of a hard paywall (several volunteering heavy advertising); an Indian reviewer proposes 3–5 free habits with premium above — a report experiment. Report 59 (Tappsk): the cap held at 2 habits for five years generates a steady 4.4–5.1% objection per era with no sign of decay; three is the number reviewers repeatedly propose as enough to evaluate. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a fixed cap of 3, unchanged over 17 months, produces a steady trickle of cap reviews from otherwise satisfied users; the report's alternative to a raise is a time-limited 4th habit — a pressure valve rather than a moved wall. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the purest defended cap — one goal at a time, free, by design (US listing: 'the app only allows you to set one goal at a time'); praised by 148 (6.46%, mean 4.87) and 28 (ONE_GOAL_CONVERT) say they resented it and came to agree ('At first I was saying let me add another goal!, but as I kept going I came to think this is how it should be'); the request for more (REQ_MULTI 44, mean 4.39) is growing (4.7% of 2025–26) and is narrower than 'many habits' — keep a completed habit while starting the next; reviewers volunteer the valve themselves: unlock a second goal only after a first 30-day cycle. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 3-item cap is defended by users as a focusing device (#7013, #4439, #6073) and §8.8 says keep it; the objection never went away (every era) but fell from 6.1% (E3) to 1.5% (E6). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): at one habit the cap is 'an aggressive but coherent strategy' whose cost side is precise (2.50★ from those who hit it) and whose conversion effect is unmeasured; the decision should be made 'on strategy grounds, not on review grounds'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the 3-board cap was tolerated ('Man kann aber auch gut ohne Leben'; 'without huge limitations') while widgets were free and rejected ('totaal niks') once they were not — the pressure valve here was the free widget, and removing it is what broke the cap.

title: Undo / un-complete is a visible button — never a gesture-only path
statement: Report 23: the only undo for an accidental completion was a shake gesture available immediately after the action; 77 reviews (1.06%, mean 3.38) across 12 storefronts called it unacceptable, several found the only workaround was resetting all history, and some deleted the app over it. Keep the gesture, add a button and a long-press-to-uncomplete path. Report 43: the Done and Info buttons sat adjacent for four years and swipes were mis-read ('I was constantly marking things as done when I really wanted to mark them as skipped… so I deleted it'; 'Tap targets for your most common actions… are tiny'); undo an accidental Done requested. Report 48: can't edit / delete a log 32 (3.22). Report 52: 'tap again to undo' was removed (2021) and a mistaken tap can only be marked 'failed'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'eu cliquei numa tarefa errado e contou mas como eu desfaço isso???????' (4★); a slow undo, wants swipe-to-undo (4★); §8.2 #9 a fast, obvious undo. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): UX_NO_TICK — 'Daily habits, tick mark not available' (in, 1★): whether the tick is missing or merely hard to find, 'the outcome was a one-star review in a habit app over the core action'; §8.3.2 make the completion gesture unmissable. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): REQ_UNDO_CHECKIN / DEF_CHECKIN_SPAM — 'Check in too many times' (4★): a second tap should undo; v2.0.1 restored a long-press check-in configurator.

title: Disclose product limits in the listing — an undisclosed cap or scope becomes a refund request
statement: Report 23: reviewers said the task cap was not disclosed in the App Store description and asked for refunds on that basis; the 68 'no value / it's just a checklist' 1★ reviews (0.94%) and most of the 123 price objections are expectation failures the listing could pre-empt.

title: A one-off free promotion (App of the Week, partner promo) acquires durable users
statement: Report 23: a Starbucks 'Pick of the Week' promo in 2015–16 drew 13 reviews at mean 4.62, and one of those users was still active in July 2025 — ten-year retention from a free promo on a paid-up-front app. Report 34 (counter-case): a ~29 Jun 2023 free-lifetime giveaway brought 27 short 5★ reviews in three days and a wave of non-English users asking for a language the app did not have; no durable-retention evidence. Report 41: two early users were given the full version free at the 2020 launch and rated 5★. Report 50: two 5★ reviewers ask for a referral / discount programme ('rewards for recommending the app to friends… in the form of discounts') while 37 evangelise it — S3: build one. Report 76 (Way of Life): a podcast mention (Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose, 2014–2016) shows up in reviews for a decade and converts the same day — an earned-media wave (E4 'the podcast wave', 26 of 51 MKT_PRESS) behaves like a promotion. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a third-party giveaway (AppAdvice lifetime promo) drew a 1★ when the code could not be redeemed — a promotion is only an acquisition if the redemption works. Report 85 (Habitica): the counter-case — an App Store feature on 2018-02-26 landed on a day the servers could not register new users: 22 reviews that day, 67 in the month at 2.91★ ('Downloaded the app this morning because of the App Store recommendation', 1★); a promotion the service cannot serve converts into a 1★ wave. Report 86 (Today): launched 8 March 2016 as an Apple Editors' Choice (MKT_EDITORS 6) — and crashed immediately for a large fraction of users while gating the free tier at one habit: 209 reviews that month at 3.11★, 54 on a single day, 228 reviews (12.77% of the ten-year corpus) permanently attached to the listing at 3.25★; 'When I saw this was an editors choice app I checked it out… all I get is the screen that says today. And then everything crashes' (1★).

title: App-icon badge count of outstanding habits, with an active-hours window
statement: Report 23: a badge count of tasks still open today, limited to an active-hours window, is named by many reviewers as the core motivator of a paid one-time tracker. Report 41: app badge counter broken / absent (3). Report 43: 20 reminders per day named as a cap. Report 55: a badge countdown of outstanding habits motivates some and can't be removed for others. Report 76 (Way of Life): the app-icon badge draws NEG_BADGE 13 ('badge nags', 4.38★) and BUG_BADGE 5. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a Focus tab exists and one reviewer questions why (UX_FOCUS_TAB_POINTLESS 1, kr 3★). Report 83 (Roubit): 'alarms that repeat until done' — NOTIF_TOO_PERSISTENT 3 against PRAISE_REMINDERS 9.

title: A 'graduated' state — keep tracking a mastered habit without it occupying an active slot
statement: Report 23: the single most persuasive argument for more capacity, made repeatedly, is that people want to keep tracking a habit that has become automatic while starting a new one; a mastered/graduated state that keeps history but frees the slot answers it without raising the cap. Report 48: end dates and archiving requested by 23 (4.09). Report 50: archive completed habits requested (2) — a completed short-term goal cluttering the screen. Report 53: archive without losing history (274-vote review). Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 'Once you complete 30 days and start a new habit, the old habit is no longer notified' (3★) — §8.5: after a cycle offer 'keep tracking this quietly' beside 'set the next goal', graduated habits kept as a low-key streak while one goal stays active; measure 60- and 90-day continuation, not goals created. Report 76 (Way of Life): archive exists (PR_ARCHIVE 14 at 4.93★, 'pause habits') with NEG_ARCHIVE_UX 5 ('cannot find archived items', 4.80★) and REQ_ARCHIVE 10 ('keep data of removed habits'). Report 86 (Today): REQ_ARCHIVE 11 restated across five years and four languages — a formed habit can only be deleted, taking its history; the most-upvoted request in 1,785 reviews.

title: Text fields must handle IME composition — Hangul and CJK input
statement: Report 23: the task-title field mangled Hangul (typing 약 stored 야ㄱ), reported four separate times over five years and never fixed, producing 1★–4★ reviews from otherwise-satisfied Korean users in the storefront with the worst refund rate. Report 28: CJK font fallback rendered Japanese glyphs for Chinese text and silently truncated habit names; a localisation update once turned every 'r' into a black square — audit font fallback and string handling whenever a language ships. Report 30: the onboarding name field rejected Arabic input — 'it won't accept any name' — 2 of 3 Saudi reviews, both 1★; a hard block at first launch for an entire locale. Report 57: a Sep 2020 update stopped the note keyboard appearing (21 of 22 reviews in three days).

title: A deliberate completion gesture — press-and-hold with haptic and sound, not a bare tap
statement: Report 23: press-and-hold completion is described as physically satisfying and as accident-proofing, attested inside the two largest positive themes; some criticise it. Copying 'tap to complete' loses something real; pair any tap model with a visible undo. Report 36: 'very satisfying to hold down a button … and get actual physical feedback from my phone … Much nicer than just tapping a complete button on a reminder list'. Report 47 (counter-evidence): a long-press that opens a record screen before 'done' is counted as too many taps by 14 (mean 2.86) — a deliberate gesture must complete the check-in, not open a form. Report 48 (counter-evidence): a redesign that made every log a double click cost ten reviews in three months from loyal payers — see [[C264]].

title: Sync merges an append-only, timestamped event log — never last-writer-wins state replacement
statement: Report 23: after a 2022 migration to direct iCloud sync, complaint-framed sync went from 1.42% of 2015–17 reviews to 7.60% of post-2022 reviews (mean 2.90) and data loss from 0.33% to 4.62% of the era; failure modes were a device overwriting newer state with older state, deleted tasks resurrecting, Watch completions never reaching the phone, and completions un-completing seconds later. A customer review spells out the correct architecture: immutable timestamped events applied in order. Report 48: duplicate entries 32 (2.31), 20 of them in the 2015 sync rewrite. Report 50: to-do entries lost and unrecoverable for a Premium user (Apr 2026). Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the recording tap is lost — tapping the ring shows the undo hint instead of recording ('A pop-up saying cancel with the top-right button appears; when I reluctantly delete it I'm back to day one'; BUG_INPUT 20, 2017 → 2026), counts stick at 7 or 4, and 'fairly often, wipes out the previous day's record' (BUG_COUNT 12, BUG_RESET 7); defects are in 48% of 1★ — 'For a product whose whole promise is an unbroken record, a lost day is the worst possible failure'; §8.1: log every tap so a lost day can be restored. Report 76 (Way of Life): no sync at all for 16 years — REQ_SYNC 139 — so this corpus has zero sync-conflict complaints; the data-loss path is the phone change, not the merge. Report 86 (Today): a restore flow that overwrote the backup it was reading and wiped the restore data (jp, 'Farewell, Today') — restore must be non-destructive.

title: Audit the funnel per market and per channel — storefronts diverge on billing and funnel stage, not on the product, and written reviews are a complaint channel that under-rates it against public ratings
statement: Report 24: Latin-American and Gulf storefronts (Brazil 4.266, Mexico 4.381, Peru 4.511, Ecuador 4.593; bill_core 2.35–6.42%) carry the same product that rates 2.1–2.6 in the US/UK/AU/CA during 2024–26 at 42–52% billing disputes; Brazil stays at 4.002 through the worst era. Language-neutral ratings rule out a classifier artefact. Whatever is different in how the product is sold there is the model — and rich English-language markets were the worst, not the best. Report 25: Argentina (mean 2.95, monetisation friction 40%, billing 10%) and the Spanish-language block (blocker 36% more common, paywall register markedly more hostile) vs Great Britain (mean 4.06, zero blocker, zero confusing-UX) — the same product, different market experience; check Argentine pricing display and trial mechanics. Report 26: Germany (63.6% 5★, 19.83% friction), France (20.37%), Australia (18.52%) and Canada (cap 10.09%) vs Russia (85.3% 5★, 7.34% friction) and Vietnam (86.8%, 5.15%) on the same product — though Russia's low friction may be a payment-availability effect: if users cannot reach the paywall, low friction is not satisfaction. Report 28: China (n=12) has zero ad complaints while its three critical reviews are all localisation — if ad inventory does not serve there, CN is a natural control for the ad-free product. Report 30: Russia is the product's real market (only continuous 13-month stream, most purchase attempts, most nuanced feedback, substantive mean 3.20) and where the payment flow is visibly breaking; Spanish-language organic reviews (AR/MX/UY, 0/6 templated, mean 2.33) are the harshest in the corpus while ES/CL are 16/24 templated at 4.75. Report 31: Australia shows the monetisation and integrity story without the crash wave (friction 43.5%, entitlement 14.0%, billing 19.7%, launch 9.3%); Canada is the worst large storefront (2.10, 57.7% 1★); Brazil and Mexico are wave-dominated (launch 28.6% / 28.1%, upsell only 2.2% / 3.5%); Switzerland was offered 10 CHF and charged 59 CHF; Hong Kong and India show 26.7% / 17.1% entitlement failure. Report 33: storefronts differ sharply — cn blocked (57.8%), de subscription-averse (price 14.7%, subscription 9.2%), kr the account-deletion centre (5.5%), jp highest payer share (16.0%) and Watch / update complaints, ru Mac/web 10.1%, vn happiest (4.61). Report 42: Brazil (41.8% cap complaints, 9 of 12 lag reports), the US (all six multi-count complaints, near-zero cap), Russia (5 of 7 crashes, 4 of 6 data losses, no payment rail) and Japan (both reviews 1★ on price) each fail differently on the same product. Report 43: 18 of 20 crash reports are US (4.40% vs 0.87%) — more likely a reporting-behaviour artefact than a device fact, unresolvable from reviews. Report 46: the same product is loved and disputed differently per storefront — Germany 3.95 with every monetisation theme 2–4× global, Russia 4.43 calling the price fair, China objecting to the payment shape not the cap, India negotiating, Turkey regional price, Spain the harshest cap objection (mean 2.00) beside Catalan praise. Report 47: Japan (mean 3.54) carries almost all the monetisation shock and the payers; Korea (4.33) requests and forgives (6 of 13 KR crash reviews still 5★); the same product rates 3.70 in JP + KR and 4.25 elsewhere. Report 48: 'Praise is remarkably uniform; grievance is local' — simplicity and flexibility land within a few points everywhere while price sensitivity clusters in CA / AU / DE / CN and localization in RU / CN; China splits sharpest (crash 12.33%, localization 12.33%, simplicity at 5.00★). Report 50: the cap change is invisible in the US (all four US cap statements say 5) and concentrated in Turkey, Australia and Mexico (four of Mexico's five reviews in 18–24 Aug 2026) — hypothesis: it lands hardest where the subscription is expensive relative to local purchasing power. Report 53: Spanish- and Portuguese-language storefronts carry 34.1% monetisation friction against 21.3% globally; Germany's top theme is price (18.00%); Taiwan's is reliability (37.5%) with only 8.9% friction. Report 54: payer and cap-complaint rates are identical in the high-volume group and globally (11.9%), so those are product properties, while price objection (CN 16.7%), restore failure (non-US) and outcome language (US 24.4%) are market-specific. Report 57: the same product shows three market problems — Korea (tenured base worn down by regressions), the US (top-of-funnel lost to a 30-second ad; ads and uninstalls 15.15%), Japan (would convert at ¥2,000, converts at zero at ¥4,500). Report 59 (Tappsk): monetisation pain is geographic and product love is not — without the Russian storefront praise (76.8%), ease and the free-limit objection are unchanged while billing falls 3.2% → 1.4% and payment access 0.7% → 0.0%; billing 3.7% in Russian-speaking storefronts vs 1.0% in English-speaking; high-star reviews hide support tickets (CONTRA_RATING 155: 102 are 4–5★ reviews whose text reports a crash, charge or refund request — 'Возможно ли вернуть деньги после списания', 5★), so star-filtered monitoring misses refund requests. Report 60 (Mindway): the US vs rest-of-world split is a funnel-stage split — the US has bought and been disappointed (under-built 7.92% vs 1.74%, billing 9.90% vs 0.87%), the rest of the world has been stopped at the door (paywall cap 11.30% vs 5.94%); whether the billing rate improved after 2024 or the US share of reviews simply fell (85.3% → 26.8%) cannot be separated from review text (Q3). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 45 written reviews vs 536 public ratings (8.40%), written mean 3.111 vs public 4.52 — 'the written corpus is a complaint channel, not a satisfaction measure'; per storefront the gap runs to −3.56 (UA: 39 ratings at 4.56 vs two 1★ reviews) and Ireland's one 1★ review is its entire public rating; Argentina is the one storefront where the June burst shows in the public number (3.82). (Consolidation after report 62: the title was widened from 'Audit the sales funnel per market — the same product can rate 4.3 in one storefront and 2.1 in another on billing alone' to cover the channel dimension the batch added; the original storefront finding stays in the statement.) Report 64 (Critique AI): written vs public gap −1.84 to −2.92 in every storefront with ≥ 5 reviews (US 180 @ 2.66 vs 9,557 @ 4.73); high-spend ('rich') markets carry the friction (2.53, 47.9% 1★) against volume markets (2.91, 34.3%) — the paywall binds where the creator's audience is; the US argues the amount (price 30.0% > hardwall 29.4%) and is where people get in (22.2% vs 11.5%), while GB argues the wall's existence (40.0% vs 20.0%); the app ranks worst in the US (48th) where 43% of written reviews come from. Report 65 (Rabit): written 3.677 vs public 4.76 (−1.08; −0.30 Vietnam to −2.10 Portugal) — 'both are correct, and the store number is the better estimate of average satisfaction while this report is the better guide to what is broken'; six 5★ reviews carry price complaints or crash reports — here stars under-report dissatisfaction; non-Brazilian reviewers left faster over the 2023 changes. Report 67 (Habio): corpus mean 2.35 vs US public 4.28 (3,932), gb 3.68, ca 4.04, au 3.71, fr 3.05, de 2.65, mx 3.31, es 2.93; 'the complaint does not depend on the market' — non-seeded means near 1★ everywhere, only the mechanism varies (workbook gb / es, language bait fr / de, cancellation and support au / de); the US is two corpora (555 of 886 flagged; non-seeded US 1.35). Report 68 (Ultiself): public exceeds corpus mean in 12 of 20 storefronts; kz 4.04 corpus mean but 2.38 outside E5, il 4.48 carried by 51 Hebrew 5★ one-liners, ng 4.98 all praise with 8 shared bodies and the 'post one review per day' text; the harm concentrates in ae (2.02, 72.0% billing), by (2.78, 26.3% web billing), ua (2.98) and cl (3.04 vs public 4.26) — the ua + kz + by group outside E5 is 61.5% billing against 29.9% for the US outside E5. Report 69 (TheFor): a positive-skew corpus — 71.25% 5★, written 4.525 against ~4.87 US public on a 30% write rate; storefront inversions (za 2.50 vs 4.40; de 5.00 vs 4.13) each explained by one or two reviews; 29 probed storefronts with zero reviews read as absent distribution, not rejection. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): a corpus that agrees with its public rating (4.73 vs 4.78) because reviewers are mostly those who succeeded; 17 contradictions are all 1–3★ with wholly positive text. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the written corpus stops 648 days before extraction while the app shipped 9 more releases (Challenges, Persona Notifications, Journal) — 'this report describes the app as it was up to late 2024'; the silent public raters are harsher (a 2★ and two 1★ with no text); zero paying reviewers, so every monetization data point is a refusal; GB, CA, AU and VN hold ratings but no text. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 85.20% 5★, 27.20% low-information reviews rising to 36.00% in 2026 ('the informative corpus is closer to 180 reviews than 250'), zero feature requests in 2026, a grant cohort of 15 all 5★, 21.5% of public ratings written; the Christmas cluster contains six 1★, so it is seasonal, not solicited. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): Japan's 103 text reviews are 3.27% of its 3,151 ratings and carry a 24.27% 1★ share against 3.11% public; JP written 3.49 vs rest of world 4.31 is 'engagement depth, not national sentiment' (27.08% of non-JP reviews are sentiment-only; every churn, defect and friction report is Japanese); Brazil holds 100 public ratings but 4 short reviews. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 41 text reviews on 451 public ratings — ratings-weighted 4.67 vs corpus 4.00 (France −1.34: 3.40 vs 4.74); 4 of 25 5★ carry a monetization objection and two are wholly negative in substance ('Me gustaría que fuera gratuito', author handle 'Gratuito porfa') — 'Star rating is unreliable as a sentiment proxy in this corpus'; gb and jp rate but write nothing. Report 76 (Way of Life): a praise corpus (any-praise 81.88%, 1–2★ 3.67%) where a 'Meaningful' complaint is dozens of reviews; CONTRA_RATING 47 (0.61%) — 29 high-star reviews reporting problems, 7 low-star praise ('I absolutely love this app', 1★); the public mean exceeds the corpus mean in 21 of 22 storefronts; E6 is both the highest-rated era (4.70) and the most polarised (1–2★ 5.2%); removing burst days shifts no headline by more than 0.4 pp. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly, 71 reviews): (1) one review is 1.41% so the spec's bands cannot discriminate — every headline carries a Wilson CI, 'where a band and an interval disagree, trust the interval'; (2) 14 of 71 (19.72%) are content-free 5★ and 3 more 5★ are complaints — 17 of 50 five-star reviews (34%) evidence no satisfaction; excluding low-info makes both the strongest positive and the strongest negative larger; (3) money complaints changed register, not volume — 7 at 1.57★ before v3.0, 7 at 3.86★ since, so 'the recent ratings no longer carry the monetization problem' (2026 Q3: 5 of 9 money-negative at 4.44★); (4) 18 of 28 storefronts contributed exactly one review, averaging 3.33★, and five of six 1★ come from them — where almost nobody writes, the one who does is the annoyed one; (5) 71 text reviews on 339 public ratings, 4.31★ vs 4.58★, the US public base has zero 1★/2★ across 37; (6) zero refund / cancellation / renewal mentions is 'a genuine blank, not a clean bill of health'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker, 172 reviews): 937 public ratings vs 172 text (18.4%), 4.781★ vs 4.599★; France 57 ratings / 2 text; the distribution is prompted (in-app review request) and the tail is inverted — 11 one-star, 6 at 2★+3★ — 'the signature of a transaction failing rather than a product gradually underperforming'; 10 edited reviews carry their last-edit date; 5 rating-vs-text contradictions (a 5★ 'given in advance', a 5★ whose body is only a complaint, a 1★ that calls it a 'Great app'); a 'six seven' meme review kept; the rating decline (4.89 → 4.02) cannot be separated from a composition shift as the YouTube/Reddit launch cohort aged out. Report 82 (Lasting Change, 175 reviews): corpus 1.880★ vs public 3.838★ — a 1.958★ gap, over two stars in every high-volume storefront ([[C300]]); 72.00% one-star; the Anglophone UK+AU+CA block is the most negative population (mean 1.20★, 94.0% 1★, praise 2%, trust_collapse 84%) with a plausible mechanism — they can read the English listing, T&Cs and warning reviews and have consumer-protection routes they use; 90.9% of the corpus comes from high-spend markets, consistent with a $50–$131 funnel targeting high-ARPU geographies; a rising era mean (1.69 → 2.41) is a measurement artefact — nine of fifteen late positives are under 60 characters while money harm hit its highest share; the developer's home market (Lithuania) is the only storefront perfect on both measures; no rating elasticity ('they are asking for their money back'), no rating recovery, no defence of the company by any user. Report 83 (Roubit, 500 reviews): the positively selected case — public 4.658★ vs corpus 4.156★ (+0.502), small in Korea and the US, +1.13★ in Japan where the text turned during bug waves while the cumulative rating still read 4.48★ — 'the text reviews are the more negative signal, and they lead it'; 31 of 33 rating/text contradictions are four- or five-star bug reports and 19 of 40 blank-screen reports are 4–5★ — 'star ratings understate dissatisfaction during bug waves'; reviews used as a support desk (SUPPORT_QUESTION 43); 145 reviews (29.00%) under 60 characters; 17 of 31 voted reviews are Japanese, 10 of them bug reports; seven solicited or invite-code reviews, all 5★. Report 84 (HabitGrid, 86 reviews): the zero-gap case — corpus 4.930★ vs public 4.939★ over 311 ratings (+0.009), every large storefront within 0.12★; 'the corpus is a complete census of text reviews and, on rating, is not distinguishable from the silent majority'; zero 1–2★ text reviews in 451 days (the only trace of a very dissatisfied user is one textless US 1★); 28 one-line 5★ (32.56%), all five-star; no churn statements; no storefront reaches 50. Report 85 (Habitica, 3,445 reviews over eleven years): the US listing shows 4.27★ from 3,324 ratings against a US corpus mean of 3.76★ and the public mean exceeds the corpus mean by 0.26–0.78★ in all eleven eligible storefronts — 'people write when something breaks'; the distribution is bimodal (5★ 44%, 1★ 14%); CONTRA_RATING 46 — 44 are 5★ reviews reporting a defect, 42 of them before 2022-12 and cn over-represented, 'consistent with reviewers treating the star field as a contact form'; single days hold 49 (crash), 22 (feature day) and 20 (outage) reviews and excluding them moves no headline more than 5.4 points; three authors on >1 storefront; 'great app!' recurs across three authors years apart. Report 86 (Today, 1,785 reviews over ten years): corpus 3.97★ vs every public storefront 4.5–4.8★ — 'do not present 3.97★ as the app's rating'; the corpus is front-loaded (45.32% in E1, 645 reviews from 2016) so 'any global percentage is mostly a statement about 2016–17'; volume decayed 45× (59.1 → 1.3 per month); CONTRA_RATING 46 — 40 are 5★ whose text is only a complaint ('Blank Screen after IOS update' — entire text) so the public average is inflated 'by a measurable population of users who write a complaint and tap five stars anyway'; Japan reports the most defects (42.11%) while rating above the mean — 'any market-health read that uses the rating alone will systematically under-weight Japanese defect signal'; RATING_LEVERAGE 16; 40 five-star reviews contain no praise at all; 152 reviews carry both praise and a bug code — 'people who like the app describing what is broken in it'.

merged_from.old_title: Audit the sales funnel per market — the same product can rate 4.3 in one storefront and 2.1 in another on billing alone
merged_from.note: reports 59, 60 and 62 attached three kinds of evidence beyond the original per-storefront rating split: removing one storefront (RU) removes billing complaints but not praise (59); a US-vs-rest split that is a funnel-stage split — bought-and-disappointed vs stopped-at-the-door (60); and written-vs-public gaps of up to −3.56 stars per storefront with a 5★ band that is 17.6% non-endorsements (62) — the point is now about what the review channel measures, not only about one billing-driven rating gap

title: Payment retries are bounded — daily dunning against a declined card reads as fraud to the customer and their bank
statement: Report 24: 584 duplicate/repeated-charge reports (1.34%, mean 1.134), 117 describing daily or near-daily retry attempts, and 123 whose bank flagged or blocked the merchant as fraud; a same-day retry loop is indistinguishable from theft from the customer's side. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'После отмены подписки приложение каждый раз пытается списать с карты средства' (after cancelling, the app keeps trying to charge the card) — off-store billing retries after cancellation and after deletion; the fix is to stop retries after deletion.

title: Content the user paid for is saveable and replayable — a library, not a stream
statement: Report 24: long-tenure paying users cannot save or re-listen to the morning coaching piece — 'the main reason, every year, I seriously consider whether or not I will even renew'; journal entries cannot be revisited; background music was removed. Missing this is a stated renewal factor for the app's best customers.

title: Statistics stay readable on the free tier — gating the progress view removes the motivation loop the category sells
statement: Report 25: statistics of any kind were paywalled in every era and the calendar view by 2026 ('Pay to even look at calendar'); the reviews that name it average 1.40 and one explains why — for someone at rock bottom, free statistics are the motivation; gating it removes the reason to upgrade rather than creating one. The report predicts, counter-intuitively, that free statistics increase conversion and proposes the A/B. Sits beside C011 (paid weekly/monthly/yearly reports): the basic progress view is free, the deep report is the paid layer. Report 31: statistics (145 mentions) and charts were a paid unlock and a purchase trigger in the one-time era. Report 46: statistics free; richer stats requested by 11. Report 60 (Mindway): the paid product has no progress view at all — 'thought this would give more feedback on completion percentage - tracking consistency. It's just a basic to do list'; 'very little flexibility or encouragement'; no reviewer in 216 describes a streak, chart, score or progress view; D3: build the tracking layer — 'the largest non-pricing gap in the report' and the capability that justifies a subscription because it cannot be replicated in Notes (E4: completion %, current streak, 30-day grid). Report 69 (TheFor): the one monetization backlash in 80 reviews is a long-tenured user who lost free stats and 'see which days were tracked' to a subscription; the listing still advertises 'Comprehensive Weekly Overview' — M3: audit what is actually gated and reconcile with the listing. Report 76 (Way of Life): charts, trends and overview are free for the 3-item tier and are the second-largest praise (PR_INSIGHTS 838); friction is about range and depth (REQ_STATS 72, REQ_DATE_RANGE 22, REQ_CALENDAR 29, NEG_CHART 38), not access. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): v2.4.0 (2026-04-27): 'Advanced analytics, which was previously part of paid Ripples+ plans, is now available to everyone' — corroborated by a free-tier user four months later ('súper útil con analíticas y todo', 5★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): week / month / year statistics are free and among the top three concrete strengths (PRAISE_STATS_VIEWS 9); a yearly percentage counted from the habit's start rather than the year is the one stats complaint (arguably a design choice; §8.2 an option rather than a fix). Report 86 (Today): PR_STATS 65 free; the statistics screen is undiscoverable ('I only stumbled on the charts in the profile section by accident!'); nobody reports buying for statistics.

title: A first-run failure escape hatch — skip setup / continue offline, with a visible error state
statement: Report 25: 51 reviews (3.90%, mean 1.63; 1.3% → 5.8% across eras) describe the app freezing on or just after onboarding with the main screen unresponsive to touch; four say reinstalling does not help and then delete the app; one names iCloud sync as the stuck state. A 'skip setup / continue offline' path and a visible error would turn some of those 1★ reviews into support tickets. Report 49: signup blocked — a name field that could not be scrolled past (Aug–Sep 2025 cluster, 23 at 1.13). Report 83 (Roubit): a white screen on launch with yesterday's routines visible and an ad required to complete them (jp 3★); §8.2 fail open — show routines when the room or store cannot load. Report 85 (Habitica): §8.2 an offline-first first run so a server error does not stop someone creating their first task — the sign-up failure waves (139 reviews, 1.55★) and NEG_OFFLINE 55 are the evidence.

title: A free-tier limit must announce itself before the user invests — at install, at setup and at the wall — never silently stop a visible progress signal
statement: Report 26: the free tier lets the garden grow to ~17% and then silently stops; 50 verified reviews (1.30%, mean 2.96) report the flower 'not growing', 17 of them naming the same 17% across April 2022 → December 2025, filed as 'Glitches 🙄', 'Bug', 'Fake Flowers' — several learned only from support that it was intentional. Users conclude the app is broken and say so publicly. A one-line in-app explanation at the moment the ceiling is hit converts a 1–3★ 'it's broken' review into a legible upgrade prompt — the cheapest high-value fix in the corpus. Report 33: the habit limit was announced only after users created habits. Report 46: the free tier cannot fill the product's own 4-row widget ('it leaves the 4th row blank… it bothers me so much'; 'makes many widgets appear broken as they tend to have a multiple of 4 rows'). Report 48: the cap 'announces itself' only after setup — 48 reviews at 1.65★ met the wall after investing effort. Report 50: own statistics locked after hitting the reduced cap (TR). Report 71 (MyStreaks): both 1★ reviewers met the cap after investing setup effort — 'i was going to make my 3rd streak and i was met with an unavoidable monthly subscription'; 'I was really excited about this app… But a paywall for more than 2 streaks?' — §8.1 #3: disclose the cap at onboarding, 'honesty about the limit before the third streak, not a change to the limit'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): §8.1 #2 show the trial state in-app from first launch — a persistent 'N days left in your free trial' — so day 8 is never a surprise; the lockout is a hard stop, not a degraded tier (one reviewer alone reports rows being cut back first). Report 75 (Habit Streak): the App Store description never states a habit-count limit, names only subscriptions, and omits the $79.99 lifetime — two reviewers say they were not warned ('il aurait pu prévenir que c'était payant'; 'man muss Geld ausgeben um die App zu benutzen, wenn nicht klärt mich bitte auf den die App wirkt perfekt' — a 2★ from a confused user calling the app perfect); §8.1 #1 'Track up to 5 habits free, forever' in the description and first onboarding screen — 'Zero engineering cost', addressing 8 of 11 low ratings; E3 disclose and measure the 1★ rate — 'the current listing makes the honest version of it impossible to test at all'. (Consolidation after report 75: title widened from 'A free-tier limit must announce itself — never silently stop a visible progress signal' to name when the announcement has to happen; the report 40-era evidence stays in the statement.) Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_DISCLOSURE 33 (0.43%, mean 2.06★) — 'not particularly clear in the iTunes store that the free app allows for only three categories' (2★); 7.73% of 1★ and 6.73% of 2★ carry it. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the free tier is one habit and the App Store description states no habit-count limit anywhere ('helps you build your new habit' — singular); three reviewers on three storefronts across ten months independently state the number (mean 2.33★), two say in as many words the boundary surprised them (MON_UNEXPECTED 2, mean 1.50★: 'What's the point of making a free app if it's unfunctional unless you buy a premium plan'; 'Ich hatte erwartet, dass mehrere Gewohnheiten frei sind'); 'A one-habit free tier is a defensible business decision. Not disclosing it is a separate, cheaper-to-fix problem, and it is the one the corpus actually punishes'; §8.1.1 one sentence in the description is 'the highest ratio of impact to effort available here' — it removes the surprise, which is what the 1★ and 2★ text objects to. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the 3-board cap and the paid widget are undisclosed in a description with no money text; §8.6 E2 disclosure A/B measuring the 1★ rate, not installs. Report 82 (Lasting Change): BILL_UNDISCLOSED 26 (14.86%) — disclosed only in the T&Cs: 'Why can't you write it loud and clear in the sales order and not hide it in the T&C fine print if you are transparent'; 'hidden in the small print rather than being clearly and prominently disclosed'; BILL_FREE_CLAIMED 7 — presented as free or a trial ('Said the app came free… I am getting charged 30.99 a month'; '$30.99 / month after the trial period, which i didnt see mentioned anywhere'); REQ_DISCLOSURE 4, all from people harmed. Report 83 (Roubit): the letter allowance is undisclosed and moves — 'you have to pay for the AI letter, but the app didn't warn you and it just stops' (2★); 'I'm not sure though' about the rule; §8.6 state the allowance before the user writes.

merged_from.old_title: A free-tier limit must announce itself — never silently stop a visible progress signal
merged_from.note: reports 71, 74 and 75 attached the disclosure-timing shape: cap complaints from reviewers who met the wall after setting up (report 71 'both object to discovering the wall after investing in setup'), an in-app trial clock proposed so 'day 8 is never a surprise' (report 74), and a cap stated on neither the listing nor onboarding (report 75); the original point was about a progress signal stopping silently

title: The reward loop needs a content runway — finite gardens, themes or levels exhaust long-term users
statement: Report 26: garden-motivation praise declined monotonically 7.93% → 8.41% → 5.65% → 5.03% → 3.76% across five years while aesthetic praise strengthened, and reviewers report running out of gardens ('when I grew all the gardens, there is nothing to do'; 'YOU NEED MORE GARDEN DESIGNS!!'; 'I'll get bored if more aren't added'). For a product whose entire retention mechanism is the garden this is the most strategically important soft signal; per-habit gardens would also soften the all-or-nothing rule. Report 28: users complete all rooms and the motivation engine stops — 16 (1.95%), including a paying customer leaving ('this one doesn't motivate me anymore'), 'after level 200 you get items less frequently, and the hype is gone', 'incentives stop after level three hundred'; one specifies the remedy — reset the house and make it dirty again, counting resets like a prestige. Report 36: a 60-day monument that is the same journey for every habit — curiosity brings people back on day 3 ('I can't stop because I'm curious about what the next reward is'; GAME+ 74, mean 4.69) and the identical journey and hard stop drive them away around day 60–120 (17 distinct, mean 2.76: 'the story is repeated for all habits … pretty boring', 8 votes; 'it's a shame that it lasts only 60 days … I could have built something infinitely'). Report 49: 'what happens after day 66' and further programmes requested (5); several describe second, third and fourth 66-day cycles. Report 50: long-tenure reviewers (9) all rate 5★; requests deepen rather than stop. Report 54: more plants / a garden or shelf (9) and richer plant behaviour (9); growth stopping at 67 days — see [[C273]]. Report 65 (Rabit): the garden is the retention mechanic (GAM_PLANT 21, mean 4.62; MOT_GOOD 21, 4.86 — 'ver minhas plantinhas crescendo me incentiva a continuar') and under-built — more plant varieties (3), a placeable garden 'more like FarmTown' with tap-a-plant-for-detail, a widget that shows the garden and warns when a plant is near death; 'the cheapest available investment in the thing people already love'. Report 83 (Roubit): carrots → coins → fragments → gems spent on furniture, themes and outfits partly through a gacha; REWARD_ECONOMY_SLOW 7 ('It is so hard to get the coins'); PAYWALL_COSMETICS 4 ('A bit greedy' — fragments cannot buy Ultimate items); BUG_REWARDS 15 (2.80★); requests for more outfits, poses, rooms and seasonal themes (14, 5.00★) — the content runway is the ask. Report 85 (Habitica): the collection loop (eggs, pets, mounts: PR_COLLECT 88) retains after novelty fades, but REQ_CONTENT 79 (2.29%) — more content, actual battles, an endgame — and 'they are all essentially the same' show the runway ends; REQ_TRADE 12.

title: A rewarded-ad unlock path for users who cannot pay (teens, students)
statement: Report 26: teens and students (25, mean 4.16; ages 10–21) cannot pay and say so, and three independently ask to watch ads instead ('I will watch ads all day long if I have to'); report 25: six reviewers volunteer 'show me ads instead' of a paywall. Demand exists in a segment converting at zero — but it conflicts with the reviews that praise having no ads (report 26: 7 at mean 5.00), so it is research, not a decision. Report 31: teens blocked by the cap and price in the 2022–23 TikTok cohort — a student / low-income price is the report's answer. Report 47: rewarded video for cosmetics was accepted ('動画を見れば使える色が増えます', 14-vote 5★, 2022) where rewarded video for logging yesterday produced 1★ — a rewarded unlock is safe on decoration, never on the record. Report 64 (Critique AI): 12 reviewers (2.86%) volunteer ads as the price of access on a teen-heavy app with no free tier; one paying adult objects ('I'd rather pay than see ads'); a free teen tier is the most-upvoted ask. Report 65 (Rabit): a coin economy earned by watching rewarded videos, with purchasable fertiliser — the videos fail and an unclosable ad blocks earning (GAM_COIN 2). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): MON_WANT_ADS 1 — a 5★ user who cannot afford the wall proposes ads instead; MONP_AFFORD_BARRIER 1 ('the moment I can afford it'). Report 83 (Roubit): a student segment (SEG_STUDENT_MINOR 13; a high-schooler 'it has helped me cope'; an elementary-schooler asking whether it keeps charging) and, from 2026-04-29, 'a new option to watch ads and earn additional rewards'; §8.5 test a student price.

title: A personal origin story in the listing builds trust — and turns any later gate into a betrayal
statement: Report 27: a solo developer's story in the listing produced 10 reviews (7.25%, every one 5★) thanking her by name — 'Thanks Emily'; 'It's clear that someone made this with joy, not for money'; 'built/maintained by an individual female developer — THANK YOU'; 'you are a hero'. The origin story does measurable acquisition work, and it is a constraint: a trust-based relationship is what makes a paywall feel like a betrayal rather than a transaction. Report 25: 'I can't believe one developer made this' and 'after interacting with the developer I decided to pay without any hesitation'. Report 59 (Tappsk): the developer's own vc.ru article brought the first users (MKT_PRESS 13) and a Russian creator is itself praised ('это еще и русский создатель а не зарубежный'). Report 71 (MyStreaks): 'Thank you to Jeff & Jami and their team for the great book & app!' — founder presence is praised in 4 reviews, all 5★. Report 76 (Way of Life): a named solo developer is part of the product — PR_DEV 268 (3.45%, mean 4.96★) rising from 2.1% of E1 to 6.7% of E6, thanked for 'steady updates' over a decade; ru 1.99×, kz 4.06×, ua 2.68×; §8.8 keep 'one-person, responsive development'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): U:developer_equity 36 (20.93%, 4.94★) — a solo, named, Reddit/YouTube-facing developer with a public roadmap was a purchase motive (MON_SUPPORT_DEV 3: 'because I like your approach'; 'to support the developer'); the equity eroded 26.4% → 12.2% as the audience changed, and the one paying customer who reports being ignored writes 'Developer doesn't respond. Waste of time' in a 1★. Report 84 (HabitGrid): U:dev_relationship 25 (29.07%), every one 5★ — 'we need more developers like this'; 'the poor guy works on it alone ❤️'; the gratitude is for keeping the app free and localising it (17 of 37 Russian reviews thank the developer, none of them report a reply). Report 85 (Habitica): 'an open-source app run by a small team that's made better by the work of volunteers' — the listing's framing is why purchasers pay (support, 23.6%) and why the 2023 dispute with volunteer moderators cut so deep (STAFF_CONTROVERSY 19 at 1.74★). Report 86 (Today): the sister app (Pillow) being 'updated, working well' while Today sat unreleased for 1,030 days is what reviewers cite when concluding the developer moved on — a studio's other products are read as evidence of intent.

title: Never interrupt the completion moment — no ad, upsell or rating prompt on the check-off tap
statement: Report 28: a forced full-screen interstitial fired on every habit check-off is the single largest fact in an 821-review corpus — 164 complaints (19.98%, mean 2.73 vs 4.35 for every other review; 52.4% of all 1★), 33 naming the per-tap mechanic as a punishment ('it feels like a punishment for doing what you were meant to do'; 'replacing the feel-good with this uncanny worry'), 30 calling the app unusable, 19 five-star reviewers still complaining, and the users most helped by the reward loop (ADHD) the most damaged by breaking it. Users are not asking for zero ads; they propose batching ('let me tick them all off and then show me an ad') or a cap per session. Report 24: checking off one habit takes 3–5 screens of celebration; report 25: upsell sheets on every action; a 2026 rating prompt fired on check-off produced a 1★ purely about the prompt. Report 29: the rating prompt fires on the first habit check-off. Report 42: a mandatory 'congratulations' trophy modal on every check-off blocks the Continue button and freezes the app for heavy users ('It takes me at least 5 minutes to mark two tasks as done'; 'pops up far too often'; messages 'not coherent') — 4 reviews; a settings toggle is the cheapest fix in the report. Report 43: the Oct 2025 redesign put a journal prompt on every skip — 'Bad design to have to do skip every time' (long-time payer, 1★). Report 46: a rating prompt 'every other time I marked a habit as complete'; a Dec 2022 completion animation on every log ('so annoying'). Report 47: the clearest evidence in the ledger — a video ad on each check-in (May–Dec 2024) produced 24 reviews at mean 1.46 and 20 exits in eight months, banners before and after were tolerated, and the 2025 upsell page after each completed task (4, mean 1.25) and the rating prompt shown to payers repeat the same mistake; the report's rule: nothing between 'tap' and 'done' — monetise elsewhere. Report 48: a post-log upgrade prompt (Jul 2024) is 'the only monetization mechanic in the corpus that users say actively reduced their intent to pay' (6 in three months); the 2021 logging redesign added taps to the same moment and was rolled back. Report 52: an ad after every check-in (2025) and a status sheet added to the check-in tap (2021) are both named as the moment the app broke. Report 60 (Mindway): the upsell interrupts the planning task itself — three reviewers (1.39%, mean 1.33) describe pop-ups 'every 5 seconds' while building a routine ([[C093]]). Report 65 (Rabit): an interstitial on habit completion from 23 Dec 2022 — 'Cada que completo un hábito me aparece un anuncio!!!'; 'vengo a desinstalarla después de ver unos 40 anuncios'; 'They don't even let you finish what you were doing' — ADS_BAD 15 (3.01%, mean 2.33), 12 of 46 reviews in the launch window (26.1%); 'An app whose entire behavioural model is complete the habit → see your plant grow → feel rewarded inserted an interstitial exactly at the reward moment'; the close button rendered under the iPhone 13 status bar and forced a restart; F5. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'app solicited a review 3 days in, after I paid for the premium version' (4★); §8.7 never prompt right after a purchase. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the review prompt fired 'after every check in' — the completion moment — and a previously-5★ paying user dropped to 1★ until it stops.

title: Sell entitlements as non-consumables — a consumable currency cannot be restored and has no 'paid member' state to honour
statement: Report 28: one consumable currency ('carrots') sells cosmetics, functional caps, ad removal and cloud sync; 10 of 24 identifiable payers (41.7%) report a purchase that did not deliver or could not be restored — 'I paid 10$ to remove ads but I still get ads'; 'cannot restore purchase on a new device'; 'I paid the 14.99… it's still saying I need to purchase'; and a $10 buyer is charged again when a new paid feature ships ('i'm already a paid member; why do i have to make another purchase?'). Reviewers cannot tell what they are buying ('I now realize just buying anything gives u cloud access') and ask for it unbundled ('just pay like two dollars to just get unlimited tasks'). An architecture problem presenting as a trust problem. Report 49: an under-18 / student free programme granted case by case is invisible to almost everyone.

title: Never monetise by routing the user's device or bandwidth for third parties — and never gate first launch behind any such opt-in
statement: Report 29: a free tracker whose whole reputation was 'actually free' (46.99% of reviews) added a launch-screen prompt in May 2026 asking users to enable 'web indexing' — letting third parties use the phone's IP to download web data — in exchange for an ad-free experience. Every reviewer who described it gave 1★ ('This app now interrupts use unless you agree to run a malware proxy downloader'; 'Didn't get past the opening screen… No thanks'; 'You PAID for this free app'); two of three quit before using the product; a reviewer had already asked 'Am I trading off data privacy for this?'; the listing's privacy label ('analytics and diagnostics') does not obviously cover it. It turned the 1★ band from bugs into privacy in one half-year. If any consent-based monetisation is used, ask after first value, in plain language, reversible, never as a gate.

title: Date arithmetic must survive month boundaries and week-start conventions
statement: Report 29: a month-rollover / weekday-offset bug was the dominant defect — 37 reviews (10.11%, mean 2.95 vs 4.73), 78.4% of them filed on days 28–3 against a 27.6% baseline ('On the last day of every month, the app has no idea what day it is… April 30 defaulted to Feb 28'; 'the 31st listed twice'; 'went backwards into April instead of forwards into July'; 'Monday thru Sunday… but the dates go Sunday thru Saturday'); it was 62.5% of all 3★ and 66.7% of 2★, peaked at 20.2% of 2025H1 and fell ~8× by 2026H1 with a residual weekday-offset tail; users taught each other to reinstall, which destroyed their local-only data. Test every date surface at month end, leap day and both week starts.

title: Never seed the launch rating with templated or bought reviews — the rating decays and the markets they cover become unmeasurable
statement: Report 30: 83 of 166 reviews (50%) matched a five-phrase list across languages ('I highly recommend it' / 'so simple, perfect' / 'the best one'…), all 5★, in two dated campaigns (EN Jul–Sep 2025, ES/NL Nov–Dec 2025), including a Dutch sentence concatenating all five phrases posted on the Russian storefront. When the campaigns stopped, the half-year mean fell 4.65 → 3.17 → 3.00 and the organic 1★ rate rose 12.5% → 44.4%; the US storefront (31 reviews, all 5★, 22 templated) and GB (nothing after the campaign) became commercially blind — the highest-spend markets yielded 8 substantive reviews averaging 3.50 against a 4.79 headline. The public rating is a decaying artefact, not an asset.
